kdl-o-001.q: Erythropoiesis (normoblastic, megaloblastic). Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the erythroid lineage?
plan: Erythropoiesis in the bone marrow: hematopoietic stem cell → common myeloid progenitor → erythroid progenitors; the main humoral regulator is erythropoietin, produced in the kidney in response to hypoxia (enhances survival and division of progenitors).

Normoblastic (normal) lineage: proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatophilic → orthochromic (oxyphilic) erythroblast → nucleus extruded → reticulocyte → erythrocyte. During maturation the cell becomes smaller, the nucleus condenses, hemoglobin accumulates in the cytoplasm, and basophilia is replaced by oxyphilia.

The reticulocyte matures in the bone marrow for ~1–3 days and in the blood for ~1–2 days; the mature erythrocyte is an anucleate biconcave disc, circulates for ~120 days and is destroyed by splenic macrophages.
Erythrocyte function: transport of O2 and CO2 via hemoglobin; its shape and membrane provide deformability.

Megaloblastic erythropoiesis – in B12 or folate deficiency DNA synthesis is impaired: nuclear maturation lags behind the cytoplasm (nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony), the cells are large (megaloblasts), erythropoiesis is ineffective – many cells die in the bone marrow itself.
In the megaloblastic state, the peripheral blood shows macrocytosis (MCV >100 fL) and hypersegmented neutrophils; in the postnatal period this is always a sign of pathology.

kdl-o-002.q: Methods of counting erythrocytes. Erythrocyte indices?
plan: Methods of counting erythrocytes: manual – counting cells in a defined volume of diluted blood in a counting chamber (Goryaev/Neubauer); automated – on a hematology analyzer by impedance (Coulter) or optical method. Today's standard is the analyzer; the chamber is only a backup/training method.

Sources of error of the chamber method: incorrect dilution, pipette error, incorrect filling of the chamber, double counting of cells on the border (only cells on the upper and left lines are counted), statistical uncertainty due to the small number of cells counted.
Hemoglobin – the reference method is hemiglobincyanide (ICSH); analyzers use cyanide-free photometric variants; hematocrit and indices are derived from values measured/calculated by the analyzer.
Erythrocyte indices: MCV = Ht/RBC (80–100 fL), MCH = Hb/RBC (27–32 pg), MCHC = Hb/Ht (hemoglobin concentration), RDW – distribution width by volume (anisocytosis; ~11.5–15%).

Classification of anemias by indices: MCV <80 – microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic, chronic disease), 80–100 – normocytic, >100 – macrocytic (megaloblastic: B12/folate; non-megaloblastic: liver, alcohol). MCV + RDW together narrow the differential diagnosis.
False results: agglutination of erythrocytes lowers RBC and raises MCV; lipemia falsely raises Hb and MCHC – in such cases examining the smear is mandatory.

pitfalls.right: the main indices are MCV, MCH (27–32 pg), MCHC and RDW; hypo-/normochromia is determined by MCHC

plan: Erythrocyte indices are values derived from RBC, Hb and Ht that show erythrocyte volume and hemoglobin content; they are used in determining the cause of anemia and in internal laboratory quality control.
MCV (mean volume) = Ht/RBC; normal 80–100 fL: microcytosis (<80), normocytosis, macrocytosis (>100).

MCH (mean amount of Hb in one erythrocyte) = Hb/RBC, ~27–32 pg; MCHC (Hb concentration in the erythrocyte) = Hb/Ht: decrease – hypochromia; increase – spherocytosis, xerocytosis or artifact (lipemia, agglutination).
RDW – SD or CV (%) of the MCV distribution curve, a measure of anisocytosis; ~11.5–15%. For example, in iron deficiency RDW is usually increased, which helps to distinguish it from thalassemia trait.
Clinical use: separate the type of anemia by MCV, then choose tests such as iron parameters, reticulocytes, B12/folate.
Each laboratory uses its own reference intervals; abnormal indices are confirmed with a peripheral blood smear.

kdl-o-004.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of reticulocytes. The IRF (immature reticulocyte fraction) parameter?
plan: Reticulocytes are young erythrocytes that retain RNA remnants; they mature for 1–3 days in the bone marrow and 1–2 days in the blood; their number reflects the activity of erythropoiesis in the bone marrow.

Normal in adults ~0.5–2.5%; because the percentage depends on the erythrocyte count, it is corrected in anemia: RPI (reticulocyte production index) = reticulocyte % × patient Ht / 45; the absolute count is also calculated.
Increase: hemolytic anemias, acute/chronic blood loss, treatment effect ("reticulocyte crisis" after giving iron, B12).

Decrease: iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anemia, aplastic anemia, MDS, B12/folate deficiency (before treatment), aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemia (parvovirus B19), hydroxyurea.

IRF is the ratio of immature (high-RNA) reticulocytes to total reticulocytes; measured on the analyzer by fluorescence intensity. The earliest sign of bone marrow regeneration: used to monitor recovery after chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation.
Reticulocyte hemoglobin (CHr/Ret-He) reflects iron available for erythropoiesis; <28 pg is a good predictor of iron deficiency.

kdl-o-005.q: Factors affecting the erythrocyte sedimentation rate?
plan: ESR is the sedimentation of erythrocytes in citrated blood over 1 hour (mm/h); a nonspecific marker of inflammation, depending mainly on the formation of "rouleaux" (stacks of coins) by erythrocytes under the influence of fibrinogen and immunoglobulins.

Reference method – Westergren (ICSH gold standard since 1973): a tube with an internal diameter of 2.5 mm and length of 190–300 mm, 3.2% sodium citrate, and the height of the plasma column is measured after 1 hour in a vertical position. ICSH 2017 gives validation requirements for alternative automated methods.

Factors increasing ESR: fibrinogen and immunoglobulins (acute phase, myeloma), anemia, female sex, pregnancy, old age; technical: high room temperature, tube tilted by 3° (ESR rises by up to ~30%), air bubbles, sunlight, vibration.
Decreasing factors: polycythemia (viscosity), sickle cells, spherocytosis (no rouleaux formation), delaying the sample for more than 2 hours, clotted blood; some drugs (statins, NSAIDs).
Reference values depend on age and sex (for example, under 50 years men ≤15, women ≤20 mm/h; after 50, ≤20 and ≤30 respectively) – the laboratory establishes its own interval.
Clinical significance: nonspecific; important in giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myeloma; in acute inflammation CRP changes faster.

pitfalls.right: the reference method approved by ICSH is based on Westergren (tube with 2.5 mm internal diameter, 3.2% citrate, vertical, 1 hour); Panchenkov is a regional historical method

kdl-o-006.q: Safety rules in laboratories (occupational safety and fire safety)?
plan: Laboratory safety system: a written safety plan and SOPs, a responsible person, regular staff training (at hiring and periodically), an emergency plan and drills.

Electrical safety: mark, take out of service and repair a damaged socket/equipment; connecting/disconnecting equipment to the mains with wet hands is prohibited; mains near water must be grounded; during repair, disconnect from power and use "lockout/tagout".

Sources of fire hazard: flammable solvents, open flame, gas cylinders. Prevention: only the minimum amount at the workplace, store solvents in a special fire-resistant cabinet, do not leave open flame unattended, keep flammables away from fire, keep aisles and emergency equipment accessible.

Action in case of fire (RACE): rescue people, raise the alarm, close doors to confine the fire, evacuate/extinguish. Using a fire extinguisher (PASS): pull the pin, aim at the base of the fire, squeeze the lever, sweep side to side.

Choose the extinguisher type to match the fire class (A – solid combustibles, B – flammable liquids/gases, C – energized equipment – with a non-conductive agent); if clothing catches fire – "stop, drop and roll", a fire blanket or emergency shower (if there is no chemical/current).

Every employee must know the location of emergency equipment: fire extinguisher, alarm, exit routes, emergency shower/eyewash, first aid kit; do not work alone, wear suitable PPE (lab coat, goggles, gloves).

kdl-o-007.q: Safety rules when working with biological material (biosafety)?
plan: Biological safety consists of measures to protect the worker, the community and the environment from infectious agents and patient specimens; the basis is a risk assessment for each task (collect information → assess risk → control strategy → implement measures → review).

Biosafety levels (BSL-1…4): BSL-1 – agents not known to cause disease in healthy adults; BSL-2 – agents causing disease of varying severity (HBV, HIV, Salmonella, etc.); work with blood, body fluids and tissues is usually carried out under BSL-2 conditions; BSL-3/4 – severe/dangerous airborne agents.

Standard microbiological practice: eating, drinking, smoking, cosmetics and food storage are prohibited in the laboratory; mouth pipetting is prohibited – use mechanical pipetting devices; wash hands after work and when leaving; long hair must be tied back.

Personal protective equipment: lab coat, gloves (not worn outside the laboratory, changed when contaminated, disposable gloves are not washed or reused), eye/face protection when there is a splash risk; remove PPE without self-contamination.

Sharps: do not recap needles by hand, do not bend/break them; place used needles and syringes immediately into a puncture-proof container; pick up broken glass not with hands but with a brush/forceps.

Reducing aerosols and splashes: aerosol-generating work (centrifuging, mixing, opening) in a biological safety cabinet or in sealed centrifuge cups; for spills, decontaminate according to an established procedure.

Decontamination and waste: disinfect work surfaces at the end of work and after every spill; decontaminate cultures and infectious material before disposal (preferably by autoclave), transport in a sealed container with a biohazard sign.

Staff health: occupational health requirements (including vaccination); after a needlestick or mucosal contamination – wash immediately, inform the supervisor and follow the post-exposure prophylaxis procedure; those working with blood follow the "bloodborne pathogens" rules.

pitfalls.wrong: Bacillus subtilis is an example of a BSL-2 agent
pitfalls.right: In BMBL 6, B. subtilis is precisely an example of BSL-1 agents (well-characterized agents not known to cause disease in healthy adults)

kdl-o-008.q: Preanalytical stage of hematological tests. Preparation of blood and bone marrow preparations for hematological examination?
plan: The preanalytical stage – more than half of laboratory errors occur at this stage: correct test ordering, patient preparation and identification, specimen collection, labeling, transport, receipt.

For CBC, venous blood in an EDTA tube (purple cap); follow the WHO-recommended order of draw (after citrate, before fluoride), fill the tube completely for the blood:anticoagulant ratio and immediately invert gently the number of times indicated by the tube manufacturer (to avoid clots and microclots).
Capillary blood: the finger is well warmed, the first drop is removed, no squeezing (admixture of tissue fluid distorts the result).

Storage and transport: the specimen at room temperature, analyze as soon as possible; with prolonged storage MCV, platelets and the differential change; clotted, hemolyzed or incorrectly labeled specimens are rejected.

Smear preparation: a thin smear with a "tail" on a clean degreased slide; rapid drying, fixation (methanol) and staining by Romanowsky; prepare the smear from EDTA blood without delay (morphological artifacts).
Bone marrow aspirate: several smears immediately from the aspirate (with particles), the rest in EDTA for flow cytometry/cytogenetics; a separate smear for Perls staining.

kdl-o-009.q: Preanalytical stage of clinical biochemical tests. Collection, storage and preparation of biomaterial for testing in clinical biochemistry?
plan: Patient preparation: for many tests – in the morning, after 8–12 hours of fasting (glucose, TG, iron); avoid physical exertion, alcohol, smoking, stress; information about medications; diurnal variation (cortisol, iron).

Specimen collection: correct identification, short tourniquet time (a prolonged tourniquet raises protein, Ca, K), avoid fist clenching (K rises), WHO order of draw (EDTA contamination raises K and lowers Ca).
Tubes: serum (with gel separator), heparinized plasma (fast result), fluoride/oxalate (glucose), EDTA (HbA1c), citrate (coagulation) – depending on the test.
Handling: centrifuge after clotting, separate serum from cells as soon as possible – glycolysis (glucose falls by ~5–7% per hour), release of K and phosphate; protect bilirubin from light.
Storage: if analysis is delayed, serum at 2–8 °C or frozen (stability is test-specific); assess hemolysis, lipemia and icterus indices and account for interference.
Criteria for specimen acceptance and rejection: wrong tube, insufficient volume, hemolysis, unlabeled specimen – recorded (quality indicators).

kdl-o-010.q: Preanalytical stage of hemostasis tests. Collection, storage and preparation of biomaterial for hemostasis testing?
plan: Anticoagulant: 3.2% (105–109 mmol/L) sodium citrate, blood:citrate ratio 9:1; the tube must be filled to at least ~90% of nominal volume – underfilling alters PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (aPTT is especially sensitive).
If hematocrit is >55%, correct the citrate volume (the plasma fraction is small – relatively too much citrate).

Collection technique: atraumatic venipuncture, short tourniquet time; with a butterfly set, because of the air space, a "discard" tube first; avoid heparin/EDTA contamination (order of draw – citrate tube before EDTA and heparin).
Mixing: gently, according to the manufacturer's instructions (without shaking); clot, hemolysis, foam – reason for rejection.

Processing: centrifuge to obtain platelet-poor plasma; store and transport the specimen at room temperature (in the cold, factor VII may be activated and VIII/vWF lost), perform the test within the specified time; freeze for special tests.
Patient information: anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs), antiplatelet agents – stated on the requisition for interpreting the result.

kdl-o-011.q: Preanalytical stage of general clinical tests?
plan: Preanalytics of general clinical tests (urine, stool, sputum, CSF, body cavity fluids) largely determines the quality of the result.

Urine: written instructions to the patient – cleansing of the external genitalia, midstream portion, sterile/clean container; for the sediment the second morning urine is preferred (in the first morning urine cells and casts undergo lysis); analysis within 1 hour at room temperature (4 hours in a refrigerator).

Stool: clean dry container, no admixture of urine or water; for coprology, diet and medications (iron, bismuth, laxatives) are taken into account; for parasitological examination – a fresh specimen (vegetative forms die quickly) or a preservative.
Sputum: in the morning, after rinsing the mouth, by deep cough (not saliva); for tuberculosis, several specimens.
CSF and punctates: sterile containers, immediately to the laboratory (cells disintegrate quickly); for cell counting – a tube with anticoagulant (for punctates).
Labeling, requisition (time, clinical information) and criteria for specimen acceptance/rejection.

kdl-o-012.q: Obtaining biomaterial for general clinical examination and preparing slides?
plan: Types of urine collection: morning (first or second), random, midstream (after hygiene), 24-hour (preservative, volume measurement), catheter/suprapubic puncture (for culture).

Urine sediment preparation: 5–12 mL of well-mixed urine is centrifuged in a conical tube at ~400×g for 5 minutes, the supernatant is removed, the sediment is gently mixed and examined under a coverslip (×100 and ×400; phase-contrast or staining if needed).

Stool preparations: native (in physiological saline), with Lugol's solution (starch, protozoan cysts), Sudan III (fats), and if needed enrichment methods (formalin-ether/ethyl acetate sedimentation) for helminth eggs.
Sputum: smear from purulent flecks – native, for Gram and Ziehl-Neelsen staining.
CSF: counting cells in a chamber, cytocentrifuge preparation and Romanowsky staining; a separate sterile specimen for microbiology.
General requirement: rapid analysis, standardized volume and centrifugation, biosafety.

kdl-o-013.q: Preanalytical stage of cytological tests. Obtaining biomaterial and preparing slides for cytological examination?
plan: Gynecological material: from the cervical transformation zone and the endocervical canal with a special brush/spatula; avoid intercourse, douching, vaginal medications and spermicides for 48 hours beforehand; water-based lubricant and menstrual fluid interfere little with interpretation in liquid-based cytology.

Slide: conventional smear – an even thin layer, immediate wet fixation (95% alcohol or spray fixative; drying artifacts); liquid-based cytology – the material is rinsed into a preservative solution (monolayer preparation, possibility of additional HPV testing).

Non-gynecological material: sputum, bronchial wash/brushing, body cavity fluids (with anticoagulant, rapid delivery or cooling), urine, fine needle aspirate (smears – air-dried and wet-fixed; the remainder for a cell block/molecular tests).
Staining: Papanicolaou (wet-fixed), Romanowsky-type stains (air-dried), and if needed immunocytochemistry on cell blocks.
On the requisition: date of last menstrual period, hormones/contraceptives, pregnancy, previous results and treatment, clinical diagnosis – needed for interpretation.
Labeling, adequacy (cellularity, transformation zone component) and recording of "unsatisfactory" specimens.

kdl-o-014.q: Modern theory of blood formation. Regulation of hematopoiesis?
plan: Modern hierarchical model: self-renewing hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) → multipotent progenitors → common myeloid (erythrocyte, megakaryocyte, granulocyte, monocyte) and common lymphoid (B, T, NK) progenitors → mature cells; newer research shows differentiation as a continuous process.
Ontogeny: yolk sac and AGM region → fetal liver and spleen → after birth, bone marrow (and lymph nodes) is the main site of hematopoiesis.
Regulation: growth factors and cytokines – erythropoietin (erythropoiesis), interleukins (IL-3, IL-6, IL-7, etc.), colony-stimulating factors (G-CSF, GM-CSF), thrombopoietin (megakaryocytopoiesis).
Local regulation – the "niche": bone marrow stroma, endothelium and intercellular signals determine HSC quiescence, self-renewal and differentiation.
Clinical and laboratory significance: impaired hematopoiesis presents as cytopenias, MDS, leukemias; bone marrow activity is assessed by reticulocytes and bone marrow aspirate.

Reticulocyte RNA is stained with supravital dyes (new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue) as a network/granules: blood is mixed with the dye and incubated, a smear is made, and under oil immersion the proportion of reticulocytes among erythrocytes is counted.
The drawback of the manual method is low reproducibility (few cells are counted, observer-dependent); therefore it is rarely used now.

Automated method – flow cytometry: staining with a fluorescent dye that binds RNA (for example thiazole orange), measurement on a laser analyzer; percentage, absolute count, IRF and CHr/Ret-He are reported.
Interpreting the result: normal ~0.5–2.5%; in anemia, correction by RPI = reticulocyte % × Ht/45; the absolute count is also taken into account.
Significance: increased in hemolysis and blood loss (bone marrow response), decreased in hypoproliferative anemias (iron, B12/folate deficiency, aplasia); assessing treatment effect.

kdl-o-016.q: Leukopoiesis. Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the leukocyte lineage?
plan: Leukopoiesis begins from common myeloid (granulocytes, monocytes) and common lymphoid (B, T, NK) progenitors; regulated by G-CSF, GM-CSF and interleukins.

Granulocytic lineage: myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte (neutrophil/eosinophil/basophil direction) → metamyelocyte → band → segmented. During maturation the nucleus condenses and segments; after the primary (azurophilic) granules, specific granules appear.

Neutrophils – phagocytosis and first defense against bacteria; eosinophils – parasites and allergic reactions; basophils – histamine, allergy; monocytes become macrophages and dendritic cells in tissues.
Lymphocytes: B lymphocytes – antibodies (becoming plasma cells), T lymphocytes – cellular immunity and regulation, NK cells – cytotoxicity against virus-infected and tumor cells.
Normal values in adults: leukocytes 4.5–11×10⁹/L; neutrophils 40–60%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 2–8%, eosinophils 0–4%, basophils 0.5–1% (varies by laboratory).

kdl-o-017.q: Methods of counting leukocytes. Counting leukocytes in the Goryaev chamber?
plan: Methods: automated (hematology analyzer – impedance and/or flow cytometry, the main practical method) and manual – in a counting chamber (Goryaev/Neubauer).

Principle of the chamber method: blood is diluted with an acetic acid solution (erythrocytes are lysed, the dye stains the nuclei), the chamber is filled, and after the cells settle they are counted in the designated large squares; result = cells counted / volume counted × dilution factor, expressed in ×10⁹/L.
Technical rules: chamber and coverslip clean, blood well mixed, cells on the border are counted by the "upper and left" rule; with very few or many cells the dilution is changed.
Errors: pipetting and dilution errors, clots, incomplete lysis of erythrocytes, nucleated erythrocytes counted as leukocytes (correction needed), statistical uncertainty when few cells are counted.
Normal in adults 4.5–11×10⁹/L; >11 – leukocytosis, decrease – leukopenia; on an analyzer, platelet clumps can give false leukocytosis – checked with a smear.

plan: The differential is the percentage ratio of leukocyte types; manually, 100 (preferably 200) cells are counted under oil immersion in a smear stained by Romanowsky, then absolute counts are calculated (percentage × WBC).

Smear quality: thin, with a "tail", evenly distributed; counting along a path covering the edge and middle parts of the smear (cells are distributed unevenly – large cells are more numerous at the edges).
Normal (adults): neutrophils 40–60%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 2–8%, eosinophils 0–4%, basophils 0.5–1%; interpretation is based on absolute counts.

Automated differential (5 populations) on the analyzer; with an abnormal result, a "flag" or suspected blasts, a smear is examined manually. The uncertainty of manual counting is especially large for rare cells (blasts, immature granulocytes).

Interpretation: neutrophilia and a "left shift" (increase in bands) – bacterial infection/stress; lymphocytosis – viral infections, CLL; eosinophilia – allergy, parasites; monocytosis – chronic infections; basophilia – myeloproliferative diseases.

kdl-o-019.q: Calculating leukocyte indices and their clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Leukocyte indices are ratios of differential parameters; the most studied is the neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio (NLR) = absolute neutrophils / absolute lymphocytes.
In healthy adults NLR is approximately in the range 0.78–3.53 (population data); there is no single strict cutoff – disease-specific cutoffs are used.

NLR rises in physiological stress (cortisol, catecholamines: neutrophilia + lymphopenia), sepsis, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, tumors and other inflammation; it has been studied as a prognostic marker.
Factors affecting NLR: age, sex hormones, steroid use, G-CSF or chemotherapy, hematological diseases, HIV, obesity – taken into account in interpretation.
Other ratios (platelet/lymphocyte, lymphocyte/monocyte) are also used; traditional "intoxication indices" are not clearly standardized – interpreted only together with clinical data.

kdl-o-020.q: Leukemoid reactions of myeloid, lymphomonocytic and eosinophilic type?
plan: A leukemoid reaction is a reactive (non-neoplastic) blood change resembling leukemia; in the myeloid type neutrophils are usually >50×10⁹/L, mainly mature forms, with no myeloproliferative neoplasm.
Causes of the myeloid type: severe bacterial infections, sepsis, hemorrhage, hemolysis, tumors (paraneoplastic), drugs (glucocorticoids, G-CSF), intoxications.

Difference from CML: in a leukemoid reaction basophilia and blasts are usually absent, leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) is high, BCR::ABL1 (Philadelphia) is negative, polyclonal; it normalizes after the underlying cause is removed.
Lymphocytic (lymphomonocytic) type: viral infections (EBV, CMV), whooping cough, etc. – lymphocytosis, atypical (reactive) lymphocytes; to distinguish from CLL – flow cytometry (clonality).
Eosinophilic type: eosinophils >0.5×10⁹/L, sometimes very high – allergy, helminth infestations, drug reactions, rheumatological diseases; exclude clonal eosinophilic neoplasms.

kdl-o-021.q: Thrombocytopoiesis. Morphological and functional characteristics of the cells of the platelet lineage?
plan: Thrombocytopoiesis in the bone marrow: myeloid progenitor → megakaryoblast → promegakaryocyte → megakaryocyte (endomitosis – polyploid, large, multilobed nucleus); the main regulator is thrombopoietin, produced in the liver.
Proplatelet projections form from the cytoplasm of the mature megakaryocyte and fragment in the bloodstream to yield platelets.
A platelet is an anucleate, small disc-shaped cell fragment; lifespan ~7–10 days, aged ones are removed in the spleen and liver; normal 150–400×10⁹/L.

Structure: membrane glycoproteins (GPIb-IX-V – adhesion via vWF, GPIIb/IIIa – aggregation via fibrinogen), granules (alpha – vWF, fibrinogen, PDGF; dense – ADP, serotonin, calcium), open canalicular system.

Function: primary hemostasis – adhesion, activation (shape change, granule secretion, thromboxane A2), aggregation; accelerating coagulation via the procoagulant phospholipid surface; clot retraction.

kdl-o-022.q: Methods of counting platelets. Testing the functional state of platelets?
plan: Platelet counting: on the analyzer by impedance (by volume), optical (light scatter) and fluorescent methods; the ICSH/ISLH reference method is immunological flow cytometry with CD41/CD61 antibodies (RBC/platelet ratio).
Manual methods (chamber, assessment on a smear) are laborious and imprecise; the smear is important for checking the analyzer result (clumps, giant platelets).

False thrombocytopenia: EDTA-dependent agglutination, clot in the specimen, giant platelets; confirmation – see clumps on the smear and recount in a sodium citrate tube (with correction for dilution).
False increase: microcytes, schistocytes, cell fragments (in leukemias) counted as platelets.

Testing function: light transmission aggregometry (with inducers ADP, collagen, epinephrine, ristocetin, etc.) – the gold standard; PFA-100/200 (closure time; sensitive to vWF, prolonged in low Ht and thrombocytopenia); bleeding time – insensitive, abolished in many places.
Additional analyzer parameters: MPV, PDW, immature platelet fraction (IPF) – help to suggest the mechanism of thrombocytopenia (production or destruction).

pitfalls.right: in practice the analyzer (impedance/optical/fluorescence), the reference is immunological CD41/CD61; Fonio is an approximate historical method

pitfalls.right: bleeding time is insensitive, has low reproducibility and has largely been replaced by PFA-100; function – aggregometry/PFA

kdl-o-023.q: Methods of counting platelets, their advantages and disadvantages?
plan: Impedance method: change in electrical resistance as cells pass through an aperture; advantage – fast, cheap, reproducible; disadvantage – relies on volume: giant platelets are not counted, microcytes/schistocytes are counted as platelets.

Optical (light scatter) and fluorescent methods: based on size and density or RNA dye; higher specificity, more accurate at low values; but they too are not free of interference from fragments and clumps.
Immunological method (CD41/CD61, flow cytometry) – the reference method; the most accurate but expensive, not in routine – for calibrating analyzers and for complex specimens.
Manual: chamber (phase contrast) and assessment on a smear – require no special equipment but are laborious and imprecise; the smear is irreplaceable for seeing clumps and morphology.
With any method: know the errors of EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia, clot in the specimen, late analysis; confirm a critically low result with a smear and, if needed, a citrate specimen.

plan: Groups of analyzer parameters: red lineage (RBC, Hb, Ht, MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW, reticulocytes), white lineage (WBC and 5 populations in percent/absolute counts), platelets (PLT, MPV, PDW) and warning signs (flags, histogram/scattergram).

Measurement principles: impedance (cell volume and number), Hb – photometry (reference – hemiglobincyanide), optical scatter and fluorescent flow cytometry (differential, reticulocytes); Ht and indices are calculated values.

Interpretation sequence: first Hb – anemia/polycythemia; by MCV and RDW the type of anemia; WBC and absolute differential; platelets; then comparing all parameters with clinical data and previous results.
False results: cold agglutinins/agglutination (RBC↓, MCV↑, MCHC↑), lipemia (Hb and MCHC↑), EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia, platelet clumps (false leukocytosis), nucleated erythrocytes.
With any abnormal result, "flag", or suspicion of blasts or atypical cells, examining the peripheral blood smear is mandatory; MCHC is also used in the internal control of analyzer performance.

plan: Anemia is a decrease in Hb below the norm for age, sex and physiological state (per WHO approximately <130 g/L in men, <120 g/L in non-pregnant women); insufficient oxygen transport.

Pathogenetic classification: 1) blood loss (acute, chronic); 2) impaired erythropoiesis – iron, B12/folate deficiency, anemia of chronic disease (inflammation), bone marrow failure (aplasia, MDS, infiltration), kidney disease; 3) increased destruction of erythrocytes – hemolytic (inherited: membranopathies, enzymopathies, hemoglobinopathies; acquired: immune, mechanical, infectious, toxic).
Morphological classification by MCV: microcytic (<80 fL), normocytic (80–100), macrocytic (>100); by MCH/MCHC – hypo-/normochromic; RDW as an addition.
By bone marrow response: reticulocytes increased (regenerative – hemolysis, blood loss) or low (hyporegenerative – impaired production); assessed with RPI.

Laboratory algorithm: CBC + indices + reticulocytes + smear → in microcytosis ferritin/TSAT; in macrocytosis B12, folate (MMA if needed); in normocytosis signs of hemolysis (LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin, direct antiglobulin test), kidney function, inflammation.

pitfalls.wrong: the benzidine test for detecting hemolysis (hemoglobinuria)
pitfalls.right: benzidine is carcinogenic (bladder cancer) and is no longer used in medical laboratories; blood/hemoglobin in urine is detected on a test strip by peroxidase activity and by microscopy

plan: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common anemia; causes: chronic blood loss (menorrhagia in women, GI bleeding), increased demand (pregnancy, growth), malabsorption (celiac disease, gastrectomy, H. pylori), inadequate dietary intake.
Stages: first the stores are depleted (ferritin↓), then iron delivery is impaired (TSAT↓, CHr↓), and finally Hb falls – Hb is a late sign.

Laboratory criteria: ferritin <30 ng/mL or TSAT <20% – absolute iron deficiency (StatPearls); AGA/ASH recommend ferritin <45 ng/mL for IDA; WHO 2020: <15 µg/L in healthy adults, <70 µg/L in infection/inflammation; serum iron varies through the day and is unreliable alone.
Blood: microcytic hypochromic anemia, RDW↑, anisopoikilocytosis, "pencil" cells, target cells; reticulocytes low/normal; thrombocytosis may occur.
Differentiation: thalassemia trait (ferritin normal, RDW often normal, Hb electrophoresis), anemia of chronic disease (ferritin normal/high), sideroblastic anemia.
Response to treatment: 1–2 weeks after iron is given, reticulocytes rise, then Hb; looking for the cause (source of bleeding) is mandatory.

cutoffs.value: healthy ≥5 years and adults <15; <5 years <12; in infection/inflammation adults <70, <5 years <30

kdl-o-027.q: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
plan: Peripheral blood: Hb decreased, MCV <80 fL, MCH and MCHC low (hypochromia), RDW increased; the smear shows microcytes, anisopoikilocytosis, elliptocytes ("pencil" cells), target cells.
Reticulocytes normal or low (absolute count low), CHr/Ret-He <28 pg; platelets often normal or reactively increased.

Bone marrow (rarely needed for diagnosis): erythroid hyperplasia, predominance of small early erythroid cells with "ragged" cytoplasm; with Perls stain (Prussian blue) there is no iron in macrophages and sideroblasts are sharply reduced.
Bone marrow iron is the gold standard for assessing stores, but invasive; in practice replaced by ferritin and TSAT.
Differentiation: in anemia of chronic disease, iron in bone marrow macrophages is preserved/increased; in sideroblastic anemia – ring sideroblasts.

pitfalls.right: IDA: microcytic hypochromic anemia (MCV, MCH, MCHC low) + ferritin <30 ng/mL or TSAT <20%

kdl-o-028.q: Anemias related to vitamin B12 deficiency?
plan: Causes: pernicious anemia (antibodies to intrinsic factor or parietal cells – B12 is not absorbed), gastrectomy, ileal disease/resection, vegetarian diet, drugs (metformin, nitrous oxide), parasite (fish tapeworm).

Mechanism: B12 is a cofactor of methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; in deficiency DNA synthesis is impaired → megaloblastic erythropoiesis, homocysteine and MMA rise.

Clinical: anemia, glossitis, jaundice (ineffective erythropoiesis/hemolysis), neurological disturbances (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, neuropathy, cognitive impairment) – may occur even without anemia.

Laboratory: macrocytic anemia (MCV >100), hypersegmented neutrophils, often leuko- and thrombocytopenia; B12 <200 pg/mL – deficiency, 200–300 – borderline (measure MMA and homocysteine); MMA is more specific for B12 deficiency (normal in folate deficiency).
Confirming pernicious anemia: antibodies to intrinsic factor (specific), antibodies to parietal cells; the Schilling test is no longer performed.
A rise in reticulocytes 3–5 days after treatment confirms the diagnosis; differentiate from folate deficiency.

pitfalls.wrong: B12 is determined by a "radioimmunoassay"
pitfalls.right: the modern method is a competitive protein-binding (intrinsic factor) immunoassay on automated analyzers (chemiluminescent/fluorescent detection); in a borderline result, MMA and homocysteine

cutoffs.value: <200 – deficiency; 200–300 – borderline (MMA/homocysteine); >300 – normal
MCV <80 – microcytic; 80–100 – normocytic; >100 – macrocytic

kdl-o-029.q: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias related to vitamin B12 deficiency?
plan: Peripheral blood: macrocytic (MCV >100 fL) hyperchromic anemia, macro-ovalocytes, anisopoikilocytosis, Howell-Jolly bodies and Cabot rings may be present; neutrophils are hypersegmented (≥5 lobes).
Often pancytopenia (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia); reticulocytes low (ineffective erythropoiesis).
Bone marrow: hypercellular, erythroid hyperplasia, megaloblasts – large cells, nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony (nucleus "young", cytoplasm hemoglobinized); giant metamyelocytes and bands.
Biochemistry: signs of ineffective erythropoiesis/intramedullary destruction – LDH and indirect bilirubin increased; B12 low, MMA and homocysteine high.
Bone marrow examination is usually not required – vitamins and metabolites suffice; if necessary it is taken before treatment starts (megaloblastosis disappears quickly after treatment).

pitfalls.wrong: determining B12 by "radioimmunoassay"
pitfalls.right: automated competitive protein-binding immunoassay + MMA/homocysteine if needed

cutoffs.value: <200 – deficiency; 200–300 – borderline (MMA/homocysteine); >300 – normal
MCV <80 – microcytic; 80–100 – normocytic; >100 – macrocytic

kdl-o-030.q: Hemolytic anemias. Clinical and laboratory parameters?
plan: Hemolytic anemia is shortened erythrocyte survival; intravascular (hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria) and extravascular (in spleen/liver macrophages, spherocytes) hemolysis.

Classification: inherited – membranopathies (hereditary spherocytosis), enzymopathies (G6PD, pyruvate kinase deficiency), hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemias); acquired – autoimmune (warm/cold antibodies), alloimmune (incompatible blood, hemolytic disease of the newborn), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC), infectious (malaria), toxic, PNH.
General laboratory signs: reticulocytosis, LDH↑, indirect bilirubin↑, haptoglobin↓ (the most sensitive); in intravascular hemolysis free Hb, hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria.
The smear points to the cause: spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, warm AIHA), schistocytes (microangiopathy), sickle and target cells, Heinz bodies/"bite" cells (G6PD), parasites.

Depending on the cause, special tests: with suspected immune hemolysis the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test; in inherited forms, membrane, enzyme (e.g. G6PD) and hemoglobin studies – in a specialized laboratory.

kdl-o-031.q: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in hemolytic anemias?
plan: Peripheral blood: normocytic (MCV may be slightly raised owing to reticulocytosis) anemia, polychromasia, many reticulocytes, sometimes nucleated erythrocytes.

Cause-specific morphology: microspherocytes (spherocytosis, AIHA), schistocytes (microangiopathic hemolysis), sickle cells, target cells (thalassemia, hemoglobinopathy), "bite" cells (oxidative hemolysis), agglutination (cold antibodies).
Bone marrow: hyperplasia of the erythroid lineage (increased erythroid/myeloid ratio) – a compensatory response; bone marrow is usually not needed for diagnosis.
Aplastic crisis (for example parvovirus B19) – reticulocytes fall sharply, erythroid aplasia in the bone marrow.
Interpret together with biochemistry: LDH↑, indirect bilirubin↑, haptoglobin↓; direct antiglobulin test.
Leukemias are clonal neoplastic diseases of hematopoietic cells; they begin in the bone marrow and spill into the blood.

Etiology/risk factors: ionizing radiation, benzene, prior chemotherapy, genetic syndromes (Down), prior MDS/MPN; pathogenesis – genetic alterations (translocations, mutations), for example t(9;22) BCR::ABL1, t(15;17) PML::RARA.

Classification: acute (blasts predominate) and chronic (mature cells predominate); myeloid and lymphoid; the current standard is WHO 5th edition (2022) and ICC 2022: types defined genetically and by differentiation.
Diagnostic work-up: CBC and smear, bone marrow aspirate/trephine biopsy, cytochemistry, flow cytometry (immunophenotype), cytogenetics, FISH and molecular tests (PCR, NGS).
In acute myeloid leukemia the classical threshold is ≥20% blasts in blood or bone marrow; in WHO-2022 this threshold has been removed for most genetically defined types.

pitfalls.wrong: leukemias are classified only by morphological/cytochemical (FAB) classification
pitfalls.right: the current classification is WHO-HAEM5 (2022) and ICC: defining genetic alterations take priority, immunophenotype and genetics are mandatory; FAB (M0–M7) is a past classification

cutoffs.value: ≥20% blasts in blood/bone marrow (with immunophenotype); in WHO-2022 this threshold is not required for many genetic types
<5% blasts in bone marrow + recovery of blood counts

kdl-o-033.q: Acute leukemias. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in acute leukemias?
plan: Acute leukemia is clonal proliferation of immature blast cells and suppression of normal hematopoiesis.

Peripheral blood: anemia (normocytic), thrombocytopenia, leukocytes increased, normal or decreased; blasts (high nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, fine chromatin, nucleoli); "leukemic hiatus" – no intermediate forms between blasts and mature cells.
Bone marrow: hypercellular, many blasts – ≥20% for AML (in some genetic types the threshold is lower/absent); normal lineages suppressed.
Identifying the myeloid type: Auer rods, myeloperoxidase positivity; in APL promyelocytes with many Auer rods and the risk of DIC – an emergency.
Confirmation: flow cytometry (myeloid/B/T lineage), cytogenetics and molecular tests (for example t(15;17) PML::RARA, FLT3, NPM1) – for classification and prognosis.
Remission: <5% blasts in the bone marrow, recovery of blood counts.

cutoffs.value: ≥20% blasts in blood/bone marrow (with immunophenotype); in WHO-2022 this threshold is not required for many genetic types

kdl-o-034.q: Chronic myeloid leukemia. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture?
plan: CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm; in ~90–95% of patients t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, the BCR::ABL1 fusion protein (mainly p210) – a constitutively active tyrosine kinase.

Peripheral blood (chronic phase): marked leukocytosis, granulocytes of all maturation stages (many myelocytes and segmented forms – "two-peak" distribution), basophilia and eosinophilia, blasts <2%, platelets often increased.
Bone marrow: markedly hypercellular, hyperplasia of the granulocytic lineage, small megakaryocytes; Ph+ cytogenetics.
Phases: chronic → accelerated (increase in blasts and basophils) → blast crisis (myeloid or lymphoid).
Confirming the diagnosis: cytogenetics or FISH (t(9;22)), RT-PCR (BCR::ABL1); monitoring treatment – quantitative RT-PCR (molecular response).
Difference from a leukemoid reaction: basophilia, BCR::ABL1 positivity, clonality.

kdl-o-035.q: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture?
plan: CLL is the accumulation of monoclonal B lymphocytes of mature appearance; the most common leukemia in adults.

Diagnostic criterion: >5×10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes in the blood with a characteristic immunophenotype (if fewer – monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, MBL); lymphocytosis persisting for more than 3 months requires a smear and immunophenotyping (French CLL Study Group).
Peripheral blood: lymphocytosis, small mature lymphocytes, "smudge" cells (Gumprecht shadows); in later stages anemia and thrombocytopenia (marrow infiltration or autoimmune).
Immunophenotype (flow cytometry): CD19, CD20 (weak), co-expression of CD5 and CD23, kappa or lambda light chain restriction (clonality).
Bone marrow: not required for diagnosis; diffuse or nodular lymphocytic infiltration – affects prognosis.
Additionally: assess autoimmune cytopenias (hemolysis, thrombocytopenia) and susceptibility to infection; prognostic genetic markers – in a specialized laboratory.

cutoffs.value: >5×10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes (characteristic immunophenotype); <5×10⁹/L – MBL
cutoffs.guideline: French CLL Study Group (based on iwCLL)

kdl-o-036.q: Multiple myeloma. Clinical and laboratory parameters?
plan: Multiple myeloma is a tumor of clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow; a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) or free light chains are produced.

Diagnosis (IMWG): clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow ≥10% (or plasmacytoma) + a myeloma-defining event: CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, lytic bone lesions) or SLiM biomarkers (plasma cells ≥60%, involved/uninvolved free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm on MRI).
Laboratory: protein electrophoresis (M-spike) and immunofixation (serum and urine), free light chains (kappa/lambda ratio), total protein, albumin, calcium, creatinine.
Blood: normocytic anemia, erythrocytes in "stacks of coins" (rouleaux) on the smear, ESR markedly raised; rarely circulating plasma cells.
Urine: Bence Jones protein (light chains) – a test strip detects it poorly, electrophoresis/immunofixation is needed.
Bone marrow: number and clonality of plasma cells (immunophenotype), cytogenetics/FISH – prognosis.

cutoffs.value: clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma) + CRAB or SLiM (≥60% plasma cells, FLC ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm on MRI)

plan: Medical ethics are the moral principles governing a health worker's attitude toward the patient, colleagues and society; deontology is the study of professional duty and rules of conduct.
Core principles: putting the patient's interest first, non-maleficence, patient autonomy and voluntary informed consent, non-discrimination (diagnosis and services only according to medical need).

Confidentiality: test results and the patient's personal data are medical confidentiality – disclosed only to authorized persons; this obligation continues after the patient's death. In the laboratory: do not give a result to a stranger by telephone, do not leave forms in view, restrict access to the electronic system.

Professional competence and accountability: continuous learning, professional development; honesty – record and correct errors without concealing them (it is forbidden to "fix" a result); report critical results to the physician immediately.
Relations with colleagues: respect and cooperation, clear communication between the laboratory technician, physician and nurse; do not criticize a colleague in front of the patient.
In Uzbekistan the code of ethics and deontology of medical workers was approved by MoH Order No. 88 of 24 March 2022 – know its main requirements (check the text on lex.uz).

kdl-o-038.q: In gastrointestinal diseases – the significance and laboratory diagnosis of H. pylori?
plan: H. pylori is a gram-negative spiral bacterium of the gastric mucosa; associated with chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and the risk of MALT lymphoma.

Non-invasive tests: 13C-urease breath test (the most reliable for active infection and for checking eradication), stool monoclonal antigen test (active infection), serology (IgG) – shows past exposure, does not assess active infection or treatment outcome.
Invasive (endoscopic) tests: rapid urease test, histology, culture and antibiotic susceptibility, PCR (clarithromycin resistance mutations).
Preanalytics: stop PPIs ≥2 weeks, antibiotics and bismuth preparations ≥4 weeks (except for serology) – otherwise false negatives.
Confirming eradication: ≥4 weeks after finishing treatment – UBT or stool antigen; serology is not used for this purpose.

kdl-o-039.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of stool examination?
plan: Stool analysis helps to assess digestive function (stomach, pancreas, liver-biliary tract, intestine), inflammation, bleeding and infections/infestations.

Coprology: macroscopic (amount, consistency, color, mucus, blood, worms), chemical (pH, occult blood, stercobilin, bilirubin), microscopic (muscle fibers, neutral fat and fatty acids, starch, fiber, leukocytes, erythrocytes, parasites).

Modern targeted tests: occult blood – immunochemical test (FIT, colorectal cancer screening), calprotectin (intestinal inflammation), elastase-1 (pancreatic exocrine insufficiency), H. pylori antigen, pathogen antigens and PCR panels.
Steatorrhea: screening with Sudan III, quantitative fecal fat (>7 g/day) – reference.
Interpretation with clinical data and diet; correct specimen collection and rapid delivery.

kdl-o-040.q: Macroscopic and chemical examination of stool. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Macroscopic: amount, shape and consistency, color (acholic – bile duct obstruction; black/tarry – upper GI bleeding or iron/bismuth; bright red blood – lower parts), odor, mucus, pus, undigested food, worms and segments.

Chemical: pH, occult blood – instead of guaiac tests (pseudoperoxidase; diet and drugs interfere), an immunochemical test specific for human hemoglobin (FIT) – no dietary restriction, more sensitive; stercobilin (absence – obstruction), bilirubin (when intestinal flora is disturbed).
Special protein markers: calprotectin – intestinal inflammation (distinguishing IBD from IBS), elastase-1 – pancreatic exocrine function.
Fat digestion: screening with Sudan stain, quantitative fecal fat.
Clinical significance: source of bleeding, malabsorption and maldigestion, inflammation, tumor screening (FIT).

pitfalls.right: benzidine is not used (carcinogenic); now an immunochemical test specific for human hemoglobin (FIT) or guaiac tests

kdl-o-041.q: Microscopic examination of stool. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Preparations: native (physiological saline), Lugol (starch, iodophilic flora, protozoan cysts), Sudan III (neutral fat), with acetic acid (fatty acids, soaps).

Food remnants: muscle fibers (creatorrhea – gastric and pancreatic insufficiency), neutral fat (steatorrhea – lipase insufficiency), fatty acids and soaps (bile insufficiency, impaired intestinal absorption), starch (amylorrhea), digestible fiber.
Elements of the intestinal wall: mucus, leukocytes (inflammation – colitis, invasive diarrhea), erythrocytes, epithelium; Charcot-Leyden crystals (eosinophilic inflammation, parasites).
Parasites: eggs and larvae of helminths, vegetative forms and cysts of protozoa (fresh specimen, enrichment methods if needed).
A tentative conclusion based on coprological syndromes; for confirmation – special tests (elastase, calprotectin, antigen/PCR).

cutoffs.value: fecal fat >7 g/24 h; elastase <100 µg/g (100–200 indeterminate)

plan: Urine is formed in the nephron: filtration in the glomeruli (primary urine – protein-free ultrafiltrate of plasma, ~180 L per day), reabsorption and secretion in the tubules, concentration in the collecting ducts.
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the main indicator of kidney function; in practice eGFR is calculated from creatinine (and cystatin C).

Proximal tubule: glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, Na and most of the water are reabsorbed; loop of Henle – concentration gradient via the countercurrent mechanism; distal tubule and collecting ducts – final regulation under aldosterone (Na/K) and ADH (water).
Laboratory reflection: glucosuria (if filtered glucose exceeds reabsorption capacity), proteinuria (glomerular or tubular damage), urine density/osmolality (concentrating ability).
Kidney disease is classified by KDIGO by eGFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3).

kdl-o-043.q: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
plan: Physical properties: amount (in adults ~600–2000 mL/day), color (bilirubin, blood, hemoglobin/myoglobin, drugs), clarity (turbidity – salts, leukocytes, bacteria, mucus), odor, relative density (1.002–1.035; urinometer, refractometer or test strip) – renal concentrating ability.

Chemical examination – test strips: pH (4.5–8), protein (mainly albumin; alkaline pH – false positive), glucose (when the reabsorption threshold is exceeded), ketones (acetoacetate/acetone, β-hydroxybutyrate is not detected), blood (erythrocytes, hemoglobin, myoglobin – peroxidase activity), leukocyte esterase, nitrites (some bacteria), bilirubin, urobilinogen.
Interferences: ascorbate (false negative blood, glucose, nitrite, leukocyte esterase), concentrated or dilute urine, drugs (phenazopyridine).
Confirmatory tests: for protein – sulfosalicylic acid (all proteins) and quantitative UPCR/ACR, for blood – microscopy, glucose and ketones in blood.
Preanalytics: midstream, morning urine, analysis within 1 hour or storage at 4 °C.

pitfalls.right: the test strip detects blood by peroxidase activity with a safe chromogen, confirmed by microscopy; benzidine is not used in medical laboratories

plan: Preparation: 5–12 mL of well-mixed fresh urine, centrifuged at ~400×g for 5 minutes, resuspended in a standard volume; under a coverslip at low (×100) and high (×400) magnification; phase contrast/staining, polarization for crystals.

Organized elements: erythrocytes (normal 0–5/field; dysmorphic erythrocytes and acanthocytes – glomerular source), leukocytes (0–5; many – infection, inflammation), epithelium (squamous, transitional, renal tubular), casts.

Casts: hyaline (a few are normal; concentrated urine, exertion), erythrocyte (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis), leukocyte (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis), granular (tubular damage), waxy (severe CKD), fatty (nephrotic syndrome).
Unorganized elements: crystals (oxalates, urates, uric acid, triple phosphates – infection; cystine – cystinuria), bacteria, fungi, trichomonads, sperm.
Automated urine particle analyzers (flow cytometry, digital imaging) – screening; abnormal results are confirmed by microscopy; the result is standardized per unit volume (/µL).

kdl-o-045.q: Methods of determining protein in urine?
plan: Qualitative/semi-quantitative: test strip (bromophenol blue – "protein error"; sensitive mainly to albumin, detects light chains poorly; false positive in alkaline urine); turbidimetric sulfosalicylic acid test – precipitates all proteins.

Quantitative: protein in 24-hour urine (gold standard; normal ≤150 mg/day), in a random specimen the protein/creatinine (UPCR) and albumin/creatinine (ACR) ratios – a practical alternative (a morning specimen is preferred).
Albuminuria categories (KDIGO): ACR <3 (A1), 3–30 (A2), >30 mg/mmol (A3); nephrotic range – >3.5 g/day or UPCR >350 mg/mmol.
Methods (in the laboratory): albumin – immunoturbidimetry; total protein – pyrogallol red/molybdate or benzethonium chloride turbidimetry.
For paraproteins (Bence Jones) the test strip is unreliable – electrophoresis and immunofixation.
Types of proteinuria: glomerular, tubular, overflow (paraproteins), postrenal; transient (fever, exertion), orthostatic.

kdl-o-046.q: Determining erythrocytes, leukocytes, epithelial cells and casts in urine, clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Erythrocytes: blood reaction on the test strip (erythrocytes, hemoglobin, myoglobin) + microscopy; >0–5/field – hematuria; dysmorphic erythrocytes, acanthocytes and erythrocyte casts – glomerular source; isomorphic – urinary tract (stone, tumor, infection).
Leukocytes: leukocyte esterase + microscopy; leukocyturia – urinary tract infection, interstitial nephritis, tuberculosis ("sterile pyuria"); leukocyte casts – pyelonephritis.
Epithelium: squamous (from the external genitalia – a sign of contamination), transitional (bladder, urinary tract), renal tubular epithelium (acute tubular necrosis, nephritis).
Casts: hyaline, erythrocyte (glomerulonephritis), leukocyte (pyelonephritis), granular, waxy (severe CKD), fatty (nephrotic syndrome).

Quantitative assessment: per field or per /µL (automated analyzers, chamber); historical methods (Nechiporenko, Kakovsky-Addis) serve the same purpose, but standardized sediment analysis and analyzers are now preferred.

kdl-o-047.q: Urinalysis parameters in various kidney diseases?
plan: Acute glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome): hematuria (dysmorphic erythrocytes, erythrocyte casts), moderate proteinuria, oliguria; raised blood creatinine, in the poststreptococcal form ASO is high and C3 low.
Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), fatty casts and lipiduria, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia.
Pyelonephritis/urinary tract infection: leukocyturia, bacteriuria, nitrite and leukocyte esterase positive, leukocyte casts (pyelonephritis); confirm by culture.
Chronic kidney disease: low relative density (isosthenuria), proteinuria/albuminuria, granular and waxy casts; staging by eGFR and ACR.
Acute tubular necrosis: tubular epithelial cells and granular ("muddy brown") casts; diabetic nephropathy – albuminuria; urolithiasis – isomorphic hematuria, crystals.

cutoffs.value: >3.5 g/24 h or UPCR >350 mg/mmol; >150 mg/24 h – pathological

plan: The basis of modern diagnosis is the WHO-recommended rapid molecular tests (for example Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, Truenat) as the initial test: within hours they detect M. tuberculosis DNA and rifampicin resistance.
Culture: liquid (MGIT) and solid media – the "gold standard" for confirmation and full drug susceptibility (result in weeks).
Microscopy: Ziehl-Neelsen or fluorescent (auramine) staining – cheap, rapid, for assessing infectiousness and treatment progress; sensitivity is limited (many bacilli are needed).
Drug resistance: molecular (line probe assays, targeted next-generation sequencing) and phenotypic tests.
Additionally: urine LAM test in people living with HIV; latent infection – IGRA (interferon-γ release assays) or the tuberculin skin test; histology, PCR on other materials.
Biosafety: handle sputum in a BSC, reduce aerosols.

kdl-o-049.q: Staining smears by Ziehl-Neelsen. Microscopy of stained smears?
plan: Principle: acid-fast bacteria (mycobacteria), owing to mycolic acids in the cell wall, retain heated carbol fuchsin even after decolorization with acid-alcohol.

Steps: a thin even smear from the purulent part of the sputum (about 2×1 cm), drying, flame fixation; staining with carbol fuchsin with heating (without boiling), decolorizing with acid alcohol, counterstaining with methylene blue, rinsing and drying.
Microscopy: oil-immersion objective (×1000), red, thin, slightly curved rods on a blue background; a sufficient number of fields is examined (for example at least 100).
Fluorescent (auramine) microscopy – faster and more sensitive at lower magnification.
Safety and quality: prepare smears in a BSC or under safe conditions; reagent control (positive/negative control smears), external rechecking (blind rechecking).

cutoffs.value: none in 100 fields – negative; 1–9/100 – exact number; 10–99/100 – 1+; 1–10/field – 2+; >10/field – 3+

kdl-o-050.q: Microscopy of smears stained by Ziehl-Neelsen. Analysis of the results obtained?
plan: Grading of the result (WHO/IUATLD): no AFB in 100 fields – negative; 1–9 – "scanty" (the exact number is recorded); 10–99 – 1+; 1–10 per field (at least 50 fields) – 2+; >10 per field (at least 20 fields) – 3+.
Interpretation: a positive smear indicates a high probability of infectiousness; a "scanty" result agrees poorly with culture – repeat microscopy or culture/molecular test.

A negative smear does not exclude tuberculosis (sensitivity is limited) – molecular tests and culture are needed; microscopy cannot distinguish M. tuberculosis from non-tuberculous mycobacteria, or live from dead bacteria.
Smear results (conversion) are used to monitor the course of treatment.
Quality: internal control and external "blind" rechecking to reduce false positive/negative results.

cutoffs.value: none in 100 fields – negative; 1–9/100 – exact number; 10–99/100 – 1+; 1–10/field – 2+; >10/field – 3+

kdl-o-051.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of sputum examination in respiratory diseases?
plan: Sputum analysis in lower respiratory tract diseases helps to determine the type of inflammation, the causative agent of infection and tumor cells.
Macroscopic: amount, character (mucoid, purulent, bloody), color, odor, layering, inclusions (Curschmann spirals, Dittrich plugs).

Microscopic: leukocytes and epithelium (specimen quality – many squamous epithelial cells indicate saliva contamination), eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals (asthma, allergy, parasites), elastic fibers (destruction), fungi, atypical cells.
Bacterioscopy: Gram stain (bacterial pneumonia), Ziehl-Neelsen/auramine (tuberculosis); culture and susceptibility; molecular tests for tuberculosis.
Cytological examination – when lung cancer is suspected (sensitivity is limited, bronchoscopic material is preferred).

kdl-o-052.q: Macroscopic and microscopic examination of sputum?
plan: Collection: in the morning, after rinsing the mouth, by deep cough into a sterile container; not saliva; for tuberculosis, several specimens.

Macroscopic: volume, consistency, character (mucoid, mucopurulent, purulent, bloody), color ("rusty" – lobar pneumonia), odor (putrid – abscess), layers, Curschmann spirals, Dittrich plugs, fibrinous casts.

Native microscopy: leukocytes, erythrocytes, epithelium (squamous – saliva contamination; columnar), alveolar macrophages (siderophages – heart failure), eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, elastic fibers, fungal elements.
Stained preparations: Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen/auramine, Romanowsky (cellular composition), cytological staining (tumor cells).
Interpretation: asthma – eosinophils, spirals, crystals; bacterial infection – neutrophils and bacteria; tuberculosis – AFB; tumor – atypical cells.

kdl-o-053.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of examining transudates and exudates?
plan: Analysis of body cavity fluids (pleural, ascitic, pericardial) determines the mechanism of fluid accumulation (transudate or exudate) and the cause.
Transudate – disturbed hydrostatic/oncotic pressure (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome): protein and LDH low, few cells.

Exudate – inflammation or tumor (pneumonia/empyema, tuberculosis, tumor, pancreatitis, autoimmune): one of Light's criteria – fluid/serum protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6 or fluid LDH > 2/3 of serum ULN.
Additional tests: cell count and differential, glucose, pH (empyema), amylase, TG (chylothorax), Gram/culture, tests for tuberculosis, cytology (tumor cells); in ascites SAAG.
In heart failure on diuretics, Light's criteria may show a transudate as an exudate – the albumin/protein gradient or NT-proBNP helps.

cutoffs.value: fluid/serum protein >0.5 or LDH ratio >0.6 or fluid LDH > 2/3 of serum ULN

kdl-o-054.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of cerebrospinal fluid examination?
plan: CSF examination is important in diagnosing meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, demyelination and tumor metastases; opening pressure is measured at lumbar puncture.
Macroscopic: color and clarity (turbid – pleocytosis; red – blood; xanthochromia points to subarachnoid hemorrhage).

Cells: very few in the norm (mononuclears); bacterial meningitis – neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose; viral – lymphocytic pleocytosis (may be neutrophilic at first), normal glucose; tuberculous and fungal – lymphocytic, high protein, low glucose.
Biochemistry: protein, glucose (compare with simultaneous blood glucose), lactate; microbiology: Gram, culture, antigens, PCR (viral and bacterial panels), cryptococcal antigen.
Cytology – tumor cells; oligoclonal bands (multiple sclerosis) – specialized laboratory.
Preanalytics: deliver the specimen immediately (cells disintegrate quickly), sterile containers, account for the effect of traumatic blood in the first tube.

kdl-o-055.q: Fundamentals of cytological examination. Importance of cytological examination in the diagnosis of neoplastic diseases?
plan: Cytology is making a diagnosis from the structure of cells: exfoliative (naturally shed or washing/brushing) and aspiration (fine needle aspirate) material.
Advantages: minimally invasive, rapid, inexpensive, repeatable; screening (cervix), early detection of tumors, assessing spread (fluids, lymph nodes), monitoring treatment effect.

Criteria of malignancy: nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia and uneven chromatin, irregular nuclear membrane, prominent/multiple nucleoli, atypical mitoses, cell overlap and mutual "molding", loss of cohesion.
Limitations: does not show tissue architecture (invasion is hard to determine), specimen adequacy and reactive changes are sources of error; if needed, confirm with histology.
Additional methods: cell block, immunocytochemistry (for example TTF-1, p40, calretinin), molecular tests (HPV, mutations), liquid-based cytology.

kdl-o-056.q: General information about tumors. Cytodiagnosis of malignant tumors?
plan: A tumor is a collection of clonal cells with uncontrolled proliferation; benign (mature, expansive growth, no metastasis) and malignant (immature, infiltrative growth, metastasis) tumors; epithelial (carcinomas), mesenchymal (sarcomas), hematopoietic (leukemias, lymphomas), etc.

Cytological signs of malignant tumors: cell and nuclear pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia, uneven chromatin, large/multiple nucleoli, atypical mitoses, loss of cohesion, necrotic background ("diathesis").

Signs of histogenetic type: squamous cell carcinoma (keratinization, "fiber" and "tadpole" cells), adenocarcinoma (glandular structures, vacuolated cytoplasm, eccentric nucleus), small cell carcinoma (small "molded" nuclei, scant cytoplasm), lymphoma (diffusely scattered monotonous lymphoid cells).
Differentiation from reactive atypia (inflammation, regeneration, radiation) is a source of error; in doubtful cases the category "suspicious for malignancy" and histological confirmation.
Immunocytochemistry and molecular tests help to determine the origin of the tumor.

kdl-o-057.q: Cytodiagnosis of tumors of the respiratory organs?
plan: Material: sputum (morning, several days), bronchial wash and brushing, bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial and EBUS-TBNA aspirates, pleural fluid.
Squamous cell carcinoma: keratinized, with dense orange cytoplasm (Pap), pleomorphic cells, hyperchromatic pyknotic nuclei; immunophenotype p40+.

Adenocarcinoma: groups and glandular/papillary structures, vacuolated cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli; TTF-1 and Napsin-A positive; preserve material for molecular tests (EGFR, ALK, etc.).
Small cell carcinoma: small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclei "molded" to each other, fine chromatin, crush artifact; neuroendocrine markers.
Sensitivity depends on the material and tumor location: for central tumors sputum and washings are more effective, for peripheral ones – guided aspiration; EBUS-TBNA in diagnosis and staging.
Differentiation from reactive changes (metaplasia, regeneration, viruses).

kdl-o-058.q: Cytodiagnosis of tumors of serous membranes?
plan: Tumor cells in serous cavity fluids are mostly metastatic: adenocarcinomas of the lung, breast, ovary, GI tract, lymphomas; the primary tumor is mesothelioma.
Reactive mesothelium: single cells or small groups, "window" (slit) sign, uniform nuclei; atypia may be present – the main differential diagnostic difficulty.
Adenocarcinoma metastases: three-dimensional clusters, "balls", vacuolated cytoplasm, two populations (tumor and mesothelium); immunocytochemistry (for example epithelial markers and organ markers).
Mesothelioma: multicellular, papillary/morula-like structures, mesothelial markers (calretinin, WT1, D2-40) positive; loss of BAP1 (and MTAP/CDKN2A) supports malignant mesothelial proliferation.
Cell block and immunocytochemistry are the basis of interpretation; the result is assessed with clinical-radiological data and, if needed, biopsy.

kdl-o-059.q: Cytodiagnosis of lymph node diseases (lymphosarcoma, lymphogranulomatosis)?
plan: Fine needle aspirate of a lymph node: reactive hyperplasia (polymorphic lymphoid cells, tingible body macrophages), granulomatous inflammation (epithelioid cells, tuberculosis – caseation, AFB), metastatic tumors (foreign epithelial cells), lymphomas.

Hodgkin lymphoma ("lymphogranulomatosis" – an obsolete name): on a reactive background (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells) large Reed-Sternberg cells (binucleate, with large nucleoli) and Hodgkin cells; immunophenotype CD30+, CD15+, usually CD20− and CD45−.
Non-Hodgkin lymphomas ("lymphosarcoma" – an obsolete term): a population of monotonous lymphoid cells; classification by WHO using morphology, immunophenotype (flow cytometry – clonality), genetics.
Cytology raises suspicion of lymphoma, but for full classification an excisional biopsy or histological material and immunohistochemistry are usually needed.
Additionally: collect the aspirate separately for flow cytometry, microbiology for tuberculosis.

kdl-o-060.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of examining the hormonal background?
plan: The hormonal background is assessed in two ways: colpocytologically (by the proportion of squamous epithelial cells in a vaginal smear) and by directly measuring sex hormones in blood serum; in current practice the main method is serum hormones, cytology is supplementary.

Material: the smear is taken from the proximal part of the lateral vaginal wall (without cervical material) – this area is most sensitive to hormones; conditions: no inflammation and cytolysis, no recent local/systemic drugs, radiotherapy or surgery; for full assessment – serial smears through the cycle.

Maturation index (MI) – percentage ratio of parabasal : intermediate : superficial cells (only single cells are counted); in a menstruating woman roughly 0:35:65; a "left shift" such as 90:10:0 – atrophy, postpartum period, progestin-only contraception.

Karyopyknotic index (KI) – ratio of superficial cells with pyknotic nuclei to all mature squamous cells (200–400 cells in 3–4 fields); peak at ovulation ~50–85%, also high in estrogen-producing ovarian tumors; the eosinophilic index (EI) changes in parallel with KI.

Maturation value (MV, Meisels): superficial cell – 1.0, intermediate – 0.5, parabasal – 0; percentages are multiplied and added (0–100; for example 0:35:65 → 82.5): 100 – only superficial cells (high estrogen effect), 0 – only parabasal (atrophy).

Clinical significance: approximate assessment of estrogen effect, atrophy, effect of hormone therapy/contraceptives; limitations – inflammation, infection, cytolysis and cervical material distort the result; the result is compared with serum hormones (estradiol, progesterone, LH, FSH, prolactin) and clinical findings.

kdl-o-061.q: Advantages and disadvantages of vaginal smear staining methods (Romanowsky, Papanicolaou, Gram and methylene blue staining)?
plan: Papanicolaou staining (wet fixation, hematoxylin + OG-6 + EA): shows nuclear structure clearly, the cytoplasm is transparent (seeing through layers), distinguishes keratinization and degree of maturation – the standard for cervical screening and tumor cytology; disadvantage – multi-step, requires time and reagents.

Romanowsky-type stains (air-dried): quick, simple, show cytoplasm and granules, microorganisms and blood cells well; disadvantage – nuclear detail and keratinization are poorer, cells enlarge on air-drying.

Gram staining: microflora (lactobacilli – gram-positive rods, Gardnerella/anaerobes, "clue" cells, gonococci – gram-negative diplococci) – the Nugent score for bacterial vaginosis (the reference laboratory method); disadvantage – not for cell morphology.
Simple methylene blue staining: quick, cheap – shows leukocytes, "clue" cells, diplococci tentatively; low specificity, gives no Gram characteristics.
Chosen according to the purpose: tumor screening – Papanicolaou; microflora/STI – Gram (and wet mount, NAAT if needed).

kdl-o-062.q: Preparing a PAP smear: requirements for the patient and for taking the smear, as well as for staining?
plan: Requirements for the patient: days outside menstruation are preferred (in liquid-based cytology menstruation interferes little), avoid intercourse, douching, vaginal medications, spermicides for 48 hours beforehand; with acute inflammation, treat first.

Taking the smear: speculum (if needed moistened with water only), the cervix clearly visible; from the transformation zone and endocervix with a special brush (cervex-brush, cytobrush) or spatula; visible suspicious areas.
Slide: conventional – spread evenly thin on the slide and fix wet immediately (avoid drying artifact); liquid-based – rinse the brush in a vial with preservative.
Staining: Papanicolaou (hematoxylin – nucleus; OG-6 and EA – cytoplasm), reagent quality checked with control slides.

Adequacy criteria: sufficient squamous cellularity, transformation zone component (endocervical/metaplastic cells), not obscured by blood, inflammation or drying; otherwise recorded as "unsatisfactory".

kdl-o-063.q: Cytological examination of smears from the vaginal portion of the cervix by the Bethesda 2001 system: smears within normal limits and reactive changes?
plan: The current system is Bethesda 2014 (an update of the 2001 edition): specimen adequacy, general category and descriptive interpretation.
NILM (negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy): normal superficial, intermediate, parabasal cells; endocervical cells and transformation zone component.
Organisms falling under NILM: Trichomonas vaginalis, Candida, flora change suggesting bacterial vaginosis ("clue" cells), Actinomyces, herpes virus effect.

Reactive changes (NILM): inflammation (including repair), radiation effect, changes associated with an intrauterine device; atrophy (postmenopause – predominance of parabasal cells); predominance of intermediate cells under progesterone.
Distinguishing reactive changes from ASC-US and other lesions: nuclear enlargement is uniform, chromatin fine, nucleoli may be present, N/C ratio preserved.

pitfalls.wrong: "Bethesda 2001" is the current system
pitfalls.right: The Bethesda system was revised in 1991, 2001 and most recently in 2014 – the current edition is 2014

kdl-o-064.q: Cytological examination of smears from the vaginal portion of the cervix by the Bethesda 2001 system: pathology of the squamous epithelium?
plan: ASC-US – changes suggestive of SIL but insufficient in quantity/quality for a definite SIL; triage with a high-risk HPV test.
ASC-H – atypical cells in which HSIL cannot be excluded (often small, of metaplastic type); referral for colposcopy.
LSIL (corresponds to CIN1, HPV effect): nuclear enlargement in mature (superficial/intermediate) cells, hyperchromasia, koilocytes (perinuclear "cavity" and nuclear atypia).
HSIL (CIN2/CIN3): in smaller, immature cells high N/C ratio, hyperchromasia, irregular nuclear membrane; squamous cell carcinoma – keratinized pleomorphic cells, nucleoli, tumor diathesis.
Results are managed together with HPV testing and colposcopy/biopsy.

kdl-o-065.q: Analyzing the results of cytological examination of smears from the vaginal portion of the cervix by the Bethesda 2001 system?
plan: Structure of the report: specimen type (conventional or liquid-based), adequacy (satisfactory/unsatisfactory, transformation zone component), general category, descriptive interpretation (NILM or epithelial cell abnormality), ancillary tests (HPV) and recommendations.
Squamous epithelial abnormalities: ASC-US, ASC-H, LSIL, HSIL, squamous cell carcinoma; glandular epithelium: AGC (endocervical/endometrial/not otherwise specified), AIS, adenocarcinoma.
Risk level: ASC-US and LSIL – low risk (HPV and follow-up/colposcopy), ASC-H, HSIL, AGC – high risk (colposcopy and biopsy).
Factors affecting interpretation: inflammation, atrophy, hormonal status, previous treatment; clinical data must be on the requisition.
Quality: second reading (blind rescreening), cytology-histology correlation, monitoring the ASC/SIL ratio.

kdl-o-066.q: Importance of the PAP smear in the prevention of cervical cancer?
plan: The PAP test is cytological screening that detects cervical precancer (SIL/CIN) and early cancer; regular screening has significantly reduced the incidence of and mortality from cervical cancer.

The cause of cancer is almost always persistent infection with oncogenic HPV; from precancer to cancer usually takes 15–20 years (5–10 years with weakened immunity) – a "window" for screening and treatment.

WHO recommendation: from age 30, screening with a high-performance (HPV) test every 5–10 years (in people living with HIV from age 25 every 3–5 years); cytology is used for triage of HPV-positive women and when an HPV test is unavailable.

Limitation of the PAP test – the sensitivity of a single test is moderate (regular repetition is required), dependent on specimen quality and the reader; liquid-based cytology and HPV co-testing improve effectiveness.
Primary prevention – HPV vaccination of girls aged 9–14; WHO 90–70–90 targets.

cutoffs.value: from age 30 a high-performance (HPV) test every 5–10 years; in people living with HIV from age 25 every 3–5 years

kdl-o-067.q: Role of human papillomavirus in the development of cervical cancer?
plan: Almost all cervical cancers are associated with oncogenic (high-risk) HPV types; HPV 16 and 18 in ~76% of cases.
Most HPV infections clear spontaneously; persistent infection leads to precancerous changes in transformation zone cells (LSIL → HSIL); 15–20 years to cancer (5–10 years with weakened immunity).
Risk factors: immunodeficiency (HIV – faster progression to cancer), persistent high-risk types (16/18).
Laboratory diagnosis: high-risk HPV DNA/RNA tests (primary screening, triage), genotyping (16/18), koilocytosis in cytology; HPV also causes other tumors (anogenital, oropharyngeal).
Prevention: HPV vaccination (girls aged 9–14), HPV-based screening and treatment of precancer.
Qualitative analysis is determining the composition of a substance, quantitative analysis is measuring the concentration or activity of a component.
Principles of quantitative measurement: the measured signal (absorption, fluorescence, electrical potential, etc.) depends on concentration; calibrator and calibration curve.
Methods: chemical (titrimetry, gravimetry – historical), physicochemical (photometry, ion-selective electrodes, chromatography, immunoassay, mass spectrometry).
Metrological aspects: units of measurement (SI), traceability, accuracy (trueness and repeatability), measuring range.
Quality assurance: internal quality control and external assessment.

kdl-o-069.q: Physicochemical and chemical methods (chromatography, spectro-, photometry, densitometry, etc.)?
plan: Chromatography: distribution between a mobile and a stationary phase; by mechanism – adsorption, partition, ion exchange, gel filtration, affinity; by technique – paper, thin layer, column, gas, high-performance liquid (HPLC), LC-MS/MS.
Clinical use: HbA1c and hemoglobin variants (ion-exchange HPLC), steroids and drug monitoring (LC-MS/MS), toxicology (GC-MS), newborn screening.
Spectrophotometry/photometry: absorption of monochromatic light is proportional to concentration (Beer–Lambert law); "blank" and calibrator; end-point and kinetic measurement (enzymes).
Other optical methods: turbidimetry, nephelometry, fluorimetry; densitometry – quantification of electrophoresis fractions.
Electrochemical methods: ion-selective electrodes (Na, K, Cl), gas analyzers.
