kdl-o-070.q: Technical characteristics of an automatic biochemical analyzer, installing the analyzer and its maintenance?
plan: Technical characteristics: type of analysis (discrete, random access), throughput (tests/hour), sample and reagent volume, photometer (wavelengths), ISE module, reaction cuvettes and incubation temperature (37 °C).
Installation: manufacturer's requirements – room temperature and humidity, stable power supply (UPS), water quality (deionized), space and ventilation; installation is done by an engineer.
Before putting into use: installation and operational tests, method verification, staff training.
Maintenance: daily (cleanliness of probe and cuvettes, reagents), weekly/monthly preventive maintenance schedule, calibration and controls.
Documentation: equipment log, faults and repairs, service contract; label a faulty analyzer and do not use it.
kdl-o-070.note: Technical parameters of analyzers are general; exact values depend on the manufacturer's documents.

kdl-o-071.q: Operating principles of an automatic biochemical analyzer. Programming a biochemical analyzer?
plan: Operating cycle: sample identification (barcode), dispensing sample and reagent, mixing, incubation at 37 °C, photometric measurement, calculation and transmission of the result to the LIS.
Measurement modes: end-point, two-point (fixed time), kinetic; bichromatic measurement; electrolytes by ISE.
Automatic functions: calibration, controls, automatic re-dilution (when out of range), hemolysis/lipemia/icterus indices, carry-over control.
Programming: entering test parameters (wavelength, volumes, time, calibrator values, linearity limit, units, reference intervals), control materials and rules.
After programming a new method – verification (precision, trueness, range) and documentation.

kdl-o-072.q: Operating principles of a semi-automatic biochemical analyzer. Programming a biochemical analyzer?
plan: Semi-automatic analyzer: the operator prepares and mixes the sample and reagent manually, the analyzer aspirates, thermostats, measures and calculates.
Measurement modes: end-point, fixed time, kinetic; calculation by standard (factor).
Programming: test name, wavelength, temperature, aspiration volume, delay and measurement time, standard concentration or factor, linearity limit, units.
Sources of error: pipetting, mixing, timing, air bubbles, contamination of the flow cell and carry-over.
Quality: in each run a blank, calibrator and controls; daily cleaning and flushing.

plan: The concept of an open system: the analyzer allows entering parameters for reagents of other manufacturers.
Sources of parameters: the reagent instructions (wavelength, volume ratio, time, calibrator, linearity), the analyzer manual.
Verification after programming: repeatability, trueness (control/EQA materials, comparison), measuring range, carry-over, checking reference intervals.
Documentation: parameter sheet, verification report, change control (who, when, what).
Regular control: internal quality control, Westgard rules, checking when the reagent lot changes.

kdl-o-074.q: Immunoturbidimetric and colorimetric methods of determining some proteins?
plan: Immunoturbidimetry: immune complexes of the antigen (the protein being determined) and antibody form turbidity in solution; the decrease in transmitted light is measured on a photometer; latex-enhanced variants for low concentrations (for example hs-CRP).

Immunonephelometry: light scattered by immune complexes is measured at an angle – more sensitive at low concentrations; for CRP, immunoglobulins, complement, apolipoproteins, transferrin, ceruloplasmin.
Advantages: specific, automated, fast; limitation – with antigen excess the "prozone" (hook) effect gives a falsely low result, lipemia and turbidity interfere.

Colorimetric methods: total protein – the biuret reaction (peptide bonds with Cu²⁺ give a violet complex); albumin – dye binding (bromocresol green BCG, bromocresol purple BCP); BCG overestimates albumin in inflammation and hypoalbuminemia, BCP is more specific.
Colorimetric methods are cheap and simple but cannot determine individual proteins (CRP, IgG, etc.) – immunochemical methods are needed for that.

kdl-o-075.q: Proteins. Importance, structure, physicochemical properties and function?
plan: Proteins are polymers of 20 kinds of L-amino acids linked by peptide bonds; levels of structure: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix, β-sheet), tertiary (spatial), quaternary (subunits).

Physicochemical properties: amphoteric nature and isoelectric point (the basis of electrophoresis), colloidal properties, oncotic pressure, precipitation and denaturation (temperature, acids, heavy metals), absorption of UV light.

Functions: catalytic (enzymes), transport (albumin, transferrin, hemoglobin), protective (immunoglobulins, complement), structural (collagen), regulatory (hormones, receptors), hemostasis (coagulation factors), oncotic pressure.
Fractions of plasma protein electrophoresis: albumin, α1 (α1-antitrypsin), α2 (α2-macroglobulin, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin), β (transferrin, β-lipoprotein, complement), γ (immunoglobulins).
Laboratory significance: total protein (biuret) and albumin (BCG/BCP), electrophoresis (M-spike, acute phase, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis patterns), individual proteins by immunochemical methods.
Acute-phase proteins are plasma proteins whose concentration changes in the liver under the influence of cytokines (mainly IL-6) in inflammation, infection and injury.
Positive reactants (increase): CRP, serum amyloid A, procalcitonin, fibrinogen, ferritin, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, hepcidin, α1-antitrypsin.
Negative reactants (decrease): albumin, prealbumin (transthyretin), transferrin, retinol-binding protein, antithrombin.

CRP changes quickly (rises within hours, falls quickly after the cause is removed); <3 mg/L (0.3 mg/dL) normal; very high values are more often in bacterial infection; hs-CRP – cardiovascular risk (<1, 1–3, >3 mg/L).
Procalcitonin – in bacterial infection and sepsis; an aid in starting/stopping antibiotic therapy (~0.25 ng/mL in respiratory infections, ~0.5 ng/mL in sepsis; ≥80% decrease over time).
ESR is an indirect marker (depends on fibrinogen and immunoglobulins), changes more slowly than CRP; consider the acute-phase effect when interpreting ferritin and albumin.

plan: 70–90% of bilirubin comes from the hemoglobin of aged erythrocytes: in macrophages heme oxygenase converts heme to biliverdin, and biliverdin reductase converts it to indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin; the rest comes from myoglobin, cytochromes and ineffective erythropoiesis.

Indirect bilirubin is insoluble in water and is transported in the blood bound to albumin to the liver; in the hepatocyte, with the participation of UGT1A1, it is conjugated with glucuronic acid (direct bilirubin) and excreted into the bile.
In the intestine bacteria convert it to urobilinogen; part is reabsorbed (urobilinogen in urine), the rest is converted to stercobilin and colors the stool.

Disorders: hemolysis – indirect bilirubin rises; conjugation defects (Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar); hepatocellular injury – both fractions; cholestasis/obstruction – direct bilirubin, bilirubin in urine, stool becomes pale.
Laboratory: total and direct bilirubin (diazo reaction), indirect = total − direct; bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine; ALT/AST, ALP/GGT, hemolysis markers.

kdl-o-078.q: Carbohydrates, classification, biological significance. Absorption of carbohydrates in the gastrointestinal tract?
plan: Classification of carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose), oligosaccharides and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, fiber); complex carbohydrates – glycoproteins, glycosaminoglycans.
Biological significance: the main source of energy (glucose is the main substrate for the brain and erythrocytes), storage (glycogen), structural and receptor functions (glycoproteins, glycolipids).

Digestion: in the mouth salivary α-amylase starts it, in the small intestine pancreatic amylase breaks down starch, brush-border enzymes (maltase, isomaltase, sucrase, lactase) hydrolyze to monosaccharides.

Absorption: glucose and galactose – with Na⁺ via SGLT1 (secondary active transport), fructose – passively via GLUT5; from the enterocyte into the blood through basolateral transporters, then via the portal vein to the liver.

Clinical-laboratory link: in lactase deficiency and other disaccharidase deficiencies – osmotic diarrhea; starch in stool (amylorrhea) – a sign of digestive insufficiency; blood glucose is measured by modern enzymatic methods (hexokinase, glucose oxidase).

pitfalls.wrong: blood sugar by the Hagedorn–Jensen and ortho-toluidine methods, "sugar curves" with a 50 g load
pitfalls.right: modern methods are enzymatic (hexokinase – 340 nm, glucose oxidase–peroxidase); the diagnostic OGTT uses 75 g anhydrous glucose

kdl-o-079.q: Neuroendocrine regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus?
plan: Glucose homeostasis: insulin (β cells) is the only glucose-lowering hormone: it enhances glucose entry into tissues, glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and inhibits gluconeogenesis and lipolysis; counter-regulatory hormones – glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone, thyroid hormones.
Nervous system: sympathetic activity (adrenaline) enhances glycogenolysis and glucagon secretion; incretins (GLP-1, GIP) increase insulin secretion after a meal.
Type 1 DM – autoimmune destruction of β cells, absolute insulin deficiency; markers: autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, insulin, ZnT8), low C-peptide; tendency to ketoacidosis.
Type 2 DM – insulin resistance and relative insulin secretion deficiency; associated with obesity and metabolic syndrome; C-peptide initially normal/high.
Other types: gestational DM, monogenic (MODY), diseases of the exocrine pancreas, drug- or endocrinopathy-related.
Diagnostic criteria are the same for both types: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 75 g OGTT 2-hour value ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms.

cutoffs.value: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 (126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 h); 75 g OGTT 2-hour ≥11.1 (200); HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP/DCCT); random ≥11.1 with symptoms; without unequivocal hyperglycemia – two abnormal results

kdl-o-080.q: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
plan: Diabetes criteria (ADA/WHO, venous plasma): fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 hours), 2-hour glucose at 75 g OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP-certified method standardized to DCCT), or random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms of hyperglycemia.
For a diagnosis without unequivocal hyperglycemia, two abnormal results are needed (two tests from one sample or on two different days).
Prediabetes (ADA): fasting 5.6–6.9 mmol/L (impaired fasting glucose), OGTT 2-hour 7.8–11.0 (impaired glucose tolerance), HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.

Conditions in which HbA1c is unreliable: sickle cell and other hemoglobinopathies (method-dependent), second–third trimester of pregnancy, hemodialysis, recent blood loss/transfusion, erythropoietin therapy, G6PD deficiency, HIV – in these only plasma glucose is used.

Preanalytics: because of glycolysis, glucose at room temperature falls by ~5–7% per hour – centrifuge the sample immediately or use a tube with a glycolysis inhibitor; a glucometer result is not for diagnosis.
Determining type and complications: autoantibodies, C-peptide; ketones; urine albumin/creatinine ratio, eGFR, lipids; in pregnancy at 24–28 weeks a 75 g OGTT (92/180/153 mg/dL ≈ 5.1/10.0/8.5 mmol/L).

pitfalls.right: fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) in venous plasma; 6.5 is the diagnostic threshold of HbA1c (%)

pitfalls.right: <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) at 2 hours is normal; 7.8–11.0 – impaired glucose tolerance; ≥11.1 – diabetes

kdl-o-081.q: Laboratory diagnosis of complications of diabetes mellitus?
plan: Acute complications: diabetic ketoacidosis (glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L or a history of diabetes, β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L, pH <7.30 and/or HCO3 <18 mmol/L – 2024 consensus), hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (glucose >33.3 mmol/L [>600 mg/dL], effective osmolality >320, without significant ketoacidosis), hypoglycemia (level 2 <3.0 mmol/L).

Diabetic nephropathy (kidney disease): urine albumin/creatinine ratio – A2 3–30 mg/mmol, A3 >30 mg/mmol (confirmed in 2 of 2–3 samples within 3 months), eGFR (creatinine, CKD-EPI) – at least once a year.
Glycemic control: HbA1c (usually every 3–6 months), home/continuous glucose monitoring; fructosamine – when HbA1c is unreliable.
Risk of macroangiopathy: lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, non-HDL cholesterol).
Others: urinalysis (glucosuria, ketonuria, proteinuria, infection), electrolytes (potassium in DKA), B12 level in those taking metformin.

kdl-o-082.q: Structure, classification and biological role of lipids?
plan: Lipids are compounds insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents; classification (LIPID MAPS): fatty acids, glycerolipids (triacylglycerols), glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, sterols (cholesterol), prenols, etc.

Simple lipids – esters of fatty acids and glycerol (triglycerides); complex – phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, -ethanolamine, -serine), sphingomyelin, glycolipids; steroids – cholesterol and the bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D formed from it.

Biological roles: energy storage (triglycerides), membrane structure (phospholipids, cholesterol, sphingolipids), signaling molecules (eicosanoids, steroid hormones), thermal insulation and mechanical protection, transport of fat-soluble vitamins.
In the blood lipids are transported within lipoproteins: chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL, HDL; apolipoproteins serve as structural components, enzyme cofactors and receptor ligands.
Clinical and laboratory significance: lipid profile (total cholesterol, TG, HDL, LDL, non-HDL cholesterol), apoB, Lp(a) – assessing the risk of atherosclerosis.

Disorders of lipid metabolism: primary (inherited – familial hypercholesterolemia, familial hyperchylomicronemia – LPL or apoC-II deficiency, etc.) and secondary (diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, obesity, alcohol, drugs).

Pathogenesis of atherosclerosis: apoB-containing lipoproteins (mainly LDL) are retained in the vessel intima and oxidized → macrophages become foam cells → inflammation, plaque; LDL and other apoB-containing lipoproteins are a direct cause of ASCVD.

Laboratory assessment: total cholesterol, TG, HDL, LDL (calculated or direct), non-HDL cholesterol, apoB (fasting not required), Lp(a) – a risk modifier: measure at least once in adults; EAS 2022 consensus: <30 mg/dL (<75 nmol/L) – risk excluded, 30–50 mg/dL – gray zone, >50 mg/dL (>125 nmol/L) – risk confirmed; >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) – lifetime risk equivalent to HeFH; ESC/EAS 2019: inherited very high level ≥180 mg/dL (≥430 nmol/L). There is no universal "normal" for Lp(a); mg/dL↔nmol/L conversion depends on the assay.
Target values depend on the overall cardiovascular risk (ESC/EAS 2019: in very high risk LDL <1.4 mmol/L).
Fredrickson (WHO) classification: I (chylomicrons), IIa (LDL), IIb (LDL + VLDL), III (remnants), IV (VLDL), V (chylomicrons + VLDL) – a historical phenotype classification.

kdl-o-084.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of determining total cholesterol, calculating the atherogenic index?
plan: Determination of total cholesterol: enzymatic method (cholesterol esterase → cholesterol oxidase → H2O2 + peroxidase/4-aminophenazone, Trinder reaction) – the standard on automated analyzers.

Clinical significance: alone it estimates risk poorly – together with HDL, LDL, TG; increase – primary hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, pregnancy; decrease – severe liver disease, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, emaciation.
Non-HDL cholesterol = total cholesterol − HDL – reflects all atherogenic lipoproteins, fasting not required; a secondary target in modern guidelines.
The "atherogenic index" (total cholesterol − HDL)/HDL – used in regional practice; in international guidelines risk is assessed by LDL, non-HDL cholesterol, apoB and an overall risk score.
Preanalytics: for a lipid profile fasting is usually not required (repeat fasting if TG is very high); the result may change after an acute illness.

kdl-o-085.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of determining low- and high-density lipoproteins (LDL, HDL)?
plan: LDL is the main carrier of cholesterol in the blood (~2/3), contains apoB-100; atherogenic. HDL returns cholesterol from the periphery to the liver (reverse transport), apoA-I; low HDL is a risk factor.
Determining LDL: Friedewald formula (mg/dL: LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5) – only when TG ≤400 mg/dL (≈4.5 mmol/L); more accurate calculation methods (Martin–Hopkins, Sampson) or direct homogeneous methods.
HDL – direct homogeneous enzymatic methods (on automated analyzers); non-HDL cholesterol = TC − HDL.
Clinical significance: LDL is the main indicator of treatment and target (by risk category, in very high risk <1.4 mmol/L); apoB – additional, especially with high TG, diabetes, obesity.
LDL increase: familial hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis; HDL decrease: obesity, insulin resistance, smoking, high TG.

cutoffs.value: very high risk <1.4 (and a reduction of ≥50%); high <1.8; moderate <2.6; low <3.0

plan: The main method is enzymatic: lipase hydrolyzes TG to glycerol and fatty acids; glycerol is oxidized by glycerol kinase and glycerol-3-phosphate oxidase to produce H2O2; with peroxidase a colored product (GPO-PAP, Trinder) is measured photometrically.
Free glycerol (for example heparin, glycerol-containing drugs, sample storage) falsely raises the result – a glycerol blank if needed.
Preanalytics: TG rises after a meal – a high result (or suspected pancreatitis) is rechecked fasting (≈10–12 hours); a lipemic sample interferes with other tests.
Interpretation: target <1.7 mmol/L (<150 mg/dL); at >5.6 mmol/L (500 mg/dL) the risk of acute pancreatitis rises sharply; with high TG the Friedewald formula is unsuitable.
Increase: secondary – diabetes, obesity, alcohol, hypothyroidism, CKD, drugs (estrogens, steroids); primary – familial hypertriglyceridemia, LPL/apoC-II deficiency.

plan: Enzymes are biological catalysts (mostly proteins) that lower activation energy; active site, substrate specificity; most require a cofactor/coenzyme (often vitamin derivatives).

Structure: simple and complex (apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme); oligomeric enzymes, isoenzymes (forms catalyzing the same reaction but differing in structure and tissue distribution – for example LDH1–5, CK-MM/MB/BB).
International classification (IUBMB, EC numbers) – 7 classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases, translocases.

Units of activity: the international unit (U – 1 µmol substrate/min) and the katal; in the clinic U/L, the conditions of determination (temperature 37 °C, pH, substrate) affect the result – IFCC reference procedures.
Clinical significance: enzymes are markers of disease (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, amylase, lipase, CK) and laboratory reagents (methods for glucose, cholesterol, urea).

pitfalls.wrong: 6 classes of enzymes
pitfalls.right: The IUBMB classification has 7 classes: EC 7 – translocases (added in August 2018)

kdl-o-088.q: Kinetics of enzymatic processes. Regulation of enzyme activity. Enzymopathies?
plan: Enzyme kinetics: the reaction rate depends on substrate concentration (Michaelis–Menten); Vmax is the rate when all active sites are saturated, Km is the substrate concentration at half-maximal rate (inversely related to affinity).

Factors affecting the rate: temperature, pH, enzyme and substrate concentrations, cofactors, inhibitors; in the laboratory activity is measured with saturating substrate under standard conditions (37 °C).

Inhibition: competitive (Km rises, Vmax unchanged – overcome by increasing substrate), noncompetitive (allosteric site; Vmax decreases, Km unchanged), uncompetitive (both decrease); irreversible inhibitors (for example organophosphates – cholinesterase).

Regulation of activity: allosteric regulation, covalent modification (phosphorylation), activation of proenzymes (zymogens) (trypsinogen, coagulation factors), induction/repression of synthesis, compartmentalization.

Enzymopathies: inherited enzyme defects – phenylketonuria, galactosemia, glycogen storage diseases, G6PD deficiency, pseudocholinesterase deficiency; acquired – changes in enzyme activity in diseases.

Enzyme diagnostics is identifying organ damage from changes in enzyme activity in the blood (and other fluids); intracellular enzymes enter the blood as a result of damage (necrosis, membrane permeability).

Organ specificity and isoenzymes: liver – ALT, AST, GGT, ALP; pancreas – lipase (more specific), amylase; muscle – CK; bone – the bone isoenzyme of ALP; prostate – (historically acid phosphatase, now PSA).
The level and dynamics of enzyme activity depend on the extent of damage, the enzyme's half-life and its localization in the cell.
Analytical standardization: IFCC reference procedures at 37 °C and certified materials – so that results are comparable between laboratories; the result is in U/L.
Enzymes as reagents: enzymatic determination of metabolites such as glucose, cholesterol, TG, urea, creatinine.

kdl-o-090.q: Methods of determining total protein and albumin?
plan: Total protein: the biuret method – in an alkaline medium peptide bonds form a violet complex with Cu²⁺; standard on automated analyzers; refractometry – approximate.

Albumin: dye-binding methods – bromocresol green (BCG; also reacts with other proteins, overestimates in inflammation and hypoalbuminemia) and bromocresol purple (BCP; more specific); immunoturbidimetry – for urine and low concentrations.
Preanalytics: a prolonged tourniquet causes hemoconcentration (protein rises); in plasma fibrinogen raises total protein somewhat.

Hypoproteinemia/hypoalbuminemia: decreased hepatic synthesis (cirrhosis), loss (nephrotic syndrome, enteropathy, burns), malnutrition, inflammation (negative acute phase); hyperproteinemia: dehydration, paraproteinemia (myeloma), chronic inflammation.
Albumin/globulin ratio and electrophoresis – determining the cause of raised globulins.

kdl-o-091.q: Determining CRP, RF, ASO. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: CRP is an acute-phase protein; immunoturbidimetry/nephelometry (quantitative) or latex agglutination (semi-quantitative); <3 mg/L normal; rises sharply in bacterial infection; hs-CRP – cardiovascular risk.

Rheumatoid factor (RF) – autoantibodies to the Fc portion of IgG (mainly IgM); latex agglutination or nephelometry; occurs in rheumatoid arthritis but is not specific (other rheumatic diseases, infections, healthy elderly); anti-CCP is more specific.

ASO (antistreptolysin-O) – antibodies to streptolysin O of group A streptococcus; begin to rise ~1 week after infection, peak at 3–6 weeks; a sign of recent streptococcal infection (rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis); dynamics in paired sera are important.
Disadvantages of latex tests: semi-quantitative, prozone effect, subjective reading; quantitative immunoturbidimetric methods are preferred in modern practice.
Results are interpreted with the clinical picture: RF/ASO alone is not a diagnosis.

kdl-o-092.q: Residual nitrogen. Azotemias. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: "Residual nitrogen" is the nitrogen in the protein-free filtrate (urea ~50%, amino acids, uric acid, creatinine, ammonia, etc.); this summary parameter is historical, individual components are measured now.

Azotemia is an increase of nitrogenous substances (urea, creatinine) in the blood: prerenal (reduced renal perfusion – dehydration, heart failure, hemorrhage; the urea/creatinine ratio is usually >20:1 (in mg/dL)), renal (parenchymal damage), postrenal (urinary tract obstruction).
Productional (extrarenal) increase of urea: high protein intake, catabolism, GI bleeding, glucocorticoids.
Assessing kidney function: creatinine (the enzymatic method is preferred) and eGFR, cystatin C if needed; urea and uric acid are auxiliary.
Decrease of urea: severe liver failure, protein deficiency, pregnancy, fluid overload.

Sample: serum/plasma (ammonium heparin is not used – ammonia contamination), urine.
Expressing the result: urea (mmol/L) or blood urea nitrogen (BUN, mg/dL); know the conversion.
Clinical significance: types of azotemia, urea/creatinine ratio (high in the prerenal state), dialysis adequacy; urea depends more on diet and catabolism than GFR does.

Clinical significance: CKD and acute kidney injury; creatinine clearance and urine albumin/creatinine ratio.

kdl-o-098.q: Methods of determining sodium, potassium, chloride. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Sodium is the main extracellular cation (normal ~136–145 mmol/L), determines osmolality and volume; potassium is the main intracellular cation (~3.5–5.0 mmol/L), membrane potential, heart rhythm; chloride is the main anion, acid-base balance.

Method – ion-selective electrodes (ISE): direct (undiluted – blood gas analyzers) and indirect (diluted – large biochemistry analyzers); with indirect ISE, hyperlipidemia and hyperproteinemia give false hyponatremia.

Potassium preanalytics: hemolysis, fist clenching, prolonged tourniquet, K-EDTA contamination, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis (in serum) give false hyperkalemia – when in doubt remeasure in heparinized plasma; storage in the cold also raises K.
Hyponatremia: water excess (SIADH, heart/liver failure), Na loss (diuretics, vomiting, adrenal insufficiency); hypernatremia – water loss, diabetes insipidus.
Hyperkalemia: renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, drugs, cell breakdown, acidosis; hypokalemia: diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, hyperaldosteronism, alkalosis.
Chloride: falls in metabolic alkalosis (vomiting), rises in hyperchloremic acidosis; used in interpreting the anion gap (Na − (Cl + HCO3)).

kdl-o-099.q: Methods of determining calcium, phosphorus. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Calcium in the blood occurs in three forms: ionized (~half, biologically active), protein-bound (mainly albumin) and complexed with anions; total calcium by photometric methods, ionized by ISE.
Albumin correction: corrected Ca (mg/dL) = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL); when albumin or pH changes, measuring ionized calcium is preferable; normal about 8.8–10.4 mg/dL (2.2–2.6 mmol/L).
Hypercalcemia: primary hyperparathyroidism (PTH high), tumors (PTHrP, osteolytic metastases), vitamin D excess; work-up – PTH, PTHrP, 25(OH)D.
Hypocalcemia: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, CKD, magnesium deficiency, acute pancreatitis; first correct for albumin.
Phosphorus (phosphate) is determined photometrically; hyperphosphatemia – renal failure, hypoparathyroidism; hypophosphatemia – hyperparathyroidism, malnutrition; hemolysis distorts the result.

kdl-o-100.q: Iron metabolism. The role of transferrin, ferritin, hepcidin?
plan: Iron absorption in the duodenum: dietary Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ and enters the enterocyte; basolateral exit via ferroportin, then it is oxidized and binds to transferrin.
Transferrin carries iron in the blood and delivers it to cells via transferrin receptors; TIBC is the total iron-binding capacity of transferrin, TSAT = serum iron/TIBC.
Ferritin is the intracellular iron storage protein; serum ferritin reflects stores (low – deficiency), but as an acute-phase protein it rises in inflammation.
Hepcidin is a liver hormone that degrades ferroportin: with iron excess and in inflammation (IL-6) it rises, reducing absorption and release from macrophages; in deficiency and hypoxia it falls.
Clinical reflection: iron deficiency (ferritin↓, TSAT↓, transferrin↑), anemia of inflammation (ferritin normal/↑, TSAT↓, hepcidin↑), iron overload/hemochromatosis (TSAT and ferritin↑).

healthy women >150, men >200; unwell adults >500

kdl-o-101.q: Methods of determining iron. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Serum iron: photometric methods – release from transferrin in an acid medium, reduction of Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and a colored complex with a chromogen; in the morning, fasting (varies through the day), non-hemolyzed sample.
TIBC (or transferrin by immunoturbidimetry) and TSAT (iron/TIBC × 100%); TSAT <20% – low iron delivery.

Ferritin – immunochemical method; marker of stores: WHO 2020 – <15 µg/L in healthy adults, <70 µg/L in infection/inflammation; in clinical practice ferritin <30 ng/mL or TSAT <20% – absolute deficiency; in inflammation ferritin <100 ng/mL and TSAT <20% suggest coexisting deficiency (StatPearls Anemia).
Additional: soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR), reticulocyte hemoglobin (CHr) – identifying iron deficiency against a background of inflammation.
Clinical significance: iron deficiency, anemia of inflammation, iron overload/hemochromatosis (raised TSAT and ferritin) and monitoring iron therapy.

kdl-o-102.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of transaminases and methods of determination?
plan: ALT and AST are enzymes that transfer an amino group from an amino acid to α-ketoglutarate (coenzyme – pyridoxal phosphate, a derivative of vitamin B6).

Determination: kinetic UV method (IFCC reference procedure, 37 °C) – the product formed oxidizes NADH in a reaction with an auxiliary enzyme, and the decrease in absorbance at 340 nm is measured; historical colorimetric end-point methods are poorly standardized.
ALT is mainly in the liver – more specific for hepatocellular injury; AST in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, erythrocytes.
Interpretation: very high values – acute viral/toxic/ischemic hepatitis; AST:ALT >2 – alcohol-related injury; isolated AST elevation – muscle (compare with CK) or hemolysis.
Preanalytics: hemolysis falsely raises AST; physical exertion, some drugs.

kdl-o-103.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of amylase and cholinesterase and methods of determination?
plan: α-amylase breaks down starch; pancreatic and salivary isoenzymes; determined in serum and urine.
Determination: kinetic methods with a chromogenic substrate (an IFCC reference procedure at 37 °C exists); historical iodometric methods are obsolete.

Clinical significance: acute pancreatitis (2 of 3 criteria: abdominal pain, lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN, imaging); lipase is more specific and persists longer; amylase also rises in salivary gland diseases, macroamylasemia, renal failure.

Cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase) is synthesized in the liver; decrease – reduced hepatic synthetic function, organophosphate poisoning (proportional to severity), cachexia; in inherited deficiency the effect of succinylcholine is prolonged.
Cholinesterase activity is determined by a kinetic photometric method; together with albumin and PT/INR the result helps assess liver function, and in poisoning the severity.

cutoffs.value: 2 of 3: typical pain; lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN; imaging

kdl-o-104.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of alkaline and acid phosphatase and methods of determination?
plan: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) – isoenzymes: non-tissue-specific (liver, bone, kidney) and specific (intestinal, placental, germ cell); the main part in the blood is liver and bone.
Determination: kinetic method with a chromogenic phosphate substrate (IFCC reference procedure, 37 °C); isoenzymes can be separated by electrophoresis or immunoassay (bone ALP).

Increase: cholestasis (together with GGT), bone diseases (Paget, metastases, osteomalacia, rickets, hyperparathyroidism), growth period, pregnancy (placenta), after a fatty meal the intestinal isoenzyme (in blood groups O and B) – fasting collection is recommended.
Acid phosphatase was historically a marker of prostate cancer; replaced by PSA as more accurate; tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase is a marker of osteoclast activity.
Interpretation: when ALP is raised, determine the source by GGT (liver) or bone markers.

kdl-o-105.q: Clinical and diagnostic significance of gamma-GTP and methods of determination?
plan: GGT is a membrane enzyme (liver, bile duct epithelium, kidney, pancreas); takes part in glutathione metabolism.
Determination: kinetic photometric method with a chromogenic substrate (IFCC reference procedure, 37 °C).
Increase: cholestasis (if it rises together with ALP – confirms the hepatic source of ALP), alcohol abuse, enzyme-inducing drugs (anticonvulsants), MASLD, oxidative stress.
Specificity is low – not a diagnosis by itself; in monitoring alcohol, together with other markers (for example carbohydrate-deficient transferrin).
In bone diseases GGT is normal – helps to distinguish the cause of raised ALP.

kdl-o-106.q: Vitamin-coenzymes and their role in metabolism. New properties of vitamin D as a hormone?
plan: Water-soluble vitamins as coenzymes: B1 (thiamine pyrophosphate – pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenases), B2 (FAD/FMN), B3 (NAD/NADP), B5 (CoA), B6 (pyridoxal phosphate – transaminases), B7 (biotin – carboxylases), B9 (folate – one-carbon groups), B12 (methionine synthase, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase), C (hydroxylases).
Laboratory reflection of deficiencies: B12/folate – megaloblastic anemia, homocysteine and MMA; B6 – decreased transaminase activity; B1 – raised lactate.

Vitamin D is in essence a hormone (a secosteroid): formed in the skin under UV rays (D3) and from food; 25(OH)D in the liver, 1.25(OH)2D in the kidney (the active form, calcitriol); regulates gene transcription via the VDR.

The classical role of vitamin D – absorption of calcium and phosphate in the intestine, bone mineralization, calcium homeostasis together with PTH; "new" (extraskeletal) effects – the immune system, cell growth and differentiation – are being actively studied.

Assessing status: serum 25(OH)D (not 1.25(OH)2D); StatPearls definition: <12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) – deficiency, 12–30 ng/mL (30–77 nmol/L) – insufficiency; other guidelines set the deficiency threshold at <20 ng/mL – definitions differ; 1 ng/mL = 2.5 nmol/L; differences between methods are large – standardized (VDSP, traceable to LC-MS/MS) methods.

cutoffs.value: <12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) – deficiency; 12–30 ng/mL (30–77 nmol/L) – insufficiency (other guidelines set the deficiency threshold at <20 ng/mL); 1 ng/mL = 2.5 nmol/L
cutoffs.guideline: StatPearls (Vitamin D Deficiency); definitions differ by guideline

plan: Filtration markers: creatinine (the enzymatic method is preferred) and eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021), cystatin C (little dependent on muscle mass; eGFRcr-cys is more accurate); urea – auxiliary.
Damage markers: albuminuria – urine albumin/creatinine ratio: A1 <3, A2 3–30, A3 >30 mg/mmol; protein/creatinine ratio; urine sediment (erythrocytes, casts).
Definition of CKD: abnormality of kidney structure or function for >3 months; classification – cause, GFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3).
Markers of complications: potassium, bicarbonate (acidosis), calcium-phosphorus and PTH (mineral-bone disorder), Hb (renal anemia), lipids.
In acute kidney injury – a rapid rise in creatinine and decreased urine output; in the prerenal state the urea/creatinine ratio is high.

kdl-o-108.q: Biochemical markers of myocardial infarction and risk factors?
plan: Myocardial infarction (4th universal definition): a rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit + clinical evidence of ischemia (symptoms, new ECG changes, pathological Q waves, imaging).
Troponin (I or T) is the main marker: rises at 3–4 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours, persists up to 7–14 days; with high-sensitivity troponin 1–3 hour algorithms.
Old markers: CK-MB – limited significance, only when troponin is unavailable (reinfarction); myoglobin – early but nonspecific; AST and LDH are no longer used in diagnosing MI.
Troponin also rises without infarction: myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, renal failure – dynamics and the clinical picture are important.

Risk factors and their laboratory reflection: dyslipidemia (LDL, non-HDL cholesterol, Lp(a)), diabetes (glucose, HbA1c), CKD (eGFR, albuminuria), inflammation (hs-CRP); non-modifiable – age, sex, heredity; smoking, hypertension, obesity.

cutoffs.value: >99th percentile URL; if the baseline is high, a >20% change in series – acute
cutoffs.guideline: 4th universal definition of MI (via StatPearls Cardiac Biomarkers)

kdl-o-109.q: Laboratory diagnosis of osteoporosis and monitoring treatment?
plan: The diagnosis of osteoporosis is mainly by DXA (T-score) and assessment of fracture risk; laboratory tests do not make the diagnosis, but identify secondary causes and monitor treatment.
Baseline panel: calcium (albumin-corrected), phosphate, ALP, creatinine/eGFR, liver tests, 25(OH)D, TSH, PTH; testosterone in men; CBC.
Looking for secondary causes (when suspected): celiac serology, protein electrophoresis (myeloma), 24-hour urine calcium, cortisol (Cushing), prolactin, magnesium.

Bone turnover markers: the reference markers recommended by IOF/IFCC – bone formation P1NP, resorption β-CTX; not for diagnosis but for monitoring response to treatment and compliance; preanalytics matter (morning, CTX fasting).
Treatment monitoring: with antiresorptive therapy a fall in CTX, with anabolic therapy a rise in P1NP; monitoring calcium and vitamin D levels.

kdl-o-110.q: The role of the liver in metabolism?
plan: Carbohydrate metabolism: glycogen synthesis and breakdown, gluconeogenesis – maintaining blood glucose in the fasting state.

Protein metabolism: synthesis of albumin, coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X, etc.), transport proteins, acute-phase proteins; transamination of amino acids; conversion of ammonia to urea (ornithine cycle).
Lipid metabolism: β-oxidation of fatty acids, synthesis of ketone bodies, synthesis of cholesterol and VLDL, formation of bile acids.
Detoxification and excretion: bilirubin conjugation and excretion into bile, metabolism of drugs and toxins, inactivation of hormones; storage of vitamins and iron.
Laboratory reflection: synthetic function – albumin, PT/INR; damage – ALT, AST; cholestasis – ALP, GGT, bilirubin; in liver failure urea is low, ammonia high, cholinesterase low.
Hepatocellular injury: ALT (more specific for the liver) and AST; AST:ALT >2 – suggests alcohol-related disease; very high aminotransferases – acute viral/toxic/ischemic hepatitis.
Cholestasis: disproportionate rise of ALP and GGT, direct bilirubin; R ratio = (ALT/ULN)/(ALP/ULN): >5 hepatocellular, 2–5 mixed, <2 cholestatic pattern.
Synthetic function: albumin, PT/INR (reflects function better than enzymes), cholinesterase.

Etiological tests: viral hepatitis (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HCV, HCV RNA and HBV DNA if needed), autoimmune markers, ferritin/iron (hemochromatosis), ceruloplasmin (Wilson disease), alpha-1 antitrypsin.
Fibrosis and tumor: noninvasive indices (FIB-4, etc.), AFP (surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma – together with ultrasound).
Steatotic liver disease (MASLD) – with cardiometabolic factors; lipid profile, glucose/HbA1c.

kdl-o-112.q: Fundamentals of hormonal regulation. The role of thyroid hormones in metabolism?
plan: Hormonal regulation: hypothalamus (liberins/statins) → pituitary (tropic hormones) → peripheral glands; negative feedback; hormones act through receptors (membrane or nuclear).
Thyroid gland: TRH → TSH → synthesis of T4 and T3 (iodine, thyroid peroxidase); T4 is deiodinated to active T3 in the tissues; in the blood mostly bound to proteins, the free fraction is active.

Effects on metabolism: raise basal metabolic rate and oxygen consumption (Na/K-ATPase, heat production), stimulate carbohydrate metabolism and protein anabolism, affect lipolysis and cholesterol metabolism; necessary for growth and development.
Laboratory: TSH is the first-line test; if TSH is altered, free T4 (distinguishing subclinical and overt hypo-/hyperthyroidism), free T3 if needed; anti-TPO – autoimmune cause.

Clinical reflection: in hypothyroidism basal metabolism is reduced (weight gain, cold intolerance, raised cholesterol), in hyperthyroidism the opposite (weight loss, tachycardia); subclinical hypothyroidism – TSH high, free T4 normal.
Gout is the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and tissues; underlying it is prolonged hyperuricemia.

Definitive diagnosis: finding MSU crystals in synovial fluid or a tophus on polarized-light microscopy (needle-shaped crystals) – the "gold standard"; this is a sufficient criterion in the ACR/EULAR 2015 criteria.
Serum uric acid: supports the diagnosis but does not make it alone – it may be normal during an attack, and hyperuricemia occurs without gout; measured when not on urate-lowering therapy.
Synovial fluid analysis: leukocytes raised (inflammation), Gram stain and culture to exclude septic arthritis; differentiation from calcium pyrophosphate crystals (pseudogout).
Additional: creatinine/eGFR, urinary urate excretion and urinary stones, metabolic syndrome parameters (glucose, lipids).

kdl-o-114.q: Modern concept of hemostasis. The hemostatic system in the norm?
plan: Hemostasis is the balance of the systems that stop bleeding and keep blood fluid: the vessel wall (endothelium), platelets, coagulation factors, anticoagulants and fibrinolysis.

Primary (vascular-platelet) hemostasis: vasoconstriction, adhesion of platelets to the subendothelium via vWF (GPIb), activation (release of ADP, thromboxane A2) and aggregation via fibrinogen (GPIIb/IIIa) – the platelet plug.

Secondary (coagulation) hemostasis – the modern cell-based model: initiation (the tissue factor–VIIa complex generates a small amount of thrombin), amplification (thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII, XI), propagation (a lot of thrombin on the surface of the activated platelet) → fibrin, stabilized by XIIIa.

Natural anticoagulants: antithrombin (neutralizes IIa, Xa, IXa; heparin potentiates it), the protein C/protein S system (inactivates Va and VIIIa; activated with thrombomodulin), TFPI (inhibits TF–VIIa/Xa).
Fibrinolysis: tPA and urokinase convert plasminogen to plasmin, plasmin degrades fibrin (D-dimer is formed); PAI-1 and α2-antiplasmin limit it.
The classical "cascade" (extrinsic and intrinsic pathway) is retained to explain laboratory tests: PT – extrinsic and common pathway, aPTT – intrinsic and common pathway.

kdl-o-115.q: Disorders of the hemostatic system. Hypo- and hypercoagulation. DIC?
plan: Causes of hypocoagulation (bleeding): thrombocytopenia and platelet function disorders, von Willebrand disease, hemophilias (VIII, IX), vitamin K deficiency and warfarin, liver diseases, DIC, anticoagulants.

Hypercoagulation/thrombophilia: inherited (antithrombin, protein C/S deficiency, factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation) and acquired (antiphospholipid syndrome, tumors, pregnancy, estrogens, immobilization, surgery).

DIC is systemic activation of coagulation (sepsis, trauma, obstetric complications, tumors, APL): microthrombi and bleeding due to consumption of factors/platelets; stages – hypercoagulation, transition, hypocoagulation (consumption coagulopathy).

Laboratory signs of DIC: falling platelets (over time), sharp rise of D-dimer/fibrin markers, prolonged PT, decreased fibrinogen, schistocytes on the smear; overt DIC by the ISTH score ≥5 (platelets, fibrin marker, PT, fibrinogen).
Screening tests: platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen (Clauss), thrombin time, D-dimer; if needed factor activities, mixing test, vWF, lupus anticoagulant.

pitfalls.wrong: most of the answer to the question on "disorders of hemostasis" is about "homeostasis" (constancy of the internal environment)
pitfalls.right: the question is about disorders of hemostasis (blood clotting and its inhibition) – hypo-/hypercoagulation, DIC

cutoffs.value: ≥5 points: platelets, D-dimer (fibrin marker), prolonged PT/INR, fibrinogen <1 g/L

plan: Primary hemostasis: platelet count, smear (morphology, clumps), platelet function – light transmission aggregometry (gold standard), PFA-100/200; vWF antigen and activity; bleeding time – insensitive, abolished in many places.
Coagulation screening: PT (extrinsic and common pathway; reported as INR), aPTT (intrinsic and common pathway), fibrinogen (Clauss method), thrombin time.
Clarifying tests: activity of individual factors (VIII, IX, XI, etc.), mixing test (deficiency or inhibitor), lupus anticoagulant, factor XIII.
Tests for anticoagulants and thrombophilia: antithrombin, protein C, protein S, activated protein C resistance, genetic tests (factor V Leiden, prothrombin).
Fibrinolysis: D-dimer (excluding VTE, DIC), fibrinogen and fibrin degradation products; global tests – thromboelastography/thromboelastometry, thrombin generation assay.
Correct preanalytics (3.2% citrate, 9:1, room temperature) is mandatory for all tests.

Vitamin K antagonists (warfarin): monitored by PT/INR; INR = (patient PT / normal PT)^ISI – eliminates differences in thromboplastin sensitivity; target in most indications 2–3, in a mechanical mitral valve 2.5–3.5.

Unfractionated heparin: aPTT (usually 1.5–2.2 times prolongation from baseline) or anti-Xa activity (more accurate, aPTT is sensitive to the effect of factors and the acute phase); at high doses the activated clotting time.
Low-molecular-weight heparins: monitoring is usually not required; in renal failure, obesity, pregnancy, children – anti-Xa.
Direct oral anticoagulants: no routine monitoring; when needed a specially calibrated anti-Xa or diluted thrombin time; PT/aPTT do not reliably reflect their effect.
With all anticoagulants: platelets (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia), Hb, kidney and liver function; take preanalytics and sample timing into account.

pitfalls.right: in these conditions PT is prolonged, so the prothrombin index (normal PT/patient PT) falls; anticoagulant monitoring by INR (INR = (patient PT/control PT)^ISI)

pitfalls.right: laboratory monitoring: warfarin – INR (2.0–3.0 in most), UFH – aPTT (1.5–2.2×) or anti-Xa, LMWH – anti-Xa

plan: Distinguishing types of allergy: IgE-mediated (type I) and non-IgE-mediated reactions; laboratory tests are interpreted together with the history.
General laboratory signs: eosinophils in blood and in nasal smear/sputum; total IgE – nonspecific (also raised in helminthiasis), a normal value does not exclude allergy.
Specific IgE (in vitro immunoassay) shows sensitization to an allergen; sensitization does not always mean clinical allergy.
Skin prick test: read at 15–20 minutes, a wheal ≥3 mm larger than the negative control is positive; histamine – positive control; antihistamines make the result falsely negative.
Additional: component-resolved diagnostics, provocation tests (under specialist supervision), tryptase in anaphylaxis; compare with clinical data in interpretation.

cutoffs.value: wheal at 15–20 minutes ≥3 mm larger than the negative control

plan: The vagina and the vaginal portion of the cervix are covered with stratified squamous (non-keratinizing) epithelium: basal/parabasal, intermediate and superficial layers.

Cells: parabasal (small, round, nucleus relatively large), intermediate (polygonal, vesicular nucleus – the yardstick for nuclear size), superficial (large polygonal, pyknotic nucleus – shed under the influence of estrogen).

Hormonal influence: estrogen (follicular phase) matures the epithelium up to the superficial layer and leads to glycogen accumulation; progesterone arrests maturation at the intermediate layer (luteal phase, pregnancy); in estrogen deficiency (menopause) – first intermediate, then predominance of parabasal cells (atrophy).
Function: protective barrier; glycogen is the substrate for lactobacilli, and lactic acid maintains the acidic environment.

Laboratory significance: approximate assessment of the hormonal background and atrophy on cytological smears, distinguishing reactive changes from precancerous lesions; in inflammation, hormonal assessment is unreliable.

kdl-o-120.q: Microscopic examination of vaginal discharge. Staining smears by Gram, Romanowsky and methylene blue?
plan: Material: with a speculum from the posterior fornix and lateral walls of the vagina, separately from the cervical canal and urethra; wet mount (in physiological saline – motility of trichomonads, "clue" cells) and 10% KOH (fungal hyphae/buds, "whiff" amine odor test), pH measurement.

Gram staining: lactobacilli (gram-positive rods), Gardnerella/anaerobic morphotypes, "clue" cells – the Nugent score for BV (0–3 normal, 4–6 intermediate, 7–10 BV); gonococci – intracellular gram-negative diplococci in leukocytes (low sensitivity in women – NAAT needed).

Romanowsky staining: cellular composition (leukocytes, epithelium), trichomonads (nucleus and flagella), fungi; methylene blue – rapid tentative staining (leukocytes, "clue" cells, diplococci), gives no Gram characteristics.
Parameters evaluated: leukocyte count (inflammation), type and number of epithelial cells, "clue" cells, type and amount of flora, fungi, trichomonads, diplococci.

Limitations of microscopy: in trichomoniasis the sensitivity of a wet mount is ~44–68%, in Candida the culture method is more sensitive; negative microscopy does not exclude infection – NAAT or culture.

cutoffs.value: ≥3 of 4: homogeneous thin discharge, "clue" cells, vaginal pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH
0–3 lactobacilli predominate; 4–6 intermediate; 7–10 BV

plan: "Vaginal dysbacteriosis" – in modern terminology mainly bacterial vaginosis (BV): replacement of lactobacilli by anaerobic bacteria (Gardnerella, etc.).
Clinical-laboratory Amsel criteria (3 of 4): homogeneous thin discharge; pH >4.5; fishy odor on adding KOH ("whiff" test); "clue" cells on microscopy.
Laboratory reference method – the Nugent score on a Gram-stained smear: 0–3 – lactobacilli predominate (normal), 4–6 – intermediate flora, 7–10 – BV.
Molecular tests: BV NAAT/multiplex PCR panels (only in symptomatic women); culture for Gardnerella is not recommended (it occurs in healthy women as well).
Differential: candidiasis (fungi in KOH, normal pH), trichomoniasis (NAAT), aerobic vaginitis, cytolytic vaginosis; exclude mixed infections.

cutoffs.value: ≥3 of 4: homogeneous thin discharge, "clue" cells, vaginal pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH
0–3 lactobacilli predominate; 4–6 intermediate; 7–10 BV

kdl-o-122.q: Variants of presentation of vaginal dysbacteriosis?
plan: Normal (lactobacilli-predominant) flora: Nugent 0–3, pH ≤4.5, few leukocytes.
Bacterial vaginosis: loss of lactobacilli, predominance of anaerobes/Gardnerella, "clue" cells, pH >4.5, "whiff" odor, usually without inflammation (few leukocytes); Nugent 7–10.
Intermediate flora: Nugent 4–6 – lactobacilli reduced, Gardnerella morphotypes have appeared.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis: fungal elements (budding cells, pseudomycelium), pH usually normal; trichomoniasis: trichomonads, many leukocytes, raised pH – microscopy has low sensitivity, NAAT preferred.
Other variants: cytolytic vaginosis (excess lactobacilli, cytolysis), atrophic state (parabasal cells, little flora), leptothrix (long filamentous bacteria – usually not pathogenic).

cutoffs.value: ≥3 of 4: homogeneous thin discharge, "clue" cells, vaginal pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH

plan: BV is vaginal dysbiosis: replacement of hydrogen peroxide- and lactic acid-producing lactobacilli by anaerobic bacteria.
Clinical diagnosis – at least 3 of the Amsel criteria: homogeneous thin discharge, pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH, "clue" cells (epithelium covered with bacteria).
Laboratory reference method – Gram staining and the Nugent score (7–10 – BV).
Molecular tests: FDA-approved BV NAATs (for example multi-component PCR panels) – only in symptomatic women; the Pap test is not for diagnosing BV.
Culture for Gardnerella is not diagnostic; test for accompanying STIs (trichomoniasis, chlamydia, gonorrhea).

cutoffs.value: ≥3 of 4: homogeneous thin discharge, "clue" cells, vaginal pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH
0–3 lactobacilli predominate; 4–6 intermediate; 7–10 BV

plan: "Leptothrix" refers to very long, thin, filamentous bacteria seen in vaginal smears; much longer and thinner than lactobacilli, arranged in rings, as a "hair ball" or "spaghetti".
Often considered a morphotype of the genus Lactobacillus; usually not pathogenic (an "innocent bystander").
Seen in Papanicolaou- and Gram-stained smears; must be distinguished from long forms of lactobacilli and fungal pseudomycelium.

Clinical association: in one study found in ~2.8% of symptomatic women, most with normal flora; more often associated with candidiasis, less often with BV and cytolytic vaginosis; association with trichomoniasis was not confirmed.
Conclusion: it is described, but alone is not an indication for treatment; test for accompanying infections (candidiasis, etc.).

pitfalls.right: leptothrix – very long filamentous bacteria in vaginal smears (often a Lactobacillus morphotype), usually not pathogenic

plan: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular parasite (elementary and reticulate bodies); often asymptomatic; in women cervicitis, urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility; in men urethritis, epididymitis.

The main diagnostic method is NAAT (PCR, etc.): the most sensitive and recommended; in women a vaginal swab (self-collected is equivalent), in men first-void urine; rectal/pharyngeal specimens as indicated.

Other methods: cell culture (forensic cases, resistance), direct immunofluorescence and immunochromatographic rapid tests – low sensitivity; serology (IgG/IgA) – not recommended for diagnosing urogenital infection.
Test together with gonorrhea (many NAATs detect both at once); after treatment test for reinfection (after 3 months).
Cytological method (inclusions) – historical, low sensitivity.

kdl-o-126.q: Normal vaginal microflora and its disorders?
plan: In women of reproductive age the normal vaginal microflora is dominated by lactobacilli (Lactobacillus spp.): they produce lactic acid (and hydrogen peroxide) from glycogen, maintain an acidic environment (pH usually ≤4.5) and inhibit pathogens.
Estrogen provides epithelial maturation and glycogen accumulation – the substrate for lactobacilli; in menopause and estrogen deficiency the flora decreases and pH rises.
Disorders: bacterial vaginosis (lactobacilli replaced by anaerobes; Nugent 7–10, pH >4.5), candidiasis, trichomoniasis, aerobic vaginitis, cytolytic vaginosis.
Assessment: pH, "whiff" test with KOH, wet mount and Gram-stained smear (Nugent score), NAAT if needed.
Factors worsening the disorder: antibiotics, douching, multiple sexual partners, hormonal changes.

pitfalls.wrong: to the question on "normal vaginal microflora", a text about intestinal dysbacteriosis
pitfalls.right: normal vaginal flora – predominance of lactobacilli, pH ≤4.5; disorders – BV (Amsel, Nugent 7–10), candidiasis, trichomoniasis

cutoffs.value: ≥3 of 4: homogeneous thin discharge, "clue" cells, vaginal pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH

plan: TORCH is a group of infections dangerous to the fetus and newborn in pregnancy: Toxoplasmosis, "Other" (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, Zika, etc.), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex.

Most dangerous is primary infection during pregnancy (especially rubella – in the first trimester; toxoplasmosis); but 50–75% of congenital CMV occurs in mothers infected before pregnancy (reactivation/reinfection).
Consequences: fetal death, congenital malformations (congenital rubella syndrome), hearing loss (CMV), eye and CNS damage (toxoplasmosis, CMV), neonatal herpes.
Routes of transmission: transplacental, through the birth canal, after birth (breast milk – CMV).
Prevention: rubella vaccination (check immunity before pregnancy), hygiene measures (CMV, toxoplasmosis), screening and targeted testing.

Serology (ELISA/chemiluminescent): IgG and IgM; IgM alone is not a diagnosis – it persists for months, cross-reactivity and rheumatoid factor give false positives; a large share of positive TORCH IgM results are not confirmed.
IgG avidity: low avidity – recent (primary) infection, high – old infection; in toxoplasmosis and CMV interpret with gestational age in mind; confirmation in a reference laboratory.

Molecular methods: PCR in amniotic fluid (fetal toxoplasmosis, CMV); in a newborn congenital CMV – PCR in saliva or urine (in the first 2–3 weeks of life; later it cannot be distinguished from postnatal infection), urine for confirmation; IgG/IgM do not confirm congenital CMV.
Rubella: serology and PCR (nasopharynx, throat, urine); herpes: PCR from lesions.
Dynamics in paired sera (seroconversion) and pre-pregnancy screening results make interpretation easier.

kdl-o-129.q: Etiology and pathogenesis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis?
plan: The causative agent of gonorrhea is Neisseria gonorrhoeae: gram-negative, bean-shaped diplococcus, located inside leukocytes; transmitted mainly sexually, at birth to the newborn (conjunctivitis).

Pathogenesis: attachment to columnar epithelium (urethra, cervical canal, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva) via pili and membrane proteins, invasion, purulent inflammation; often asymptomatic in women, complications – pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, dissemination.
The causative agent of trichomoniasis is Trichomonas vaginalis: a pear-shaped, flagellated, motile unicellular parasite; transmitted sexually.

Pathogenesis of trichomoniasis: attachment to the epithelium of the vagina and urethra and cytotoxic effect, inflammation (many leukocytes), rise in pH; often asymptomatic in men; pregnancy complications, increases the risk of HIV transmission.
Both infections may coexist with other STIs – comprehensive testing.

Gonorrhea: NAAT is the main method (vaginal swab in women, first-void urine in men; extragenital sites); in men with symptomatic urethritis, intracellular diplococci in leukocytes on a Gram or methylene blue smear – a presumptive diagnosis (low sensitivity in women).
Gonococcal culture on selective media – to determine antibiotic susceptibility (in treatment failure), confirmation by two methods.
Trichomoniasis: NAAT – highly sensitive; wet mount (sensitivity 44–68%, falls sharply after 1 hour – examine immediately), culture (InPouch) – for resistance; the PAP test is not diagnostic.
In stained smears (Romanowsky) the shape and nucleus of trichomonads are seen, but motility is not.
In both infections also test for chlamydia, syphilis, HIV; retest after treatment.
Leishmaniasis: causative agent – Leishmania (amastigotes inside macrophages in humans, promastigotes in the vector); vector – sandflies.
Clinical forms: cutaneous, mucocutaneous and visceral (kala-azar); source – animals (dogs, rodents) or humans (depends on species and region).
Spirochetoses: leptospirosis – enters through water/soil contaminated with urine of rodents and animals, through skin and mucous membranes.
Relapsing fever (Borrelia) – via ticks or lice; fever attacks are linked to antigenic variation.
Link of pathogenesis to the laboratory: leptospires in blood in the first week, then in urine; borreliae in blood during fever – the sampling time is chosen accordingly.
kdl-o-131.note: The source on antigenic variation and vectors of relapsing fever was checked in part.

plan: Leishmaniasis: smear/biopsy from the edge of a skin ulcer, in the visceral form material from bone marrow, spleen or lymph node; on Giemsa staining amastigotes (1–5 µm, nucleus and kinetoplast).
Additionally for leishmaniasis: culture (promastigotes), PCR (species identification), rK39 serology in the visceral form.
Leptospirosis: in week 1 PCR in blood (and CSF), then in urine; serology – MAT (reference), IgM ELISA; rising titer in paired sera.
Relapsing fever: thick and thin blood smear (Giemsa/Wright) taken during a fever attack – spirochetes; they may not be found in the afebrile period.
Safety and quality: PPE when handling material, positive control slides, confirmation in a reference laboratory.
Causative agents: Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi; vector – the female Anopheles mosquito.
Life cycle: sporozoites – liver stage (hypnozoites in P. vivax/ovale – relapses), then the erythrocytic cycle and gametocytes.
Pathogenesis: destruction of erythrocytes – fever attacks and anemia; in P. falciparum cytoadherence – severe malaria (brain, kidney).
Epidemiology: tropical regions, imported cases; transfusion and vertical transmission are rare.
When suspected (travel history + fever) – urgent laboratory testing.
kdl-o-133.note: Epidemiological details only according to the CDC DPDx page.

plan: Microscopy is the main method: thick smear (finding the parasite, sensitivity) and thin smear (species identification); Giemsa staining.

Calculating parasitemia (WHO MM-SOP-09): in a thick smear parasites/µL = parasites counted × 8000 / leukocytes counted (if the actual leukocyte count is unavailable, 8000/µL is assumed); if there are ≥100 parasites per field, the proportion (%) of infected erythrocytes is calculated on the thin smear.
If negative, repeat smears at 12–24 hour intervals (3 series in total).
Rapid tests (RDT, antigens) – where microscopy is not available; confirm the result by microscopy and quantify.
PCR – for species identification and low parasitemia; serology is not for acute diagnosis.
Quality: qualification of microscopists, standard stain pH, external quality assessment.

cutoffs.value: negative smears every 12–24 hours, 3 series in total

kdl-o-135.q: Biology, morphology, laboratory diagnosis of roundworms?
plan: Nematodes are separate-sexed cylindrical worms: Ascaris, pinworm (Enterobius), whipworm (Trichuris), hookworms, Strongyloides, Trichinella.
Differences in life cycles: geohelminths (Ascaris, whipworm – egg matures in soil), contact (pinworm – autoinfection), through the skin (hookworm, Strongyloides larvae).
Laboratory: eggs in stool (wet mount, enrichment – formalin-ethyl acetate), Kato-Katz – quantitative; in enterobiasis the perianal cellophane tape test.
Morphology: Ascaris egg (fertilized/unfertilized, bumpy shell), whipworm – barrel-shaped, two polar plugs, pinworm – flattened on one side.
Additional: in strongyloidiasis methods for detecting larvae, in trichinellosis serology and muscle biopsy; eosinophilia.
kdl-o-135.note: Separate DPDx pages on Strongyloides and Trichinella were not checked.

plan: Macroscopy: adult worms passed in stool or vomit (Ascaris – large, pinkish-white), pinworms in the perianal region; rinse the worm with water and view it on a dark background.
Microscopy: wet mount and enrichment (formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation), flotation; Kato-Katz for quantitation.
Ascaris eggs: fertilized – oval, thick mammillated shell; unfertilized – elongated, sink on flotation.

Whipworm egg: 50–55×20–25 µm, barrel-shaped, two polar plugs; pinworm egg: 50–60×20–30 µm, flattened on one side, tape test in the morning before washing (once – ~50%, 3 days in a row – ~90% sensitivity).
Recording the result: species, stage (egg/larva/adult), and if needed intensity (eggs/g).

kdl-o-137.q: Biology, morphology, laboratory diagnosis of tapeworms?
plan: Cestodes are tape-like hermaphroditic worms: scolex, neck, proglottids (strobila); no intestinal cavity.

Main species: Taenia saginata (cattle), T. solium (pig; risk of cysticercosis if eggs are ingested), Hymenolepis nana (may be transmitted without an intermediate host), Diphyllobothrium, Echinococcus (humans are an intermediate host).
Laboratory: eggs in stool (Taenia eggs 30–35 µm, radially striated, T. solium and T. saginata cannot be distinguished), examination of proglottids.
Species identification: number of uterine branches in the proglottid, structure of the scolex; molecular methods.
In echinococcosis and cysticercosis – imaging and serology; taeniid eggs may be infectious – precautions.
kdl-o-137.note: A separate source on echinococcosis and diphyllobothriasis was not checked.

plan: Macroscopy: proglottids passed in stool – press between two glass slides and count the uterine branches (more in T. saginata, fewer in T. solium).
Scolex: T. solium – with hooklets (armed), T. saginata – without hooklets; Hymenolepis is small.
Microscopy: eggs in stool (wet mount, enrichment); Taenia eggs 30–35 µm, with a thick radially striated embryophore, inside an oncosphere with 6 hooklets.
Hymenolepis nana egg – thin-shelled, with filaments at the poles; H. diminuta – larger, without filaments.
Caution: T. solium proglottids and eggs are infectious to humans – gloves, decontamination.

kdl-o-139.q: Biology, morphology, laboratory diagnosis of flukes?
plan: Trematodes (flukes) are flat, leaf-shaped worms with two suckers; most are hermaphrodites (schistosomes are separate-sexed).

Life cycle: intermediate host – mollusks (in some, a second intermediate host – fish or plant); humans are infected by raw fish (Opisthorchis), water plants (Fasciola) or through the skin (Schistosoma).
Main species: Opisthorchis/Clonorchis (bile ducts), Fasciola (liver), Schistosoma (blood vessels), Paragonimus (lung).
Laboratory: eggs in stool (or bile) – the Opisthorchis egg is small (19–30×10–20 µm), with an operculum; in schistosomiasis eggs in stool/urine, serology.
Enrichment methods (formalin-ethyl acetate), repeat examination; eosinophilia.

pitfalls.right: whipworm (Trichuris) and hookworms are nematodes; trematodes include Opisthorchis/Clonorchis, Fasciola, Schistosoma

kdl-o-139.note: Separate DPDx pages on Fasciola and Paragonimus were not checked.

plan: Macroscopy: adult trematodes are rarely found in stool (after treatment or in surgical material); leaf-shaped body, two suckers.
Microscopy: eggs in stool or duodenal/bile fluid; enrichment (formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation) is more sensitive.
Opisthorchis/Clonorchis egg: 19–30×10–20 µm, operculum (lid) and "shoulders", a knob at the opposite end.
Schistosoma eggs: large, spined (lateral or terminal), in stool or urine; Fasciola egg – large, with an operculum.
One negative result is not sufficient – repeat examination; state the species and stage in the result.
kdl-o-140.note: The dimensions of the Fasciola egg were not checked, therefore no figure is given.

kdl-o-141.q: Biology, morphology, laboratory diagnosis of protozoa?
plan: Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotes; groups: amoebae, flagellates (Giardia, Trichomonas, Leishmania), ciliates (Balantidium), sporozoa/apicomplexa (Plasmodium, Toxoplasma, Cryptosporidium).
Life forms: trophozoite (vegetative, motile) and cyst/oocyst (resistant, infectious); trophozoites in liquid stool, more cysts in formed stool.
Diagnosis of intestinal protozoa: wet mount of fresh stool (motile trophozoites), cysts with Lugol, permanently stained preparation (trichrome), enrichment.
Antigen tests and PCR: giardiasis (antigen test), amebiasis (distinguishing E. histolytica from E. dispar), cryptosporidiosis.
Blood and tissue protozoa: malaria (thick/thin smear), leishmaniasis (amastigotes), toxoplasmosis (serology, PCR).
At least 3 stool specimens, preserved with a fixative.
Material: stool (fresh or fixed), blood, tissue aspirates, urogenital smears – depending on the parasite.

Stool: wet mount in physiological saline – motility of trophozoites (within 30 minutes), Lugol – cyst nuclei, permanently stained preparation (trichrome) – species identification; formalin-ethyl acetate enrichment.
Special stains: modified acid-fast stain for Cryptosporidium and Cyclospora.
Blood: thick/thin smear, Giemsa (Plasmodium, trypanosomes); tissue: Leishmania amastigotes.
Limitations of microscopy: E. histolytica/dispar cannot be distinguished; if sensitivity is low – antigen or PCR tests.
Quality: measuring with a calibrated ocular micrometer, positive control slides.
kdl-o-142.note: A separate DPDx page on acid-fast staining was not checked.

kdl-o-143.q: Diagnosis and differential diagnosis of dysentery amoeba?
plan: Amebiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica; intestinal (dysentery, colitis) and extraintestinal (liver abscess) forms.

Microscopy: in fresh stool or intestinal mucosal material, a trophozoite with phagocytosed erythrocytes is characteristic of E. histolytica; cysts (4 nuclei) are morphologically indistinguishable from E. dispar/moshkovskii.
Definitive diagnosis: stool antigen test or PCR (distinguishes E. histolytica); in liver abscess serology and imaging.

Differential diagnosis: bacterial dysentery (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter – culture), balantidiasis, inflammatory bowel diseases (calprotectin, endoscopy), non-pathogenic amoebae (E. coli, E. hartmanni).
At least 3 stool specimens; do not mistake macrophages for amoebae.
kdl-o-143.note: A separate source on bacterial dysentery and balantidiasis was not checked.

kdl-o-144.q: Etiopathogenesis and laboratory diagnosis of COVID-19?
plan: Etiology: SARS-CoV-2 is a betacoronavirus with single-stranded RNA; it enters the cell via the spike protein through the ACE2 receptor.
Pathogenesis: replication in the upper respiratory tract, in severe cases pneumonia, inflammation and coagulopathy.
Diagnosis of current infection: NAAT (RT-PCR) is the most sensitive; antigen tests are fast but less sensitive, if negative repeat after 48 hours.
Antibody tests are not for diagnosing current infection but for past infection/epidemiology.
For severity and prognosis – general laboratory parameters (lymphopenia, CRP, D-dimer, etc.) together with clinical assessment.
kdl-o-144.note: Details of pathogenesis (ACE2) were not checked against a separate source.

kdl-o-145.q: Methods of laboratory diagnosis of COVID-19, their advantages and disadvantages, rules for obtaining biomaterial for testing?
plan: Methods: NAAT (RT-PCR, isothermal amplification) – high sensitivity, requires a laboratory and time; antigen tests – fast, on site, lower sensitivity; antibody tests – not for current infection.
Biomaterial: upper respiratory tract (nasopharyngeal, nasal, oropharyngeal swab, saliva – according to the test authorization); in severe disease the lower respiratory tract.
Collection rules: PPE, a synthetic-tipped swab (per instructions), viral transport medium, correct labeling, rapid delivery and the cold chain.
Interpretation: serially repeat a negative antigen test (48 hours), compare with symptoms and contact; PCR positivity may persist for a long time.
Quality and safety: internal controls, prevention of contamination, handling specimens according to their biosafety level.

pitfalls.wrong: PCR detects "COVID-19 DNA"
pitfalls.right: SARS-CoV-2 is an RNA virus; NAAT detects genes of viral RNA (RT-PCR)

plan: PCR is a method of amplifying a specific segment of nucleic acid in vitro: template DNA, two primers, dNTPs, a thermostable polymerase (Taq).
Cycle: denaturation (~95 °C), primer annealing (~50–65 °C), elongation; the product doubles each cycle, a plateau after 30–40 cycles.
Types: conventional (detection by electrophoresis), real-time (qPCR – fluorescent dye or probe), RT-PCR (for RNA).
Clinical use: detecting infectious agents and measuring viral load, genetic mutations, tumor markers, tissue typing, forensic medicine.
Limitations: contamination (false positives), inhibitors (false negatives), primer-dimers; controls and separation of work areas are necessary.

kdl-o-147.q: Differential diagnosis of transudates and exudates?
plan: Distinguishing transudate from exudate – Light's criteria: fluid/serum protein >0.5; fluid/serum LDH >0.6; fluid LDH > 2/3 of serum LDH ULN – if at least one is met, it is an exudate.
Transudate: clear, pale yellow, low protein, few cells; causes – heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia.
Exudate: turbid, cellular, high protein and LDH; causes – infection (parapneumonic, empyema, tuberculosis), tumors, pancreatitis, autoimmune diseases, pulmonary embolism.

Light's criteria wrongly classify 15–30% of transudates as exudates (up to a third in heart failure or cirrhosis on diuretics) – in that case the serum–fluid albumin/protein gradient is more specific; NT-proBNP and additional criteria (cholesterol) are also used.
In ascites the serum–ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is used; the cause of an exudate is determined by the cell differential, glucose, pH, amylase, culture and cytology.

cutoffs.value: fluid/serum protein >0.5 or LDH ratio >0.6 or fluid LDH > 2/3 of serum ULN

plan: Phospholipids are amphipathic lipids: a backbone of glycerol (glycerophospholipids) or sphingosine (sphingomyelin), two fatty acid "tails" and a polar "head" containing phosphate.
Main representatives: phosphatidylcholine (lecithin), phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol, cardiolipin, sphingomyelin.

Functions: basis of the bilayer of cell membranes; signal transduction (phosphatidylinositol derivatives, source of arachidonic acid for eicosanoids); surface of lipoproteins; dissolving cholesterol in bile; lung surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine).
Role in hemostasis: phosphatidylserine on the surface of activated platelets is the procoagulant surface for coagulation factor complexes.
Laboratory aspect: antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin) – a cause of thrombosis; disturbance of membrane lipids changes erythrocyte shape.
Jaundice is a rise of bilirubin in the blood and staining of tissues; three main types: prehepatic (hemolytic), hepatic (parenchymal), posthepatic (mechanical, obstructive).
Hemolytic: indirect bilirubin raised, no bilirubin in urine, urobilinogen raised, dark stool; signs of hemolysis – reticulocytosis, LDH↑, haptoglobin↓; ALT/AST usually normal.
Parenchymal: both fractions raised, ALT/AST sharply raised (hepatocellular pattern), bilirubin present in urine; in severe cases albumin low, PT/INR prolonged.

Mechanical: mainly direct bilirubin, ALP and GGT disproportionately raised (cholestatic pattern), urine dark (bilirubin), urobilinogen reduced/absent, stool pale; imaging (ultrasound) shows the cause.
Inherited hyperbilirubinemias: Gilbert, Crigler–Najjar (conjugation defect – indirect), Dubin–Johnson and Rotor (direct).
