kdl-o-150.q: General rules for quality control of clinical laboratory tests?
plan: The quality assurance system covers the entire testing process (pre-pre → preanalytical → analytical → postanalytical → post-post); the standard is ISO 15189:2022.

Internal quality control: in each run (at least daily) control materials at two or more levels, Levey–Jennings charts and Westgard rules; if a run is not accepted, patient results are not released, the cause is found, corrected and recorded.
External quality assessment (interlaboratory comparison, PT) – regular participation, analysis of results and corrective actions.
Equipment and reagents: calibration, preventive maintenance, temperature control, checking reagent lots and expiry; method verification/validation.
Staff competence, SOPs, documentation and traceability; quality indicators (specimen rejection, turnaround time, critical value notifications) and internal audits.

cutoffs.value: x̄ and SD from at least 20 measurements on different days
1-2s – warning; 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s (within run), 4-1s, 10x – rejection

kdl-o-151.q: Quality of laboratory tests and the factors affecting it?
plan: The quality of a laboratory result is its fitness for a clinical decision: trueness (absence of systematic error), precision/repeatability (small random error), timely release, correct interpretation.
Preanalytical factors (more than half of errors): incorrect ordering, patient preparation, identification errors, wrong tube, hemolysis, clot, low volume, transport and storage.

Analytical factors: calibration, reagent quality and expiry, instrument malfunction, interferences (hemolysis, lipemia, bilirubin, drugs), staff qualification; detected by internal and external control.
Postanalytical factors: incorrect entry/transmission of the result, wrong unit or reference interval, failure to report a critical value, delay.
Biological factors: age, sex, circadian rhythm, pregnancy, diet, physical exertion – taken into account in reference intervals and interpretation.

kdl-o-152.q: Principles of quality control of clinical laboratory tests?
plan: Basic principles: control applies to the entire testing process, is regular and documented, statistically based, and aimed at preventing and correcting errors (continuous improvement).
Control materials should have a matrix similar to the patient sample, concentrations close to clinical decision levels, and be independent of the calibrator.
Statistical control: the mean (x̄), standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation (CV%) are determined; acceptance/rejection of a run by the Levey–Jennings chart and Westgard multirules.
External control assesses trueness (bias); method performance is compared with quality requirements.
For each nonconformity – corrective and preventive actions, records and staff training (ISO 15189).

Intralaboratory (internal) quality control: daily/per run with control materials, results are plotted on a Levey–Jennings chart and evaluated by Westgard rules – detects repeatability and short-term systematic shifts.

Interlaboratory control (external quality assessment, PT): the organizer sends identical "blind" samples, the laboratory analyzes them routinely, results are compared with the reference/peer group mean (z-score, % deviation).
External assessment shows trueness (bias) and agreement between methods and laboratories; an unsatisfactory result – root cause analysis and corrective actions.
Under ISO 15189:2022 participation in internal control and external assessment is mandatory; for tests without a PT program – alternative comparison (exchanging samples with another laboratory).
For morphological examinations (blood, cytological smears) external assessment is via images or "unknown" smears.

kdl-o-154.q: The importance of the preanalytical stage in ensuring the quality of clinical laboratory tests (permissible errors and their prevention)?
plan: The preanalytical stage is the main source of errors: in different studies ~50–70% of errors (for example 62% preanalytical, 15% analytical, 23% postanalytical).

Typical errors: ordering a wrong or unnecessary test, errors in patient identification and labeling, lack of patient preparation (fasting, drugs), wrong tube or order of draw, underfilling (citrate), hemolysis, clot, EDTA contamination, prolonged tourniquet, incorrect transport/storage, delay.
Prevention: SOPs and written instructions, staff training (phlebotomy), barcode and electronic identification, specimen acceptance criteria and rejection rules.
Monitoring: preanalytical quality indicators (% rejected specimens, % hemolysis, incorrect labeling), hemolysis/lipemia/icterus indices.
Cooperation with clinical departments and feedback; reporting and analysis of errors.

kdl-o-155.q: Constructing and using a control chart?
plan: Preparation: a stable control material is chosen; if there is no prior data, each level is measured at least 20 times on different days, and the mean (x̄) and SD are calculated; CV% = SD/x̄ × 100.
Chart: horizontal axis – date/run, vertical – concentration; center line x̄, control limits ±1s, ±2s, ±3s.
Use: in each run the control result is plotted on the chart and evaluated by Westgard rules: 1-2s – warning; 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s (within run), 4-1s, 10x – rejection.
Interpretation: a single point beyond ±3s or large scatter – more often random error; a sequential shift to one side (2-2s, 4-1s, 10x) – systematic error (calibration, reagent, instrument).
In a rejected run patient results are not released; the cause is found, corrected, and the test repeated; with a new control lot x̄ and SD are re-established; all actions are documented.

cutoffs.value: x̄ and SD from at least 20 measurements on different days
1-2s – warning; 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s (within run), 4-1s, 10x – rejection

kdl-o-156.q: The role of external quality control by examining unknown blood smears?
plan: External quality assessment for morphological examinations (blood smear): the organizer sends "unknown" smears of known diagnosis or digital images.
The laboratory evaluates the smear routinely: differential, cell morphology (blasts, atypical lymphocytes, dysplasia), erythrocyte shape, inclusions and parasites.
Results are compared with the expert answer and other participants – inter-observer agreement and clinically significant errors are identified.
Significance: testing specialist competence that cannot be replaced by automation, harmonizing terminology, training and corrective actions.
Under ISO 15189 participation in external assessment and analysis of results are mandatory; internal "blind" rereading is also used.

kdl-o-157.q: The role of the postanalytical stage in internal quality control?
plan: Postanalytical stage: checking the result (technical and clinical validation), forming the report, transmission, interpretation and archiving.

Elements of internal control: authorize a run only after control is accepted; delta check (comparison with the previous result), logical consistency (for example MCHC, anion gap), critical limits of results.
Report: correct units and reference intervals, comments (hemolysis and other interferences), patient identification and times.
Critical values – report immediately to the physician in the established manner and record; monitoring turnaround time (TAT).
Postanalytical errors (incorrect entry, transmission, interpretation) are tracked through quality indicators; specimen retention (for retesting) and confidentiality of results.

kdl-o-158.q: Ensuring quality control in performing ELISA?
plan: ELISA quality control is within the requirements of ISO 15189: it covers the preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical stages.
On each plate, kit calibrators, negative and positive controls; if their optical density and cut-off value do not meet the manufacturer's criteria – the run is invalid.
Independent (third-party) control material, run-to-run monitoring with the Levey–Jennings graph and Westgard rules; comparison when the lot changes.
Equipment: calibration of the photometer (ELISA reader) filters, washer (residual volume), pipettes and thermostat; bringing reagents to room temperature, incubation time/temperature.
Participation in external quality assessment (EQA); recording nonconformities and corrective actions.

kdl-o-159.q: Preparing biomaterials for ELISA testing. External and internal factors affecting the analytical stage?
plan: Biomaterial: usually serum or plasma (the anticoagulant stated in the kit instructions); avoid hemolyzed, lipemic, icteric samples and bacterial contamination.
Specimen collection and preparation: correct identification, completing clotting and centrifugation, separating serum quickly; storage temperature and time, avoid repeated freeze–thaw.
External (analytical) factors: reagent temperature, incubation time and temperature, pipetting accuracy, quality of washing, protection of the substrate from light, plate "edge effect".

Internal (sample-specific) factors: heterophile antibodies and rheumatoid factor (false positive/negative), hook effect at very high analyte concentration (falsely low), biotin (in streptavidin–biotin systems).
Control: kit controls, internal quality control, in a doubtful result dilution or retesting by another method.
kdl-o-159.note: A separate source on biotin interference was not checked (left as a general principle).

plan: The automated method is the main one: on a hematology analyzer by the impedance principle (the number and size of electrical pulses as cells pass through an aperture) or an optical method; MCV and RDW are obtained at the same time.

The manual method – in a counting chamber: blood is diluted to a defined degree in isotonic solution, the chamber is filled, erythrocytes are counted in designated small squares and calculated to ×10¹²/L from the volume and dilution.
Errors of the chamber method: dilution/pipetting, incorrect filling of the chamber, uneven distribution of cells, violating the rule for counting cells on the border, counting too few cells.
Errors on the analyzer: agglutination (RBC falsely decreased, MCV increased), very high leukocytosis, microspherocytes/fragments; when in doubt a smear and repeat analysis.
Normal (approximately): men 4.6–6.2, women 4.2–5.4 ×10¹²/L (depends on laboratory); erythrocytosis and erythropenia are interpreted in clinical context.

reference.note: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

kdl-o-161.q: Etiology and pathogenesis of gonorrhea, trichomoniasis, laboratory diagnosis?
plan: Gonorrhea: N. gonorrhoeae – a gram-negative intracellular diplococcus; infects columnar epithelium, purulent urethritis/cervicitis, often asymptomatic (women), complications – pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility.
Trichomoniasis: T. vaginalis – a flagellated motile protozoan; vaginitis, urethritis; often asymptomatic (men).
Diagnosis of gonorrhea: NAAT (main), in men a Gram/methylene blue smear (intracellular diplococci), culture and antibiotic susceptibility.
Diagnosis of trichomoniasis: NAAT (highly sensitive), wet mount (immediately; sensitivity 44–68%), culture; if found on a PAP test – confirm with a sensitive test.
Test together for other STIs (chlamydia, syphilis, HIV) and treat sexual partners.

kdl-o-162.q: Epidemiology, etiopathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis of malaria?
plan: Causative agents and vector: five Plasmodium species, the Anopheles mosquito; life cycle – liver and erythrocytic stages.
Pathogenesis: destruction of erythrocytes (fever, anemia), severe complications in P. falciparum.
Microscopy: thick and thin smear, Giemsa; thick – detection, thin – species.
Calculating parasitemia (WHO MM-SOP-09): in the thick smear assuming 8000 leukocytes/µL (if no actual WBC), at high parasitemia the percentage of infected erythrocytes on the thin smear.
RDT, PCR (species and low parasitemia), if negative repeat after 12–24 hours; serology is not for acute diagnosis.

cutoffs.value: negative smears every 12–24 hours, 3 series in total

kdl-o-163.q: Fundamentals of the immunoenzyme method and the essence of ELISA analysis?
plan: Principle: specific antigen–antibody binding occurs on a solid phase (plate), and the signal is measured through the color reaction of an enzyme-labeled reagent and substrate.
Main formats: direct, indirect (detecting antibodies), sandwich (detecting antigen, two antibodies) and competitive (small molecules).
Steps: coating/blocking, sample incubation, washing, conjugate, washing, substrate, stop solution, optical density at a defined wavelength.
Result: qualitative (cut-off, "gray zone") or quantitative (from a calibration curve); units are kit-specific.
Advantages and limitations: sensitive, can be automated; interferences (heterophile antibodies, hook effect) and differences between kits.

kdl-o-164.q: Equipment required for performing enzyme immunoassay and its use?
plan: Main equipment: microplate photometer (ELISA reader, working and reference filters), plate washer, thermostat/shaker-incubator, single- and multichannel automatic pipettes.
Auxiliary: centrifuge, freezer/refrigerator (reagents at 2–8 °C), timer, distilled water, disposable tips; fully automated ELISA analyzers.
Use: manufacturer's instructions, pre-run check (filters, zero value), checking that the wash channels are not clogged, regular calibration of pipettes.
Maintenance and documents: preventive maintenance schedule, equipment logs, in a malfunction stop use and recheck.
Biosafety: treat samples as potentially infectious, PPE, decontamination of waste.

kdl-o-165.q: Determining specific antibodies against infections, i.e. IgM, IgA and IgG, by ELISA, false positive (+) and negative (−) results, finding and eliminating their causes?
plan: Meaning of antibody classes: IgM – usually an early/acute response, IgG – later and persists long (past infection or immunity), IgA – mucosal response; IgG avidity – assessing the timing of infection.
Evaluating the result over time: paired sera (2–3 weeks apart) and change in titer/index.
Causes of false positives: prolonged persistence of IgM, cross-reactivity, polyclonal activation (for example EBV), rheumatoid factor, heterophile antibodies, contamination and insufficient washing.
Causes of false negatives: the "serological window" (early period), immunodeficiency and immunosuppression, hook effect, incorrectly stored sample or reagents.

Elimination: a confirmatory test (another method, immunoblot, avidity, NAAT), a repeat sample, removal of RF (for IgM), kit controls and internal quality control; interpret the result together with the clinical picture.

kdl-o-166.q: Tumor markers: use for screening, diagnosis, determining the outcome of disease, assessing the therapy being given and the effectiveness of monitoring?
plan: Tumor markers are substances produced by the tumor or the body; many rise in benign conditions as well and do not rise in every tumor.
Screening: most markers are unsuitable for screening the general population (they rise in benign conditions, and are often normal at an early stage).
Diagnosis: a single marker does not make the diagnosis – together with imaging and histology; in some cases (for example AFP, β-hCG in embryonal tumors) it helps in diagnosis and staging.
Prognosis and monitoring: the pre-treatment level, a fall during treatment – effectiveness, a renewed rise – likelihood of recurrence; serial measurement with the same method in the same laboratory.
Limitations: differences between methods, hook effect (at very high values), heterophile antibodies.

kdl-o-167.q: Structure and function of immunoglobulins, their imbalance?
plan: Structure: two heavy and two light chains, disulfide bonds; Fab (antigen-binding) and Fc (effector) portions; 5 classes – IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE.
Functions: IgG – the main secondary response, crosses the placenta; IgM – primary response, pentamer; IgA – mucosal surfaces (secretory IgA); IgE – allergy and helminths; IgD – B-cell receptor.
Quantification: nephelometry/turbidimetry, protein electrophoresis (gamma fraction), immunofixation.

Imbalance: decrease – primary and secondary immunodeficiencies (loss, immunosuppression); polyclonal increase – chronic inflammation, liver diseases, autoimmune; monoclonal increase – gammopathies (myeloma).

plan: INR expresses PT in a standardized form: INR = (patient PT / mean normal PT)^ISI; ISI is the sensitivity index of the thromboplastin reagent relative to the WHO reference.
INR was introduced by the WHO to compare results of different thromboplastins and laboratories; it is intended for monitoring warfarin (vitamin K antagonist) therapy.
Target: in most indications (VTE, atrial fibrillation) 2–3; in a mechanical mitral valve 2.5–3.5; in healthy people ~≤1.1.
Factors affecting INR: drug interactions, vitamin K-rich food, liver disease, preanalytics (underfilling the citrate tube, high Ht).

The historical "prothrombin index" and "% by Quick" depend on the reagent, so in anticoagulant monitoring they have been replaced by INR; INR is also used in liver disease (MELD), but is not fully validated for that.

plan: CRP is a pentameric acute-phase protein synthesized in the liver under the influence of IL-6; it opsonizes pathogens and damaged cells and activates complement.
Kinetics: it rises within hours of the onset of inflammation and falls quickly after the cause is removed – convenient for monitoring treatment effect (faster than ESR).
Interpretation: <3 mg/L (0.3 mg/dL) normal; moderate rise – viral infections, chronic inflammation, injury; very high (>100 mg/L) – mainly bacterial infection.
hs-CRP (high-sensitivity) – cardiovascular risk in healthy people: <1 mg/L low, 1–3 average, >3 high (in the absence of acute inflammation).
Limitations: nonspecific; in liver failure it may rise only slightly; procalcitonin is additional for distinguishing bacterial from viral infection.

plan: Macroelements: calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chlorine; microelements: iron, zinc, copper, iodine, selenium, etc.
Calcium–phosphorus metabolism is regulated by PTH, vitamin D (calcitriol) and calcitonin; bone is the main store; ionized calcium is the active fraction.
Magnesium is a cofactor of many enzymes; deficiency leads to hypocalcemia and hypokalemia.
Iron is part of hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes; transferrin carries it, ferritin stores it, hepcidin regulates it; copper is linked to iron metabolism through ceruloplasmin.
Laboratory assessment: in serum Ca (corrected/ionized), phosphate, Mg, iron parameters (iron, TIBC/TSAT, ferritin), PTH, 25(OH)D; urinary excretion.
Glucose: in venous plasma by enzymatic methods (hexokinase – the most specific; glucose oxidase–peroxidase); preventing glycolysis – rapid centrifugation or a tube with an inhibitor.
Diagnostic thresholds of glucose: fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L – diabetes, 5.6–6.9 – impaired fasting glucose (ADA); 75 g OGTT at 2 hours ≥11.1 – diabetes, 7.8–11.0 – impaired tolerance.
HbA1c: HPLC, boronate affinity, immunoassay or enzymatic method; NGSP-certified, DCCT-standardized; ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol) – diabetes, 5.7–6.4% – prediabetes.
Advantage of HbA1c – no fasting required, little day-to-day variability; disadvantage – unreliable in hemoglobinopathies, anemia, changed erythrocyte lifespan.
If the results of two tests disagree, the test exceeding the threshold is confirmed by repeating it.

cutoffs.value: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 (126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 h); 75 g OGTT 2-hour ≥11.1 (200); HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP/DCCT); random ≥11.1 with symptoms; without unequivocal hyperglycemia – two abnormal results

kdl-o-172.q: The role of ELISA in diagnosing coronavirus infection?
plan: Diagnosis of current SARS-CoV-2 infection is made by NAAT (RT-PCR) or antigen tests; detecting antibodies by ELISA is not recommended for diagnosing current infection.
The place of antibody tests: identifying past infection, epidemiological (seroprevalence) studies, in some clinical cases an aid in delayed diagnosis.
Antigen targets: nucleocapsid (N) antibodies – only after infection; spike (S) antibodies – after infection or vaccination; this difference is important in interpretation.
Limitations: delayed seroconversion, cross-reactivity, antibody level does not directly show protection.
Quality: a validated kit, controls, interpreting the result together with clinical and epidemiological data.

plan: The differential is the ratio of leukocyte types (%), always interpreted together with absolute counts; determined manually on a smear or on an analyzer.

Leukocytosis – in adults >11×10⁹/L; physiological (stress, exertion, pregnancy) and pathological (infections, inflammation, necrosis, leukemias, drugs – glucocorticoids). Types: neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, monocytosis, eosinophilia (>0.5×10⁹/L), basophilia.
Leukemoid reaction – neutrophils >50×10⁹/L without a myeloproliferative disease; hyperleukocytosis – >100×10⁹/L (usually leukemia).

Causes of leukopenia (mainly neutropenia): viral infections, some bacterial infections, drugs and chemotherapy (myelotoxic), autoimmune, B12/folate deficiency, bone marrow aplasia or infiltration, hypersplenism; agranulocytosis – a sharp decrease of granulocytes, risk of severe infection.

Morphological changes: "left shift" (bands and immature forms), toxic granulation; hypersegmentation – a sign of megaloblastic anemia; blasts – suspicion of leukemia, smear and hematologist consultation.

kdl-o-174.q: Pigment metabolism. Methods of determining bilirubin in blood serum?
plan: Pigment metabolism: heme → biliverdin → indirect bilirubin (with albumin) → conjugation by UGT1A1 in the liver → direct bilirubin into bile → in the intestine urobilinogen/stercobilin.
Determination in serum – diazo reaction: direct bilirubin without an accelerator, total bilirubin with an accelerator (Jendrassik–Grof-type methods); indirect = total − direct.
Alternative methods: vanadate/enzymatic oxidation; in newborns direct spectrophotometry.
Preanalytics: protect from light, avoid hemolysis.
Interpretation: predominance of indirect – hemolysis or conjugation disorder; predominance of direct – cholestasis or hepatocellular injury; result in µmol/L.

plan: Wet mount: from purulent, bloody flecks; leukocytes, erythrocytes, epithelium (many squamous epithelial cells – saliva contamination, low specimen quality), alveolar macrophages, elastic fibers (tissue destruction), Curschmann spirals, Charcot-Leyden crystals, fungal elements.
Gram staining: morphology of bacteria (gram-positive diplococci, etc.) and neutrophils – bacterial pneumonia; interpret together with culture.
Ziehl-Neelsen (or auramine) – acid-fast rods; result by grading ("scanty", 1+, 2+, 3+).
By Romanowsky – cellular composition (eosinophils – asthma/allergy), in cytological methods – atypical (tumor) cells.
Results are interpreted together with the clinical picture, culture and molecular tests; negative microscopy does not exclude tuberculosis.

cutoffs.value: none in 100 fields – negative; 1–9/100 – exact number; 10–99/100 – 1+; 1–10/field – 2+; >10/field – 3+

plan: Coagulation (secondary) hemostasis is the formation of thrombin and fibrin as a result of proteolytic reactions of coagulation factors.

Cell-based model: initiation (tissue factor + VIIa → Xa → a small amount of thrombin), amplification (thrombin activates platelets, V, VIII, XI), propagation (tenase and prothrombinase complexes on the platelet surface – the thrombin "burst").
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin; XIIIa cross-links fibrin fibers; vitamin K-dependent factors – II, VII, IX, X (and also protein C and S).
Laboratory assessment: PT/INR (extrinsic + common pathway), aPTT (intrinsic + common), fibrinogen (Clauss), thrombin time; factor activities.
Inhibitory systems: antithrombin, protein C/S, TFPI; their disorder – thrombophilia.

kdl-o-177.q: Microscopic examination of protozoa in stool?
plan: Specimen: fresh stool, liquid stool is examined quickly (within 30 minutes) or placed in a fixative (formalin, PVA); at least 3 specimens on different days.
Wet mount: motility of trophozoites in physiological saline; in Lugol's solution cyst nuclei and glycogen vacuoles.
Enrichment: formalin-ethyl acetate sedimentation – increases the sensitivity of finding cysts.
Permanently stained smear (trichrome, etc.) – species identification; for Cryptosporidium a modified acid-fast stain.
Morphological differentiation: E. histolytica (trophozoite with phagocytosed erythrocytes) and non-pathogenic amoebae; Giardia cyst and trophozoite; antigen or PCR if needed.
OGTT – 75 g anhydrous glucose (for children 1.75 g/kg, maximum 75 g) in 250–300 mL water is drunk within 5 minutes; venous plasma glucose is measured fasting and after 2 hours.

Preparation: 3 days of usual diet (≥150 g carbohydrate/day), overnight fast (≥8 hours), sit during the test, do not smoke; acute illness, prolonged bed rest and glucocorticoids/diuretics distort the result.

Interpretation (at 2 hours): <7.8 mmol/L normal, 7.8–11.0 – impaired glucose tolerance, ≥11.1 – diabetes (confirmation needed); if fasting glucose is ≥7.0, the test is usually not needed to confirm diabetes.
Pregnancy: at 24–28 weeks a one-step 75 g OGTT – any one of fasting ≥5.1, 1 hour ≥10.0, 2 hours ≥8.5 mmol/L is GDM; in the two-step approach a 50 g screen and a 100 g OGTT.
Disadvantages: limited reproducibility, sensitive to preanalytical errors (glycolysis) – process the sample immediately.

pitfalls.wrong: intravenous glucose administration and the tolbutamide test for "latent diabetes"
pitfalls.right: the standard for diagnosing diabetes/prediabetes: oral 75 g OGTT, fasting glucose and HbA1c (ADA criteria); IV and tolbutamide tests are absent from current criteria

plan: An orphan (rare) disease is a disease with low prevalence in the population: in the European Union <5 per 10 000 people, in the USA <200 000 patients (Orphan Drug Act, 1983).

According to experts there are more than 10 000 rare diseases (GARD; other sources >6800); a significant proportion is linked to a single-gene mutation (NHGRI), often begins in childhood, chronic and severe.
Problems: diagnostic delay, limited availability of specialists and laboratories, few and expensive treatments.
Laboratory significance: biochemical (metabolites, enzymes) and genetic tests, newborn screening.
National definitions and lists differ by country (cite local regulatory documents).
Clinical suspicion: family history, multisystem signs, developmental delay, metabolic crises.
First-stage biochemistry: blood gases, glucose, ammonia, lactate, ketones; amino acids and acylcarnitines (tandem MS), organic acids in urine, glycosaminoglycans.
Enzyme activity (lysosomal diseases, etc.) and special biomarkers.
Genetic confirmation: targeted gene tests, gene panels, exome/genome sequencing.
Specialized centers, correct collection and transport of specimens (dried blood spot, frozen sample), releasing the result with genetic counseling.

plan: Newborn screening is a population program for diseases that are treatable early and detectable before clinical signs appear.
History: the Guthrie test (phenylketonuria) and the dried blood spot (Guthrie card).
Modern method: tandem mass spectrometry – from a single blood spot amino acids and acylcarnitines, many metabolic diseases.
Specimen: dried blood spot from the heel, at a defined age (usually in the first days of life), correct filling and drying of the filter paper.
A positive screen is not a diagnosis: confirmatory biochemical/genetic tests and prompt referral; quality control of the program.

kdl-o-182.q: Methods of quality control of clinical laboratory tests?
plan: Methods of internal quality control: statistical control with control materials (two to three levels) – Levey–Jennings chart, Westgard multirules; methods based on patient data (patient averages, delta check).
Assessing repeatability – parallel measurements, CV%; assessing trueness – reference/certified materials and external assessment results (bias).
External quality assessment (PT/EQA) – interlaboratory comparison; if no program exists – sample exchange.
Method verification/validation (precision, trueness, linearity, limit of detection, interferences), calibration and maintenance of equipment.
Quality indicators, internal audit, management of nonconformities and management review (ISO 15189).

kdl-o-183.q: Rules for clinical audit of the quality and effectiveness of laboratory support of treatment and diagnostic activity in healthcare institutions?
plan: Clinical audit is a systematic comparison of the laboratory service with defined criteria and remeasurement after implementing changes (cycle: criterion → data collection → comparison → change → re-audit).
Sources of criteria: ISO 15189 requirements, clinical guidelines (test-ordering algorithms), national orders.

Indicators (quality indicators): appropriateness of test ordering and repeated unnecessary tests, proportion of rejected specimens, hemolysis %, report turnaround time (TAT), time to report critical values, external assessment results, complaints.
Effectiveness: impact of tests on clinical decisions, cost-benefit, use of resources.
Results are discussed at management review, a plan of corrective actions is drawn up and its implementation monitored.

kdl-o-184.q: The importance of the preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical stages in internal quality control of hematological tests?
plan: Preanalytical: correct anticoagulant (EDTA), filling and mixing, control of clots/hemolysis, time and temperature before analysis (specimen aging changes MCV, platelets, the differential), smear quality.

Analytical: calibration of the analyzer, daily internal control (three levels – low, normal, high) with Levey–Jennings and Westgard rules; checking the background (blank) and carry-over; inter-observer agreement for the microscopic differential.
Control based on patient data: the moving average of stable indices such as mean MCV, MCH, MCHC – detects analyzer drift early.
Postanalytical: rules for reviewing the smear on "flags" and abnormal results, delta check, reporting of critical values (Hb, platelets, leukocytes, blasts).
External assessment: for analyzer parameters and morphology ("unknown" smears).

kdl-o-185.q: Anemias, classification, pathogenesis. Constructing Levey-Jennings control charts and the Westgard rules?
plan: Classification of anemias (briefly): pathogenetic – blood loss, impaired erythropoiesis (iron, B12/folate, bone marrow failure, inflammation, kidney), hemolysis; morphological – by MCV micro-, normo-, macrocytic; by reticulocytes regenerative/hyporegenerative.
For reliable Hb and indices in diagnosing anemia, quality control of the analyzer is necessary: Levey–Jennings charts for parameters such as Hb, MCV.
Constructing a chart: measure the control material in ~20 runs, determine x̄ and SD; lines at ±1s, ±2s, ±3s.
Westgard rules: 1-2s – warning; 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s, 4-1s, 10x – reject the run; if rejected, the patient result is not released.
For example, a gradual shift of MCV to one side (10x) – systematic error (calibration, reagent) – may lead to misclassification of anemias.

cutoffs.value: x̄ and SD from at least 20 measurements on different days
1-2s – warning; 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s (within run), 4-1s, 10x – rejection

kdl-o-186.q: The importance of the preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical stages in internal quality control of general clinical tests?
plan: Preanalytical: instructions to the patient, correct collection (midstream, second morning urine for sediment), clean/sterile containers, rapid delivery (within 1 hour at room temperature, 4 hours in a refrigerator), standard requirements for stool and sputum.

Analytical – test strips: expiry and storage conditions, daily control with positive/negative control urines, adherence to reading time or an automatic reader; confirmatory tests (for example sulfosalicylic acid for protein).

Analytical – microscopy: standardized volume, centrifugation (400×g, 5 minutes) and reporting the result "per field" or per unit volume; automated urine particle analyzers and control materials for them; inter-observer agreement.
Postanalytical: checking consistency of results (for example blood on the strip and erythrocytes on microscopy, nitrite and bacteria), units, critical findings.
Participation in external assessment programs (test strips, sediment images).

kdl-o-187.q: The importance of the preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical stages in internal quality control of cytological examinations?
plan: Preanalytical: correct collection technique (transformation zone), rapid wet fixation or preservative, labeling, clinical data; assessing adequacy and monitoring the proportion of "unsatisfactory" specimens.

Analytical: staining quality (reagent changes, control slides), the screener's workload limit, second reading (for example rescreening a portion of negative smears), standard terminology (Bethesda 2014).
Monitoring indicators: ASC/SIL ratio, proportion of HPV-positive ASC-US, correlation of cytology and histology results, inter-observer agreement.
Postanalytical: completeness and accuracy of the report, recommendations, rapid delivery of critical/high-risk results, archive and ability to review.
External quality assessment ("unknown" smears/images) and continuing training; ISO 15189 requirements.

kdl-o-188.q: External quality control of cytological smears (examination of unknown smears)?
plan: Cytological external quality assessment – "unknown" smears or digital images with a diagnosis confirmed by an expert (often with histological correlation) are sent to laboratories.
The laboratory evaluates the smear routinely, giving adequacy, category and a descriptive interpretation (Bethesda).
Results are compared with the expert's interpretation and other participants; clinically significant discrepancies (for example reading HSIL as NILM) are analyzed separately.
Purpose: testing diagnostic competence, standardizing terminology, training and corrective actions.
Under ISO 15189 participation in external quality assessment and documentation of results are mandatory; supplemented by internal "blind" rescreening.

kdl-o-189.q: Specific features of the preanalytical stage in biochemical tests: storage and transport of blood samples, the effect of treatment procedures and drugs on blood parameters?
plan: Storage and transport: separate serum/plasma from cells quickly (glucose, K, phosphate, LDH change); control temperature and light (bilirubin); during transport avoid vibration and extreme cold/heat.

Glucose: glycolysis ~5–7% per hour – separate within 30–60 minutes or use a tube with an inhibitor; K: rises in chilled whole blood and with late separation, fist clenching, hemolysis, K-EDTA contamination.
Interferences: hemolysis (K, LDH, AST, phosphate rise), lipemia (photometric and indirect ISE errors), icterus; assessed by analyzer indices.
Effect of treatment procedures: drawing a sample from the infusion site (glucose, electrolytes), heparin, contrast agents, timing of hemodialysis.
Drugs: in vivo effect (diuretics – K, Na; glucocorticoids – glucose; enzyme inducers – GGT) and in vitro analytical interference (for example ascorbate interferes with peroxidase reactions).
Drugs and procedures are stated on the requisition; in a doubtful result exclude preanalytical causes.

kdl-o-190.q: Constructing Levey–Jennings control charts for biochemical parameters, the Westgard rule?
plan: For each biochemical parameter (for example glucose, creatinine, ALT) a control material of at least two levels (normal and pathological).
Initial stage: each level is measured in ~20 independent runs; x̄, SD, CV% are calculated; on the Levey–Jennings chart x̄ and lines at ±1s, ±2s, ±3s.

Westgard multirules: 1-2s – warning (check the other rules); rejection – 1-3s, 2-2s (two consecutive points beyond ±2s on the same side), R-4s (within one run, one above +2s and the other below −2s), 4-1s, 10x.
Action by type of error: random (1-3s, R-4s) – pipetting, bubbles, sample; systematic (2-2s, 4-1s, 10x) – calibration, reagent lot, lamp, temperature; correction and repeat analysis.
The choice of rules depends on the quality requirement of the method and its performance (for example sigma); all actions are documented.

cutoffs.value: x̄ and SD from at least 20 measurements on different days
1-2s – warning; 1-3s, 2-2s, R-4s (within run), 4-1s, 10x – rejection

kdl-o-191.q: The importance of the postanalytical stage in evaluating biochemical results against reference values?
plan: The reference interval is the central 95% of results of a healthy reference population; each laboratory verifies the manufacturer's or literature interval for its own population and method (verification).

Interpretation takes into account age, sex, pregnancy, circadian rhythm, biological variability; for some tests clinical decision limits are used instead of a reference interval (glucose, HbA1c, lipids, troponin 99th percentile).
The result report contains correct units, the reference interval/decision limit, an abnormality flag and comments on interference (hemolysis, etc.).
Postanalytical control: delta check, logical consistency, immediate reporting of critical values, timely release of results.
A result outside the reference interval is not always disease (5% of healthy people are outside), and a result inside does not exclude disease – clinical interpretation.

kdl-o-192.q: Hemostasis, its disorders. Hemostasis parameters. The importance of the preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical stages in hemostasis testing?
plan: Hemostasis and its disorders (briefly): primary (platelets, vWF) and coagulation; hypocoagulation (hemophilia, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC) and thrombophilia.
Main parameters: platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, thrombin time, D-dimer; if needed factors, antithrombin, protein C/S, lupus anticoagulant.
Preanalytical: 3.2% citrate, 9:1 ratio (≥90% filling), correction at Ht >55%, atraumatic puncture, order of draw, rapid delivery at room temperature, hemolysis/clot – rejection.

Analytical: calibration of the coagulometer, control each shift with two-level control plasmas (normal and pathological), Westgard rules; when the reagent lot changes update the ISI and the mean normal PT.

Postanalytical: correct calculation of INR, reporting of critical values (very high INR, low fibrinogen, low platelets), interpretation with information on anticoagulant use; external quality assessment.

in most indications 2.0–3.0 (target 2.5); in a mechanical mitral valve 2.5–3.5
1.5–2.2 times baseline

plan: Specimen type according to the kit instructions: serum/plasma (anticoagulant), in some tests CSF, saliva or other fluids.
Collection: identify the patient and the tube, correct tube, avoid hemolysis; separate serum by centrifugation after clotting is complete.
Storage and transport: defined temperature and time (short term 2–8 °C, long term frozen), avoid repeated freeze–thaw, triple packaging during transport.
Rejection criteria: marked hemolysis/lipemia, incorrect label, insufficient volume, expired specimen.
Before the run: bring the specimen to room temperature, mix, centrifuge if needed; safety measures.

kdl-o-194.q: External and internal factors affecting the analytical stage of ELISA testing?
plan: External factors: room and reagent temperature, incubation time, pipetting errors, quality of washing (residual liquid), plate edge effect, substrate left in light, photometer filters.
Reagent-related: do not mix kit lots, expiry date, correct preparation and storage.
Internal (sample) factors: hemolysis, lipemia, bilirubin; heterophile antibodies and RF (false positive/negative), hook effect (falsely low), immune complexes.
Detection: check the controls and cut-off, in an unexpected result dilution, retesting or another method.
Documentation and corrective actions; staff training.

kdl-o-195.q: Checking the quality of test systems used for ELISA testing, their sensitivity and specificity?
plan: Diagnostic sensitivity is the proportion of positive results in the diseased; specificity is the proportion of negative results in the healthy; assessed with a panel of samples of known status.
Positive and negative predictive value depend on disease prevalence; at low prevalence the proportion of false positives rises.
Verification in the laboratory: precision (repeatability), comparison with reference samples, samples near the cut-off, lot-to-lot differences.
Internal quality control (independent control material, Westgard) and external quality assessment.
Recording and interpretation: the kit insert, an algorithm for "gray zone" results (retesting, confirmatory test).
kdl-o-195.note: The definitions of sensitivity/specificity are general biostatistical concepts; a separate source was not checked.

kdl-o-196.q: Quantitative and qualitative test systems used for ELISA testing, their disadvantages, advantages, requirements for them?
plan: Qualitative tests: a positive/negative answer by the cut-off index; convenient for screening, but give no "gray zone" and no concentration.
Quantitative tests: concentration from calibrators and a curve (IU/mL, etc.); allow monitoring dynamics, depend on calibration quality.
Disadvantages: interferences (heterophile antibodies, RF, hook effect), lack of standardization between kits, results cannot be compared with another kit.
Requirements: a registered/validated kit, known sensitivity and specificity, traceability to reference materials, controls, clear instructions.
Choice: purpose (screening or confirmation), prevalence, automation and price.

kdl-o-197.q: Specific features of organizing PCR laboratories?
plan: The basic principle is preventing amplicon contamination: separate zones (reagent preparation, nucleic acid extraction, amplification, detection).
One-way workflow: movement from the clean zone to the contaminated zone; materials and staff do not go in the reverse direction.
Separate equipment, pipettes, lab coats and gloves for each zone; filter tips; an air pressure gradient if needed.
Biosafety: risk assessment, a biological safety cabinet for nucleic acid extraction; decontamination of surfaces (hypochlorite, UV).
Controls: negative (NTC), positive, internal and extraction controls; monitoring environmental contamination.

kdl-o-198.q: Personal protective equipment used when working in PCR laboratories, its types, rules of use?
plan: Personal protective equipment (PPE) is chosen on the basis of a risk assessment: lab coat, disposable gloves, goggles/face shield, a respirator if needed.
In a PCR laboratory there are two aims: to protect the worker from the infectious sample and to protect the sample/reagents from contamination.
Zone-specific PPE: separate colored/marked lab coats for each zone, left in the zone; gloves are changed often.
Order of donning and doffing, hand hygiene, used items disposed of as hazardous waste.
Staff training and regular supervision.

kdl-o-199.q: Fundamentals of DNA. Determining the sequence of nucleotides?
plan: DNA structure: deoxyribose, phosphate and four nitrogenous bases; complementary pairing A–T, C–G; double helix, antiparallel strands.
Basis of replication and PCR: the polymerase synthesizes in the 5’→3’ direction and requires a primer.
Sequencing: the chain-termination (Sanger) method – the "gold standard" for small segments; massively parallel (next-generation) sequencing – many genes/genome; modern technologies such as nanopores.
Clinical use: inherited mutations, tumor genetics, microbial identification and drug resistance.
Quality of the result: read quality, depth of coverage, bioinformatic analysis and interpretation of variants.
kdl-o-199.note: The permitted source for Sanger and NGS details was not fully checked (the genome.gov page does not contain the name Sanger).

plan: PCR components and cycle (denaturation, annealing, elongation); amplification is exponential, then a plateau.
Real-time PCR: a fluorescent dye (SYBR Green) or specific probes; the Ct value is inversely related to the starting amount – quantitative analysis.
RT-PCR – cDNA from RNA (reverse transcriptase); RNA viruses and gene expression.
Other variants: multiplex, nested, digital PCR, isothermal amplification (depending on the laboratory's purpose).
Advantages and limitations: high sensitivity and specificity; contamination, inhibitors, primer design problems.
kdl-o-200.note: Details of multiplex/nested/digital PCR were not checked in the source.

plan: Preanalytical: correct specimen, transport medium, temperature and time; preventing degradation of nucleic acids.
In each run the controls: negative (NTC), positive, extraction control and internal amplification control (detecting inhibition).
Contamination control: zones, one-way flow, cleaning surfaces, environmental swabs.
Method validation/verification: sensitivity (limit of detection), specificity, repeatability; calibration of equipment (thermal cycler, pipettes).
External quality assessment, documents, ISO 15189 requirements.

kdl-o-202.q: DNA technologies in the study of infectious diseases, rules of specimen collection. Multifactorial diseases?
plan: DNA/RNA technologies in infections: direct detection of the pathogen (PCR, NAAT), measuring viral load, genotyping and resistance mutations, epidemiological typing, sequencing.

Specimen collection rules: material appropriate to the site of infection (swab, blood, urine, CSF), a sterile DNase/RNase-free container, an appropriate transport medium; freezing/transport temperature.
Sources of error: insufficient material, delayed transport, inhibitors (heparin, etc.), contamination.
Multifactorial diseases: due to several genes and environmental factors (for example type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases); molecular tests assess risk but do not make a diagnosis.
Interpret results together with clinical and other laboratory data.
kdl-o-202.note: A separate source on multifactorial diseases was not checked.

kdl-o-203.q: Molecular methods in diagnosing infections in pregnant women and newborns?
plan: Main infections in pregnancy and in newborns: CMV, toxoplasmosis, rubella, herpes, HIV, hepatitis B, etc.
Congenital CMV: within 2–3 weeks after birth PCR in saliva (preferred) or urine; a sample taken later cannot distinguish congenital from acquired.
Toxoplasmosis: to confirm fetal infection – PCR in amniotic fluid; serology in the mother (IgM, IgG, avidity) is confirmed in a reference laboratory.
Rubella: PCR (nasopharynx, urine) and serology; in the first trimester of pregnancy the risk of transmission is high.
Advantages of the molecular method: in the newborn maternal IgG antibodies confound serology, PCR detects the pathogen directly; timing and type of specimen are important.

kdl-o-204.q: Molecular-biological methods in diagnosing sexually transmitted infections and in diagnosing papillomavirus infection and cervical cancer?
plan: In STIs NAAT is the method of choice for chlamydia and gonorrhea (vaginal swab, first-void urine); in gonorrhea culture is retained for antibiotic susceptibility.
Trichomoniasis: NAAT is much more sensitive than wet-mount microscopy.
HPV: molecular tests identifying high-risk (oncogenic) genotypes are used in screening strategy as primary or together with cytology; HPV-16/18 genotyping.
Cervical cancer screening: with a positive HPV test cytology (triage) and colposcopy; WHO recommends an HPV DNA test in screening.
Specimen and quality: correct collection device and transport medium, internal controls, avoiding contamination.
Myocardial injury – troponin above the 99th percentile; with a rise/fall – acute; with added signs of ischemia – myocardial infarction.

Cardiac troponins I and T are cardiac-specific isoforms; high-sensitivity methods accurately measure low concentrations and give rapid rule-in/rule-out algorithms (0/1 or 0/2 hours); dynamics: when the baseline value is high, a change >20% is significant.
CK-MB – auxiliary (reinfarction, when troponin is unavailable), falsely raised in muscle injury; myoglobin – early, nonspecific.
Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) – wall stress, diagnosis and prognosis of heart failure; not for diagnosing MI.
Causes of troponin rise without infarction (myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, renal failure, arrhythmias, cardiac surgery) – clinical interpretation is needed.

cutoffs.value: >99th percentile URL; if the baseline is high, a >20% change in series – acute
cutoffs.guideline: 4th universal definition of MI (via StatPearls Cardiac Biomarkers)

kdl-o-206.q: Modern laboratory diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Methods of determining glycosylated hemoglobin, glucose?
plan: Diagnostic criteria: fasting venous plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 75 g OGTT at 2 hours ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%, random ≥11.1 with symptoms; the confirmation rule.
Glucose methods: hexokinase (close to reference level, 340 nm), glucose oxidase–peroxidase; preanalytics – glycolysis, rapid centrifugation; glucometers only for monitoring.
HbA1c methods: ion-exchange HPLC, boronate affinity, immunoassay, enzymatic; NGSP/IFCC standardization; interference from Hb variants and erythrocyte lifespan.
Additional markers: autoantibodies and C-peptide (type 1/2), fructosamine, ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate), albuminuria (ACR).
Quality: two-level control, Westgard rules, external quality control; report the result in the correct units – mmol/L and mg/dL.

cutoffs.value: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 (126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 h); 75 g OGTT 2-hour ≥11.1 (200); HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP/DCCT); random ≥11.1 with symptoms; without unequivocal hyperglycemia – two abnormal results

kdl-o-207.q: Middle-molecular peptides – markers of endogenous intoxication?
plan: The concept of "middle molecules" came from nephrology: the Babb and Scribner hypothesis (1965) – substances larger than ~500 Da, poorly removed in hemodialysis and causing uremic complications (polyneuropathy).

The modern international classification (EUTox): uremic toxins – small water-soluble (<0.5 kDa; urea, creatinine), middle molecules (0.5–58 kDa; for example β2-microglobulin) and large (>58 kDa); removal of middle molecules is studied as an indicator of dialysis adequacy.

In post-Soviet laboratory practice "middle-molecular peptides" (MMPs) are a general marker of endogenous intoxication: after protein precipitation the UV absorbance of the sample is measured spectrophotometrically at 254 and 280 nm (serum, urine, saliva); an increase has been shown in studies in sepsis, burns, peritonitis, pancreatitis, renal/hepatic failure, tumors.

Limitations: the method is nonspecific (not one defined substance but the sum of various peptides and other UV-absorbing compounds), not standardized, and not given as a standard test in international clinical guidelines (not found in this review); interlaboratory comparison is difficult.

In assessing the degree of intoxication it is interpreted in practice together with internationally accepted parameters: urea, creatinine/eGFR, bilirubin, lactate, CRP/procalcitonin, leukocytes; the MMP result only over time and with the clinical picture.
kdl-o-207.note: 2026-10-09 audit: the concept and the UV 254/280 nm method were confirmed in open sources (PMC11126090, PMC5192514); MMP is not standardized as a test – the local method (reagents, normal range) should be checked by an expert.

kdl-o-208.q: The effect of insulin and other hormones on carbohydrate metabolism?
plan: Insulin is an anabolic hormone: it increases glucose entry via GLUT4 into muscle and adipose tissue and glycogen synthesis in the liver; inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis and ketogenesis.
Glucagon – increases glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis in the liver; a low insulin/glucagon ratio leads to ketogenesis.
Adrenaline – glycogenolysis and lipolysis, inhibition of insulin secretion; cortisol – gluconeogenesis, insulin resistance; growth hormone and thyroid hormones – counter-regulatory effect.
Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) – increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion after a meal.

Laboratory reflection: insulin and C-peptide (endogenous secretion; C-peptide is low with exogenous insulin), in excess of counter-regulatory hormones (Cushing, pheochromocytoma, acromegaly) secondary hyperglycemia.

kdl-o-209.q: Plasma factors participating in the blood clotting process?
plan: Plasma coagulation factors: I (fibrinogen), II (prothrombin), III (tissue factor), IV (Ca²⁺), V, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, XIII; also prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen.
Most are synthesized in the liver (VIII – endothelium/hepatic sinusoidal cells); II, VII, IX, X are vitamin K-dependent (γ-carboxylation).
Most are zymogens of proteases (II, VII, IX, X, XI, XII), V and VIII are cofactors, XIII is a transglutaminase (stabilizes fibrin), fibrinogen is the substrate.
Deficiencies: hemophilia A (VIII), B (IX), factor XI deficiency, factor VII deficiency; acquired – liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, DIC, inhibitors.
Laboratory: PT (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen), aPTT (XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, fibrinogen), activity of individual factors (PT- or aPTT-based), mixing test.

kdl-o-210.q: The extrinsic activation pathway of plasma factors in the blood clotting process?
plan: Extrinsic pathway: when a vessel is injured, tissue factor (TF) is exposed to the blood and forms a complex with VII/VIIa.
The TF–VIIa complex activates X (and IX); Xa in the prothrombinase complex with Va converts prothrombin to thrombin – the physiological start of coagulation.
TFPI quickly inhibits TF–VIIa–Xa – therefore further amplification continues through IX/VIII (intrinsic tenase).
Laboratory reflection: PT – by adding thromboplastin (TF + phospholipid + Ca²⁺) it assesses the extrinsic and common pathway; INR – monitoring VKA.
Factor VII has the shortest half-life – in vitamin K deficiency and when warfarin is started PT is prolonged first; isolated PT prolongation – probable factor VII deficiency.

kdl-o-211.q: The role of platelets in the blood clotting process?
plan: Adhesion: at the damaged wall to subendothelial collagen via vWF (GPIb-IX-V) and directly to collagen (GPVI).
Activation: shape change, granule secretion (ADP, serotonin, vWF, fibrinogen, factor V), synthesis of thromboxane A2 – recruits new platelets.
Aggregation: GPIIb/IIIa is activated and links platelets through fibrinogen bridges – the primary plug.
Procoagulant role: phosphatidylserine is exposed on the activated membrane – tenase and prothrombinase complexes assemble (thrombin "burst"); clot retraction.
Laboratory assessment: platelet count and morphology, aggregometry (ADP, collagen, epinephrine, arachidonic acid, ristocetin), PFA; effect of antiplatelet agents (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors).
The anticoagulant system consists of mechanisms that confine clot formation to the site of injury and keep blood fluid within vessels.

Physiological anticoagulants: antithrombin (a serpin; neutralizes IIa, Xa, IXa, heparin/heparan sulfate accelerates it a thousandfold), protein C – activated by thrombin with thrombomodulin, together with its cofactor protein S cleaves Va and VIIIa, TFPI – inhibits TF–VIIa and Xa.
Endothelium: thrombomodulin, heparan sulfate, prostacyclin and NO (inhibit platelets), tPA (fibrinolysis).
The fibrinolytic system – breaks down the fibrin that has formed (plasmin).

Deficiencies (antithrombin, protein C/S) and factor V Leiden (APC resistance) – risk of venous thrombosis; laboratory: functional activity tests, genetic tests; take into account the change of results during anticoagulant therapy.
Antithrombin is a serpin synthesized in the liver; inactivates thrombin, Xa, IXa (and also TF-bound VIIa); heparin sharply enhances its action – the mechanism of heparin therapy.
Protein C is vitamin K-dependent; it is activated by thrombin bound to endothelial thrombomodulin; activated protein C with protein S cleaves Va and VIIIa.
Protein S is a cofactor of activated protein C and TFPI.
TFPI limits the initiation of the extrinsic pathway (TF–VIIa–Xa).

Biological significance: local limitation of coagulation, prevention of intravascular thrombosis; deficiency (inherited, or acquired in DIC, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome) – thrombophilia; in the laboratory antithrombin, protein C, protein S activity and APC resistance.

kdl-o-214.q: The importance of fibrinolysis, pathways of activation of the fibrinolytic system?
plan: Fibrinolysis is dissolving the fibrin clot to restore vessel patency; plasminogen → plasmin (a protease) degrades fibrin and fibrinogen.

Activation pathways: extrinsic (main) – tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) from the endothelium, effective on the fibrin surface; urokinase (uPA) – in tissues; intrinsic (contact) pathway – XIIa, kallikrein; exogenous – thrombolytic drugs (alteplase, etc.).
Inhibitors: PAI-1 (inhibits tPA and uPA; high PAI-1 – risk of thrombosis), α2-antiplasmin (rapidly inactivates free plasmin – limits its action around the clot), TAFI.
Products: fibrin degradation products; D-dimer – a specific product of breakdown of cross-linked fibrin.
Laboratory: D-dimer (excluding VTE, DIC), fibrinogen, if needed plasminogen, α2-antiplasmin, PAI-1; global tests (lysis on thromboelastometry).

kdl-o-215.q: Determining blood clotting times and their clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Whole blood clotting time (Lee–White and similar methods) is a historical test: insensitive, not standardized, dependent on many factors; in the modern laboratory it has been replaced by standard plasma tests.

Plasma clotting times: PT (thromboplastin + Ca²⁺; extrinsic and common pathway; reported as INR), aPTT (contact activator + phospholipid + Ca²⁺; intrinsic and common pathway), thrombin time (fibrinogen → fibrin), fibrinogen (Clauss).
PT prolongation: VKA (warfarin), vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, deficiency of II/V/VII/X.
aPTT prolongation: heparin, hemophilias (VIII, IX), XI/XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant, DIC; the mixing test distinguishes deficiency (correction occurs) from an inhibitor.
Bedside activated clotting time (ACT) – for monitoring high-dose heparin (cardiac surgery); global viscoelastic tests (TEG/ROTEM).

kdl-o-216.q: Determining fibrinogen, fibrinolytic activity and clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Fibrinogen is factor I synthesized in the liver, a positive acute-phase protein; the result is interpreted against the laboratory's reference interval.

Determination: the Clauss method (functional) – excess thrombin is added to diluted plasma, the clotting time is inversely proportional to fibrinogen concentration and is calculated from a calibration curve; PT-derived fibrinogen and immunological methods are auxiliary.

Decrease: DIC, severe liver disease, massive bleeding and dilution, thrombolytic therapy, inherited afibrinogenemia/dysfibrinogenemia; increase: inflammation, pregnancy, tumors – a risk factor for thrombosis.

Fibrinolytic activity: D-dimer (fibrin breakdown – high NPV for excluding VTE; age-adjusted cutoff after 50), fibrin degradation products, plasminogen, α2-antiplasmin, PAI-1; the historical euglobulin lysis time is rarely used now.
Clinical significance: DIC score (fibrinogen <1 g/L adds a point), transfusion strategy, monitoring thrombolysis.

cutoffs.value: ≥5 points: platelets, D-dimer (fibrin marker), prolonged PT/INR, fibrinogen <1 g/L

kdl-o-217.q: Methods of determining total protein and drawing a calibration graph?
plan: Biuret method: in an alkaline medium Cu²⁺ ions form a violet complex with peptide bonds; the color intensity is proportional to protein concentration (photometry).

Calibration: with calibrator(s) of known concentration (usually human serum-based or an albumin standard); absorbance is measured at several concentrations and a "concentration–optical density" graph is drawn; the linearity range is checked.
The concentration of an unknown sample is found from the graph or calculated via a factor (C_st/A_st); the blank (reagent and sample blank) is taken into account.
The type of calibrator affects the result – calibration must be traceable to reference materials and verified with control materials.
Errors: interference from lipemia, hemolysis, bilirubin; diluting samples above the linearity limit; the result is interpreted against the laboratory reference interval.

kdl-o-218.q: Methods of determining urea in blood and clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Methods: urease–glutamate dehydrogenase kinetic UV method (decrease of NADH at 340 nm) – the main one on automated analyzers; urease + conductometry/ion-selective electrode; urease Berthelot colorimetric method.
Sample: serum or plasma (not ammonium anticoagulant); avoid hemolysis and ammonia contamination.
Increase (azotemia): prerenal (dehydration, heart failure, shock, GI bleeding), renal (acute/chronic kidney disease), postrenal (obstruction); catabolism, protein-rich food, glucocorticoids.
Decrease: severe liver failure (urea synthesis falls), protein deficiency, pregnancy, overhydration.
Interpretation together with creatinine/eGFR; the urea/creatinine ratio helps to suggest a prerenal state, but its diagnostic value is limited.

kdl-o-219.q: Methods of determining creatinine in blood and clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Methods: Jaffe (picrate, kinetic) – cheap, but interference from glucose, ketones, bilirubin, some drugs; enzymatic methods – more specific, preferred by KDIGO.
Standardization and quality: IDMS-traceable calibration, CV <2.3%, bias <3.7%; separate plasma within 12 hours; control for low values in children.
eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021) in the report together with creatinine; <60 mL/min/1.73 m² is considered reduced; the combination with cystatin C is more accurate.
Increase: reduced GFR (acute and chronic kidney diseases, prerenal and postrenal causes), large muscle mass, meat-rich diet.
Decrease: low muscle mass (old age, amputation, cachexia), pregnancy (GFR rises).

cutoffs.criterion: Analytical requirement for the creatinine method
cutoffs.value: CV <2.3%; bias <3.7%; calibration traceable to a reference material; enzymatic method preferred

kdl-o-220.q: Methods of determining transaminase activity (kinetic method, end-point), their advantages and disadvantages?
plan: Kinetic (continuous) method: reaction rate is measured at several points (decrease of NADH at 340 nm) – in the substrate-saturated, linear phase; the IFCC reference procedure at 37 °C (with added pyridoxal phosphate) is the international standard.
Advantages of the kinetic method: high specificity and precision, linearity control (substrate depletion is detected), automation, possibility of standardization and interlaboratory comparison.
End-point (colorimetric) methods: cheap, simple equipment; disadvantages – linearity of the reaction cannot be controlled, underestimate at high activity, poorly standardized – historical.
Errors: hemolysis (AST), lipemia, need for dilution at high activity (substrate depletion), disturbance of temperature and pH.
Result in U/L; reference intervals depend on method and temperature.

kdl-o-221.q: The role of transaminases in amino acid metabolism?
plan: Transaminases transfer an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid; the coenzyme is pyridoxal phosphate (B6).
ALT: alanine + α-ketoglutarate ⇄ pyruvate + glutamate; AST: aspartate + α-ketoglutarate ⇄ oxaloacetate + glutamate.

Significance: amino acid catabolism (nitrogen collects in glutamate, then undergoes oxidative deamination – ammonia into the urea cycle), linking amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism (gluconeogenesis substrates, glucose–alanine cycle), synthesis of non-essential amino acids.
AST takes part in the malate–aspartate "shuttle" (reducing equivalents between mitochondria and cytoplasm).
Clinical reflection: released into the blood upon cell damage – markers of damage of the liver (ALT) and other tissues (AST).

kdl-o-222.q: Determining amylase activity, clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Determination: kinetic photometric method with chromogenic oligosaccharide substrates in serum/plasma or urine (IFCC reference procedure at 37 °C); the pancreatic isoenzyme can be determined separately.
Acute pancreatitis: lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN + typical pain and/or imaging (2 of 3 criteria); amylase rises quickly and falls quickly, lipase is more specific and persists longer.
Hyperamylasemia other than in pancreatitis: salivary gland diseases (parotitis), macroamylasemia, renal failure, intestinal perforation/ischemia, ectopic pregnancy.
The enzyme level does not reflect the severity of pancreatitis.
Urinary amylase and amylase/creatinine clearance – additional (in macroamylasemia urinary amylase is low).

cutoffs.value: 2 of 3: typical pain; lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN; imaging

kdl-o-223.q: Methods of determining bilirubin. Clinical significance of the parameters?
plan: Methods: diazo (Jendrassik–Grof type; direct – without accelerator, total – with accelerator), vanadate/enzymatic oxidation; neonatal direct spectrophotometry.
The sample is protected from light; hemolysis and lipemia distort the result.
Increased indirect bilirubin: hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, Gilbert and Crigler–Najjar syndromes, physiological jaundice of newborns.
Increased direct bilirubin: hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, cholestasis, bile duct obstruction (stone, tumor), Dubin–Johnson/Rotor.
Interpretation with other tests: ALT/AST (hepatocellular), ALP/GGT (cholestasis), hemolysis markers, bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine.

kdl-o-224.q: Fundamentals of enzyme diagnostics. Some enzymes and their importance in diagnosing diseases?
plan: Basics: enzymes enter the blood when cells are damaged; organ specificity, localization in the cell (cytoplasm/mitochondria) and half-life determine interpretation; IFCC standardization.
Liver: ALT, AST (hepatocellular), ALP, GGT (cholestasis), cholinesterase (synthesis).
Pancreas: lipase (more specific), amylase – acute pancreatitis (≥3×ULN).
Muscle and heart: CK (muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis), CK-MB – heart; in diagnosing myocardial infarction high-sensitivity troponin is now the standard, the old "enzyme panel" (AST, LDH) is not used.
Bone: ALP (bone isoenzyme); prostate: PSA instead of acid phosphatase; LDH – a nonspecific marker of hemolysis, tumor burden, tissue damage.

cutoffs.value: 2 of 3: typical pain; lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN; imaging

plan: Causes of hyperenzymemia: cell damage and necrosis (hepatitis, infarction, rhabdomyolysis, pancreatitis), increased membrane permeability, induction of enzyme synthesis (GGT – alcohol, drugs), production by tumor cells, reduced enzyme clearance (amylase in renal failure), macroenzymes (macroamylase, macro-CK).
In cholestasis the synthesis of ALP and GGT increases; physiological increase – ALP in the growth period, placental ALP in pregnancy, CK after exertion.

Causes of hypoenzymemia: reduced enzyme synthesis (cholinesterase in liver failure), inherited deficiencies (pseudocholinesterase, ALP – hypophosphatasia), inhibitors (organophosphates), cofactor deficiency (transaminases low in B6 deficiency), loss of many cells (pancreatic insufficiency).
Analytical causes: hemolysis (AST, LDH), incorrect storage (loss of activity), substrate depletion.
Interpretation with the clinical picture and other tests; standardized IFCC methods.
Ketone bodies are acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone; they are synthesized in liver mitochondria from acetyl-CoA formed by β-oxidation of fatty acids.

Pathway: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase – the rate-limiting step) → acetoacetate; it is reduced to β-hydroxybutyrate or decarboxylated to acetone (exhaled in the breath – "fruity" odor).
Regulation: glucagon enhances, insulin inhibits; fasting, a carbohydrate-free diet, insulin deficiency (DKA), alcohol increase ketogenesis.
The liver cannot use ketones (lacks the enzyme SCOT); the brain (in prolonged fasting), heart and muscles use them as an energy source.
Laboratory: blood β-hydroxybutyrate (enzymatic; DKA criterion ≥3.0 mmol/L) is preferred; nitroprusside test strips in urine mainly detect acetoacetate and do not detect β-hydroxybutyrate.

cutoffs.value: glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L or a history of diabetes; β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L; acidosis: pH <7.30 and/or HCO3 <18 mmol/L (the mild DKA threshold in the severity table)

plan: Fatty degeneration of the liver (steatosis) is the accumulation of TG in hepatocytes; under the 2023 international consensus the term is "steatotic liver disease" (SLD), the metabolic form – MASLD (formerly NAFLD), the inflammatory form – MASH.

Diagnosis of MASLD: steatosis + at least 1 cardiometabolic factor (obesity, diabetes/prediabetes, hypertension, high TG, low HDL); with added alcohol – MetALD; other causes (alcohol, drugs, viral hepatitis) separately.
Laboratory: ALT/AST mildly to moderately raised or normal (normal enzymes do not exclude the disease), GGT, TG, glucose/HbA1c, lipid profile.
Assessing fibrosis risk: noninvasive indices (FIB-4 – based on age, AST, ALT, platelets), then elastography or the ELF test.
Excluding secondary causes: viral hepatitis, alcohol, drugs, Wilson disease (in the young), hypothyroidism.

Hyperlipoproteinemia is an increase of one or more classes of lipoproteins in the blood; Fredrickson (WHO) phenotypes: I – chylomicrons, IIa – LDL, IIb – LDL and VLDL, III – remnants (dysbetalipoproteinemia), IV – VLDL, V – chylomicrons + VLDL.
Primary causes: familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor, etc.), familial combined hyperlipidemia, LPL or apoC-II deficiency (type I), apoE variant (type III), familial hypertriglyceridemia.
Secondary causes: diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, alcohol, obesity, drugs.
Laboratory diagnosis: lipid profile, non-HDL cholesterol, apoB, Lp(a); lipoprotein electrophoresis if needed; excluding secondary causes (TSH, glucose/HbA1c, creatinine, urine protein, liver tests).
Risk: LDL and apoB – atherosclerosis; very high TG (>5.6 mmol/L) – pancreatitis.

cutoffs.value: optimal <1.7 (150 mg/dL); mildly raised 1.7–2.2 (150–199); high 2.3–5.6 (200–499); very high >5.6 (>500) – risk of pancreatitis

cutoffs.criterion: Lp(a) – inherited very high level (ESC/EAS 2019 guideline)
cutoffs.value: Recommendation of section 5.5: ≥180 mg/dL (≥430 nmol/L) – identify by measuring at least once in a lifetime; in the text of section 5.3.4 >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) – increased lifetime ASCVD risk (the source differs between "≥" and ">"). This is not a universal norm or a single risk threshold
cutoffs.unit: mg/dL (nmol/L value from the source itself; conversion depends on the assay)

cutoffs.guideline: EAS consensus statement 2022 (Kronenberg et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3925)

cutoffs.value: >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) – lifetime ASCVD risk equivalent to untreated heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

plan: Dietary lipids are mainly triglycerides, as well as phospholipids and cholesterol esters.

In the stomach gastric lipase breaks down part of the TG; the main digestion is in the duodenum: bile acids emulsify fat, pancreatic lipase (with colipase) breaks TG down to 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids; phospholipase A2 and cholesterol esterase also take part.
The products of digestion form mixed micelles with bile acids and are delivered to enterocytes.
In the enterocyte TG are resynthesized and assembled with apoB-48 into chylomicrons; chylomicrons enter the lymph, then the blood; LPL (activated by apoC-II) breaks them down in the tissues.

Disorders and laboratory reflection: with bile deficiency (cholestasis) or pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, steatorrhea – neutral fat and fatty acids in the coprogram; deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.
Water makes up ~60% of body weight in adults: ~2/3 inside cells, ~1/3 outside cells (interstitial and intravascular).
Water is a solvent and transport medium, thermoregulation, the medium of metabolic reactions.

Electrolytes: Na⁺ – the main cation of extracellular fluid (osmolality and volume), K⁺ – intracellular (membrane potential, neuromuscular excitability), Cl⁻ and HCO3⁻ – the main anions (acid-base balance), Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ – enzymes, contraction, hemostasis.
Plasma osmolality (~275–295 mOsm/kg) is determined mainly by Na; oncotic pressure is provided by albumin.
Disorders: dehydration/overhydration, imbalance of sodium and potassium – neurological and cardiac complications; laboratory monitoring – electrolytes, osmolality, hematocrit, protein.

plan: Osmoregulation: hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense a rise in plasma osmolality → thirst and secretion of ADH (vasopressin) → via V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts aquaporin-2 – water reabsorption.
Volume regulation: the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system – aldosterone in the distal nephron increases Na reabsorption and K excretion; its secretion is regulated by K⁺ level and the RAAS.
Natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) – natriuresis and vasodilation when volume increases.
The kidney is the final effector organ: filtration, reabsorption, concentration.
Laboratory reflection: plasma and urine osmolality, Na, K, urine Na; ADH disorders – diabetes insipidus (urine dilute, hypernatremia), SIADH (hyponatremia, urine concentrated).
Body water is divided into intracellular (~2/3) and extracellular (~1/3) compartments; extracellular fluid into interstitial (~2/3) and intravascular (plasma, ~1/3) parts.
Movement of water between the intra- and extracellular space depends on the osmotic gradient (mainly Na and glucose): if plasma is hypertonic, water leaves the cell.
Exchange across the capillary wall: the balance of hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid out) and oncotic pressure (albumin – holds fluid in) (Starling forces).
Disturbance: hypoalbuminemia and raised venous pressure – edema and fluid in cavities (transudate); in inflammation permeability rises (exudate).
Laboratory: osmolality (measured and calculated), Na, albumin/total protein, hematocrit; analysis of body cavity fluids (transudate/exudate).

Types of dehydration: isotonic (water and Na lost equally – vomiting, diarrhea, blood loss), hypertonic (more water lost – sweating, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis; Na >145 mmol/L, osmolality >300), hypotonic (more Na lost – diuretics, adrenal insufficiency).
Laboratory signs: raised hematocrit and total protein (hemoconcentration), increased urea/creatinine ratio (prerenal), high urine density/osmolality, low urine Na (if there is no renal cause).
Overhydration: isotonic (edema – heart, kidney, liver failure), hypotonic (water intoxication, SIADH – hyponatremia), hypertonic (hypertonic solutions).
In overhydration hemodilution: decrease in Ht, protein, Na.
During treatment correct Na slowly (risk of osmotic demyelination) – frequent monitoring of electrolytes.
Plasma osmolality: measured (osmometer – freezing point depression) and calculated (2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8, mg/dL; in mmol/L 2Na + glucose + urea); normal ~275–295 mOsm/kg.
Osmolal gap (measured − calculated) – an increase points to toxic osmoles (methanol, ethylene glycol, ethanol).
Sodium is the main indicator of water balance (hyper-/hyponatremia – water deficit/excess).
Signs of hemoconcentration: Ht, Hb, total protein, albumin; kidney: urea/creatinine, urine density and osmolality, daily urine output.
Special tests: ratio of urine and plasma osmolality, urine Na (volume status), water deprivation test (diabetes insipidus – under specialist supervision).

plan: DKA is hyperglycemia, ketonemia and metabolic acidosis in insulin deficiency and an excess of counter-regulatory hormones; more common in type 1 DM, but also in type 2 and during SGLT2 inhibitor use (euglycemic DKA).
Criteria (2024 consensus): glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L or a history of diabetes; β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L (or urine ketones ≥2+); pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L.

Laboratory monitoring: glucose, electrolytes (K⁺ – even with a total deficit may be normal/high at first), anion gap, bicarbonate, creatinine/urea, osmolality, blood gases, β-hydroxybutyrate; correct Na for glucose.
Difference from the hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state: in HHS glucose >33.3 mmol/L (>600 mg/dL), effective osmolarity >320 mOsm/L, no significant ketoacidosis (β-HB <3.0).
Resolution criteria are based on normalization of ketones and pH/bicarbonate; during treatment potassium and glucose are measured frequently.

kdl-o-237.q: Methods of determining glucose in blood, clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Methods: hexokinase (most specific, 340 nm), glucose oxidase–peroxidase, glucose dehydrogenase (in some glucometers); laboratory diagnosis is in venous plasma.
Preanalytics: glycolysis (~5–7%/hour) – centrifuge immediately or use a tube with an inhibitor; fasting ≥8 hours.
Diagnostic significance: fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L or OGTT at 2 hours ≥11.1 – diabetes; 5.6–6.9 – impaired fasting glucose (ADA); random ≥11.1 with symptoms – diabetes.
Hypoglycemia: <3.9 mmol/L (level 1), <3.0 (level 2 – urgent measures); causes – insulin/sulfonylurea, insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency, severe liver disease, sepsis.
Other causes of hyperglycemia: stress, glucocorticoids, endocrinopathies, pancreatitis.

kdl-o-238.q: Hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia and glucosuria – the main signs of disturbed glucose metabolism?
plan: Hyperglycemia – diabetes (fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L, OGTT at 2 hours ≥11.1), prediabetes, stress, drugs, endocrinopathies; acute complications – DKA and the hyperosmolar state.
Hypoglycemia – level 1 <3.9 mmol/L, level 2 <3.0 mmol/L, level 3 – a severe condition requiring assistance; causes – insulin/secretagogues, alcohol, insulinoma, deficiency states.
Glucosuria – when blood glucose exceeds the reabsorptive capacity of the renal tubules; also renal glucosuria (tubular defect) and use of SGLT2 inhibitors – even when blood glucose is normal.
Laboratory assessment: venous plasma glucose, HbA1c, OGTT; in hypoglycemia, during the episode insulin, C-peptide, β-hydroxybutyrate together with glucose.
Urine glucose is not a diagnostic criterion – only a guiding sign.

plan: Exogenous pathway: in the intestine chylomicrons (apoB-48) → TG are removed by LPL → chylomicron remnants are taken up by the liver via apoE.
Endogenous pathway: the liver secretes VLDL (apoB-100) → with LPL IDL → LDL; LDL delivers cholesterol to the tissues via LDL receptors.
Reverse cholesterol transport: HDL (apoA-I) takes cholesterol from peripheral tissues and returns it to the liver.
Atherosclerosis: retention of apoB-containing lipoproteins in the intima, oxidation, uptake by macrophages (foam cells) and inflammation; LDL is a causal factor of ASCVD.
Laboratory monitoring: lipid profile, non-HDL cholesterol, apoB, Lp(a); LDL targets by risk level.
