kdl-o-240.q: Determining total cholesterol, clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: Method: enzymatic colorimetric (cholesterol esterase – cholesterol oxidase – peroxidase, Trinder reaction), end-point method on automated analyzers.
Sample: serum or plasma; fasting is usually not required; hemolysis, high bilirubin, ascorbate may interfere with the peroxidase reaction.
Interpretation: not alone but with HDL, LDL, TG and overall risk; non-HDL cholesterol is calculated.
Increase: primary hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, diabetes; decrease: liver failure, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, cachexia.
Quality: standardized calibrators and control, external quality control.
LDL cholesterol is the atherogenic "bad" cholesterol; the main indicator of treatment goals.
Calculation: Friedewald (mg/dL: LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5; in mmol/L TG/2.2) – at TG ≤4.5 mmol/L (400 mg/dL); inaccurate with low LDL and high TG – Martin–Hopkins or Sampson equations.
Direct homogeneous methods – when TG is high or LDL very low.
Historical "beta-lipoprotein" (turbidimetric precipitation) methods are nonspecific – LDL cholesterol and apoB are used now.
Interpretation: target by risk category (for example in very high risk <1.4 mmol/L and a reduction of ≥50%).

plan: HDL (alpha-lipoproteins) – the main apoprotein is apoA-I; transport cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver (reverse transport).

Determination: on automated analyzers direct homogeneous enzymatic methods (other lipoproteins are blocked, HDL cholesterol is measured enzymatically); historically – precipitation of apoB-containing lipoproteins (phosphotungstate/Mg²⁺, dextran sulfate) and cholesterol in the supernatant.
Clinical significance: low HDL is a risk factor; needed to calculate non-HDL cholesterol (TC − HDL); very high HDL may not be protective.
Decrease: obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 DM, smoking, sedentary lifestyle, high TG; increase: physical activity, estrogens, alcohol.
Quality: homogeneous methods are prone to error with high TG and abnormal lipoproteins.

kdl-o-243.q: Determining the apoproteins of lipoproteins (apo-B, apo-A), clinical diagnostic significance?
plan: Apolipoproteins are the protein part of lipoproteins: apoB-100 (VLDL, IDL, LDL; one per atherogenic particle), apoB-48 (chylomicrons), apoA-I (the main protein of HDL), apoC-II (LPL activator), apoE (clearance of remnants).
Determination: immunoturbidimetry or immunonephelometry; standardized, automated; fasting is not required for apoB.
apoB reflects the number of atherogenic particles; a better risk indicator than LDL cholesterol, especially with high TG, diabetes, obesity, very low LDL.
apoA-I is a surrogate for HDL; the apoB/apoA-I ratio has been studied as a risk indicator.

Lp(a) is an LDL-like particle in which apo(a) is bound to apoB; largely genetically determined; measure at least once in adults; EAS 2022: >50 mg/dL (>125 nmol/L) – confirms risk (rule-in), <30 mg/dL (<75 nmol/L) – excludes it, 30–50 – gray zone; >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) – lifetime risk equivalent to HeFH (ESC/EAS 2019: ≥180 mg/dL). Conversion between units depends on the assay.

plan: Total calcium – photometric methods on automated analyzers (colored complex with a metallochromogen); the result is interpreted together with albumin.
Ionized calcium – ISE (blood gas analyzers), anaerobic sample, pH-dependent; preferable when albumin changes.
Albumin correction: Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin, g/dL); normal ~8.8–10.4 mg/dL.
Hypercalcemia: primary hyperparathyroidism, tumors, vitamin D intoxication, granulomatous diseases; hypocalcemia: hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, CKD, hypomagnesemia, pancreatitis.
Preanalytics: prolonged tourniquet (false increase), EDTA/citrate/oxalate tubes (false decrease), hemolysis.

plan: Calcium and phosphorus are mainly in bone (hydroxyapatite); about half of the calcium in blood is ionized (active).
PTH: released in response to hypocalcemia – increases bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion, and renal 1α-hydroxylation (calcitriol).
Calcitriol (1.25(OH)2D) – intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate; calcitonin – inhibits bone resorption (small role in humans); FGF23 – phosphaturia.

Disorders: hyperparathyroidism (Ca↑, P↓, PTH↑), hypoparathyroidism (Ca↓, P↑), vitamin D deficiency (Ca normal/↓, P↓, PTH↑), CKD (P↑, PTH↑ – secondary hyperparathyroidism), malignancy-associated hypercalcemia (PTH low, PTHrP↑).
Laboratory: Ca (corrected/ionized), phosphate, Mg, PTH, 25(OH)D, ALP, creatinine, urine calcium.

kdl-o-247.q: Determining sodium and potassium in blood serum, clinical diagnostic significance?
plan: Method – ISE: direct (undiluted, blood gas analyzers) and indirect (diluted, biochemistry analyzers); flame photometry – historical.

Sodium: normal ~136–145 mmol/L; hyponatremia – water excess (SIADH, heart/liver/renal failure) or Na loss; false hyponatremia – lipemia/paraproteinemia with indirect ISE; translocational hyponatremia in hyperglycemia.

Potassium: normal ~3.5–5.0 mmol/L; hypokalemia – diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, hyperaldosteronism, insulin; hyperkalemia – renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, drugs (RAAS blockers), acidosis, cell breakdown.
Pseudohyperkalemia: hemolysis, fist clenching, tourniquet, K-EDTA contamination, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis – recheck in heparinized plasma before treatment.
Critical values are reported urgently (risk of arrhythmia).

plan: Main methods: immunoturbidimetry and immunonephelometry (CRP, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, α1-antitrypsin, transferrin, fibrinogen antigen), immunochemiluminescence (procalcitonin, ferritin, IL-6).
Fibrinogen – the functional Clauss method (based on thrombin time, on a coagulometer); albumin – dye-binding methods.
Electrophoresis: increase of the α1 and α2 fractions (acute inflammation pattern), decrease of albumin.
Semi-quantitative latex agglutination (CRP) – fast, but imprecise; quantitative methods are preferred.
Interpretation: dynamics of CRP and procalcitonin; consider the effect of the acute phase in ferritin, albumin, transferrin results.
Cytokines are small proteins that transmit intercellular signals (interleukins, interferons, TNF, colony-stimulating factors, chemokines); autocrine, paracrine, endocrine action.
Functional groups: proinflammatory (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), anti-inflammatory (IL-10, TGF-β), Th1/Th2/Th17 profiles, hematopoietic factors.
Properties: pleiotropy, redundancy, cascades and synergism/antagonism.
Clinical significance: IL-6 triggers the synthesis of acute-phase proteins (CRP); "cytokine storm"; targets of biological therapy.
Laboratory: ELISA or multiplex immunoassay; short half-life and preanalytical factors, interference from heterophile antibodies.
Both methods are based on the interaction of light with particles formed by antigen–antibody immune complexes.
Immunoturbidimetry: the decrease in transmitted light (turbidity) is measured by a photometer in the direction of the light source – performed on ordinary biochemistry analyzers.
Nephelometry: light scattered by the immune complexes is measured at an angle (for example 90° or at a small angle) – a special nephelometer; more sensitive at low concentrations.
Attaching antibody to latex particles increases sensitivity (hs-CRP, myoglobin, etc.).

Limitations: with antigen excess (prozone/hook effect) a falsely low result – check for antigen excess on the analyzer or dilute; interference from lipemia, turbidity; dependence on the calibrator and antibody lot.
Quantitative immunochemical methods: immunoturbidimetry (latex-enhanced), immunonephelometry – the main methods.
hs-CRP – a high-sensitivity method able to measure low concentrations (fractions of mg/L) – for cardiovascular risk.
Semi-quantitative latex agglutination (on a slide) – rapid screening, titer with dilutions; imprecise, subjective.
Point-of-care (immunochromatographic/immunoturbidimetric) – in outpatient settings.
Quality: two-level control, excluding the prozone effect, reporting the result in mg/L; <3 mg/L normal, >10 mg/L – active inflammation.

plan: Ceruloplasmin is an α2-glycoprotein synthesized in the liver, the carrier of ~95% of copper in the blood.
Ferroxidase activity: oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ – necessary for loading iron onto transferrin and for iron metabolism.
A positive acute-phase protein: rises in inflammation, pregnancy, under the influence of estrogens.
Decrease: Wilson disease (ATP7B defect – copper is not loaded onto ceruloplasmin, the apoform is rapidly degraded), copper deficiency, severe liver failure, protein loss.
Diagnosis of Wilson disease: low ceruloplasmin + raised copper in 24-hour urine + Kayser–Fleischer ring (and other tests); ceruloplasmin is determined by an immunochemical (nephelometric) method.

kdl-o-253.q: Teratogenic effect of rubella, herpes, CMV?
plan: Rubella: primary infection in pregnancy (especially the first trimester) leads to fetal death and congenital rubella syndrome (severe congenital malformations); prevention – vaccination before pregnancy.
CMV: the most common infectious cause of birth defects in the USA; ~10% of infants have symptoms at birth, 40–60% of them have long-term complications; hearing loss may appear at birth or later.
Herpes (HSV): mainly transmitted in the birth canal – neonatal herpes (skin, CNS, disseminated); transplacental transmission is rare.
Laboratory: rubella – serology and PCR; CMV – saliva/urine PCR within 2–3 weeks in the newborn; HSV – PCR from lesions/CSF; IgG avidity in the mother when assessing primary infection.
The teratogenic effect depends on the timing of infection and the mother's immune status; screening and counseling.

kdl-o-254.q: Glycosylated hemoglobin, clinical and diagnostic significance?
plan: HbA1c reflects average glycemia over 2–3 months; fasting is not required, day-to-day variability is small.
Diagnostic thresholds: ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol) – diabetes (with confirmation), 5.7–6.4% – prediabetes; only an NGSP-certified method standardized to DCCT.
Monitoring: treatment target in most adults <7% (individualized); in stable patients at least twice a year, in those not meeting the target every 3 months.

Limitations: hemoglobinopathies and HbF (method-dependent), changed erythrocyte lifespan (hemolysis, blood loss, transfusion, pregnancy, iron deficiency, CKD/hemodialysis, erythropoietin) – assessed by glucose or fructosamine.
The risk of complications (retinopathy, nephropathy) is related to the HbA1c level.

plan: Principle: latex particles coated with antigen or antibody produce visible agglutination with the corresponding component in the sample.
Use: CRP, rheumatoid factor, ASO and some microbial antigens; rapid screening tests.
Qualitative and semi-quantitative performance: serial dilution of the sample, approximate concentration by the last positive dilution.
Limitations: subjective reading, prozone (hook) effect – false negative at high concentration, nonspecific agglutination; in the modern laboratory quantitative turbidimetry/nephelometry is preferred.
Quality control: positive and negative controls, reagent temperature, reading time.
Hematopoiesis is the stepwise differentiation of all blood cells from the self-renewing hematopoietic stem cell.

Hierarchy: HSC → multipotent progenitors → common myeloid progenitor (megakaryocytes, erythrocytes, granulocytes, monocytes) and common lymphoid progenitor (B, T, NK); according to new data there is less branching and differentiation is more continuous.
Sites of hematopoiesis: in the embryo the yolk sac and AGM, in the fetus the liver and spleen, after birth the bone marrow.
Regulation: erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, colony-stimulating factors, interleukins and bone marrow niche signals.
Practical significance: leukemias and MDS are clonal diseases of stem/progenitor cells; immunophenotyping (CD34, etc.) determines the cell lineage.

Morphology: a reticulocyte is an anucleate young erythrocyte, slightly larger than a mature one; on Romanowsky stain polychromatophilic (grayish-bluish), on supravital stain (new methylene blue, brilliant cresyl blue) RNA remnants as a network/granules.
Formation: after an orthochromic erythroblast extrudes its nucleus it becomes a reticulocyte; it matures into an erythrocyte over 1–3 days in the bone marrow and 1–2 days in the blood.
Function: contains hemoglobin – carries oxygen; thanks to residual RNA it continues hemoglobin synthesis for a short time.
Diagnostic significance: an indicator of erythropoietic activity – normal ~0.5–2.5%; corrected by RPI; IRF – the youngest fraction, CHr – iron availability.
Increase – hemolysis, blood loss, response to treatment; decrease – hypoproliferative anemias, aplasia, aplastic crisis.
Pathogenetic classification: blood loss; insufficient erythropoiesis (iron, B12/folate deficiency, inflammation, bone marrow failure, kidney disease); hemolysis (inherited and acquired).

Morphological (MCV): microcytic – iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic, some anemias of chronic disease; normocytic – blood loss, hemolysis, chronic disease, kidney, aplasia; macrocytic – megaloblastic (B12, folate) and non-megaloblastic (liver, alcohol, hypothyroidism, MDS).
By regenerative capacity: reticulocytes/RPI high – hemolysis, blood loss; low – impaired production.
By severity depending on the Hb level: mild, moderate, severe (WHO thresholds).
The classification determines the work-up algorithm: indices → reticulocytes → targeted tests (ferritin/TSAT, B12/folate, hemolysis markers, bone marrow).

plan: Aplastic anemia is bone marrow failure: hypocellular bone marrow and pancytopenia without infiltration and dysplasia.
Causes: idiopathic (immune – T cells destroy stem cells), drugs and chemicals (benzene), radiation, viruses (hepatitis), pregnancy; inherited (Fanconi anemia, telomere diseases).
Laboratory: pancytopenia, reticulocytopenia, normo-/macrocytic anemia; no blasts or dysplasia on the smear.
Trephine biopsy is mandatory: cellularity <25% (fat tissue predominates); aspirate is often "dry".
Severity (Camitta): severe – low cellularity + two of the following: neutrophils <0.5×10⁹/L, platelets <20×10⁹/L, reticulocytes low; very severe – neutrophils <0.2×10⁹/L.
Differential: hypoplastic MDS, PNH (testing for the PNH clone by flow cytometry), aleukemic leukemia, B12 deficiency.

cutoffs.value: cellularity <25% (or 25–50%, <30% hematopoietic) + two of: ANC <0.5; platelets <20; reticulocytes <60 (sometimes <40); very severe: ANC <0.2

plan: Acute posthemorrhagic anemia: in the first hours Hb/Ht may be normal (plasma and erythrocytes are lost together); Hb falls after plasma volume is restored or with fluid infusion – hence serial CBCs.
The anemia is normocytic normochromic; as the bone marrow response, reticulocytosis after a few days (MCV may rise slightly), reactive leukocytosis and thrombocytosis may occur.
Chronic blood loss (GI tract, menorrhagia) leads through iron deficiency to microcytic hypochromic anemia.
Laboratory monitoring: CBC, reticulocytes, blood group and crossmatch tests, coagulogram (in massive bleeding DIC – platelets and fibrinogen fall), urea (may rise in GI bleeding).
Identifying the source and assessing iron stores (ferritin).
Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation) – in infections, autoimmune diseases, tumors, CKD; one of the most common anemias in hospital.

Mechanism: IL-6 raises hepcidin → ferroportin is degraded → intestinal iron absorption and release from macrophages fall ("functional" iron deficiency); the response to erythropoietin is blunted, erythrocyte lifespan is shortened.

Laboratory: usually mild-moderate normocytic normochromic (may later become microcytic), reticulocytes low; serum iron low, TSAT low, transferrin/TIBC normal or low, ferritin normal or high (acute-phase protein), CRP high.

Distinguishing from iron deficiency: ferritin <30 µg/L – absolute deficiency (WHO: in inflammation in adults <70 µg/L); in inflammation ferritin <100 ng/mL and TSAT <20% – coexisting deficiency is likely (StatPearls Anemia); sTfR and sTfR/log ferritin, CHr help.
In bone marrow iron in macrophages is preserved, sideroblasts are few.

kdl-o-262.q: Interpreting hematology analyzer parameters and comparing them with the parameters of a complete blood count done by a routine method?
plan: The analyzer result is more accurate and reproducible than manual methods (chamber, smear), since thousands of cells are measured; in manual methods the statistical error is large because few cells are counted.

Comparison: RBC, WBC, PLT – the analyzer's impedance/optical method vs chamber; Hb – analyzer photometry vs the manual hemiglobincyanide method (reference); Ht – calculated on the analyzer, manual – microhematocrit (centrifuge).
Differential: the analyzer gives 5 populations, a manual smear of 100–200 cells shows morphology (blasts, atypical cells, erythrocyte shape, inclusions) – the methods complement each other.

Old "routine" parameters have been replaced by modern ones: for example, MCH/MCHC instead of the color index, RDW instead of manual assessment of anisocytosis, flow cytometry instead of manual reticulocytes.

When results disagree, preanalytical causes (clot, hemolysis, delay) and interferences (agglutination, lipemia, platelet clumps) are checked; with analyzer "flags" and abnormal results the smear is examined.
The analyzer's trueness is ensured by control materials and calibration, its reproducibility by internal quality control.

kdl-o-266.q: Leukemias, etiology, pathogenesis, stages. Clinical diagnostic characteristics?
plan: Leukemias are clonal neoplasia of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells; risk factors: radiation, benzene, cytostatics, inherited syndromes, prior MDS/MPN.
Pathogenesis: genetic damage (translocations – BCR::ABL1, PML::RARA; mutations – FLT3, NPM1, etc.) arrests differentiation and enhances proliferation; normal hematopoiesis is suppressed.
Stages (clinical course): initial, advanced (overt), remission (complete/partial), relapse, terminal; in CML chronic phase → accelerated → blast crisis.
Clinical diagnostic signs: anemic, hemorrhagic, infectious and hyperplastic (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly) syndromes; in blood blasts, cytopenias or leukocytosis.
Diagnosis: CBC/smear → bone marrow → cytochemistry, immunophenotype, cytogenetics/molecular; classification by WHO-2022/ICC.

kdl-o-267.q: Blood and bone marrow slide findings in chronic leukemias?
plan: CML: in blood leukocytosis, granulocytes of all stages (many myelocytes and segmented forms), basophilia/eosinophilia, blasts <2% (chronic phase); bone marrow markedly hypercellular, granulocytic hyperplasia, small megakaryocytes; Ph/BCR::ABL1 positive.

CLL: in blood >5×10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes, small mature lymphocytes, "smudge" cells; immunophenotype CD5+, CD23+, CD19+, light chain restriction; in bone marrow lymphocytic infiltration (diffuse or nodular).
Signs of acceleration/blast crisis (CML): increase of blasts and basophils, new cytogenetic changes.
For other chronic neoplasms (for example hairy cell leukemia, prolymphocytic) morphology + immunophenotype are also assessed together.
Monitoring treatment: in CML quantitative BCR::ABL1 (RT-PCR), in CLL blood counts and flow cytometry.

cutoffs.value: >5×10⁹/L clonal B lymphocytes (characteristic immunophenotype); <5×10⁹/L – MBL
cutoffs.guideline: French CLL Study Group (based on iwCLL)

plan: Nuclear signs (the most important): nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism (anisokaryosis), increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia, coarse and unevenly distributed chromatin, irregular nuclear membrane (folds, indentations), large or multiple nucleoli, multinucleation, atypical mitoses.
Cytoplasmic signs: disturbed differentiation (reduced cytoplasm, basophilia), unusual keratinization or vacuolization.
Intercellular relationships: reduced cohesion (single cells), three-dimensional clusters, overlapping, molding, cell-in-cell.
Background: necrosis, tumor diathesis, blood.
Criteria are assessed together rather than singly; reactive atypia, regeneration, radiation and viral changes can also produce nuclear changes – when in doubt additional tests and histology.

kdl-o-269.q: Cytological diagnosis of malignant tumors of the uterus and cervix?
plan: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and its precursors: HSIL (CIN2/3) – immature cells, high N/C ratio, hyperchromasia; carcinoma – keratinized pleomorphic cells ("fiber", "tadpole" forms), prominent nucleoli, tumor diathesis.
Glandular tumors: AGC, endocervical adenocarcinoma in situ and invasive adenocarcinoma (glandular clusters, nuclear atypia), endometrial adenocarcinoma cells.
Cytology is limited in detecting endometrial pathology – the diagnosis is confirmed histologically (biopsy).
The result is in Bethesda 2014 terminology, together with HPV testing and colposcopy/biopsy.
Differentiation from reactive changes, atrophy and radiation effect.

kdl-o-270.q: Bacterioscopic examination of sputum in pulmonary tuberculosis?
plan: Bacterioscopy is the detection of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) in a sputum smear by Ziehl-Neelsen (light microscope) or auramine (fluorescence microscope).
Specimen: 2 (or 3) sputum specimens, at least one early morning; smear from the purulent part; if bacilli are few – enrichment (centrifugation).
Grading: "scanty" (1–9/100 fields), 1+ (10–99/100 fields), 2+ (1–10/field), 3+ (>10/field).

Limitations: low sensitivity (especially in people living with HIV and in children), does not distinguish M. tuberculosis from other mycobacteria and does not determine drug susceptibility – WHO recommends rapid molecular tests as the initial test; microscopy is used in treatment monitoring.
Biosafety and quality: external rechecking (blind rechecking), reagent control.

cutoffs.value: none in 100 fields – negative; 1–9/100 – exact number; 10–99/100 – 1+; 1–10/field – 2+; >10/field – 3+

plan: Normal cytogram: superficial and intermediate squamous cells, metaplastic and endocervical cells from the transformation zone, few leukocytes, lactobacilli.

Inflammation/infection: many neutrophils, reactive changes; organisms – trichomonads, Candida, "clue" cells (bacterial vaginosis), herpes virus effect (multinucleated cells, "ground-glass" nuclei, molding).
Atrophy: predominance of parabasal cells; hyperkeratosis/parakeratosis; repair.
HPV effect and precancer: koilocytes, LSIL, HSIL; carcinoma – malignant cells and diathesis.
The cytogram is described in Bethesda 2014 terminology; interpretation with clinical data and HPV testing.

General signs of malignant tumor cells: nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia, uneven chromatin, large nucleoli, atypical mitoses, loss of cohesion, necrotic background.

Carcinomas: squamous cell (keratinization), adenocarcinoma (glandular structures, vacuoles), small cell (small, molded nuclei); sarcomas – spindle/pleomorphic cells; lymphomas – diffusely scattered monotonous lymphoid cells; melanoma – pigment, large nucleoli.
Material: exfoliative (sputum, fluids, urine, smears) and aspiration (fine needle aspirate).
Additional methods: cell block, immunocytochemistry (tumor origin), flow cytometry (lymphomas), molecular tests (therapy targets).
Limitations: differentiation from reactive atypia, specimen adequacy; histological confirmation if needed.
Definition: substances (proteins, glycoproteins, hormones, enzymes, genetic changes) detectable in blood, urine, tissue as a result of tumor cells or the body's response to a tumor.
Properties of the "ideal" marker and real limitations: high sensitivity and specificity are rarely found; increase in benign diseases (liver, inflammation).
Purposes of use: monitoring treatment effect and detecting recurrence – the main one; some in diagnosis, prognosis or choosing treatment (tissue markers).
Analytical aspects: immunoassay, lack of standardization between methods, serial measurements should be done in the same laboratory.
Interpretation: dynamics, together with clinical data and imaging.
Blood/serum markers: PSA (prostate), CEA (colon, etc.), AFP (liver, embryonal tumors), β-hCG (embryonal, trophoblastic), CA-125 and HE4 (ovary), CA 15-3 (breast), CA 19-9 (pancreas, bile ducts).
Other blood markers: calcitonin (medullary thyroid cancer), thyroglobulin (differentiated thyroid cancer), chromogranin A and NSE (neuroendocrine), LDH, β2-microglobulin (myeloma, lymphomas).
Tissue/molecular markers: ER/PR, HER2 (breast), mutations such as EGFR, ALK, KRAS – for choosing treatment.
Grouping by chemical nature: oncofetal antigens, glycoproteins, hormones, enzymes, genetic changes.
For each marker know the purpose (diagnosis, prognosis, monitoring) and the limitations.

kdl-o-275.q: Leukemoid reactions of the myeloid type?
plan: A myeloid-type leukemoid reaction – neutrophils usually >50×10⁹/L, mainly mature forms (bands, segmented), metamyelocytes/myelocytes may be present; there is no myeloproliferative neoplasm.
Causes: severe bacterial infections and sepsis, acute hemorrhage, hemolysis, burns, tumors (paraneoplastic, G-CSF-producing), drugs (glucocorticoids, G-CSF).
Morphology: toxic granulation, "left shift"; blasts and basophilia are usually absent.
Difference from CML: LAP is high (low in CML), no basophilia, BCR::ABL1 negative, polyclonal; normalizes after the underlying disease is treated.
Leukoerythroblastosis (immature granulocytes + nucleated erythrocytes) – points to bone marrow infiltration or severe stress.

cutoffs.value: >50×10⁹/L (no MPN)

kdl-o-276.q: Leukemoid reactions of the lymphomonocytic type?
plan: Leukemoid reactions of the lymphocytic/monocytic type – absolute lymphocytosis and/or monocytosis, often with atypical (reactive) mononuclear cells.

Causes: viral infections (EBV – infectious mononucleosis, CMV, hepatitis), whooping cough, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, stress; monocytosis – chronic infections (tuberculosis, endocarditis), inflammation.
Morphology: reactive lymphocytes – large, with broad bluish cytoplasm "embracing" erythrocytes, pleomorphic cells; differ from the monotonous small lymphocytes of CLL.
Differentiation: testing clonality by flow cytometry (polyclonal in reactive); EBV serology; if prolonged a lymphoproliferative disease is sought.
The reaction disappears after recovery from the underlying disease.
Infectious mononucleosis is an acute infection caused mainly by EBV (sometimes CMV); fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly.
Blood: leukocytosis, lymphocytosis (>50%) and atypical lymphocytes (>10%) – reactive CD8 T lymphocytes (Downey cells); thrombocytopenia and neutropenia may occur.
Heterophile antibodies (monospot): sensitivity 63–84%, specificity 84–100% (lower than EBV-specific antibodies); may be negative at the start of the illness and in children.
EBV-specific serology: VCA IgM (acute infection), VCA IgG, EBNA IgG (appears after several months – its presence in the acute period argues against acute infection); EBV DNA (PCR) if needed.
Biochemistry: transaminases are often raised (mild hepatitis).
Differential: acute leukemia and lymphomas (smear, flow cytometry), CMV, acute HIV infection, toxoplasmosis.

kdl-o-278.q: Leukemoid reactions of the eosinophilic type?
plan: Eosinophilia – absolute eosinophils >0.5×10⁹/L; very high levels are considered an eosinophilic-type leukemoid reaction.

Causes: allergic diseases (asthma, atopic dermatitis), helminth infestations (especially in the tissue phase – Ascaris migration, toxocariasis, trichinellosis, fascioliasis), drug reactions (DRESS), rheumatological diseases and vasculitis, some tumors (Hodgkin lymphoma), adrenal insufficiency.
Laboratory approach: absolute count, eosinophil morphology on the smear, stool and serological tests for helminths, IgE, signs of organ damage.
In persistent high eosinophilia, if no reactive cause is found, bone marrow and genetic studies with a hematologist to exclude clonal (hematological) causes.
After the underlying disease is treated, reactive eosinophilia decreases.

kdl-o-279.q: Malaria, species, detecting parasites in the thick drop and smear?
plan: Species causing malaria in humans: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi.

Thick drop: erythrocytes are hemolyzed, large blood volume – sensitive for finding the parasite; the thin smear is fixed in methanol – erythrocyte and parasite morphology are preserved, the species is identified.
Giemsa staining (standard pH), viewing with an oil-immersion objective; do not call it negative until enough fields have been examined.
Species differences (on the thin smear): erythrocyte size, Schüffner's dots, number of rings, gametocyte shape (banana/crescent in P. falciparum).
Calculating parasitemia and recording the result; if negative repeat, PCR if needed.
kdl-o-279.note: The morphological features of the species (Schüffner's dots, gametocyte shape) were not separately checked against the DPDx species table.

kdl-o-280.q: Inflammatory diseases of the female genital organs?
plan: Lower genital tract: vaginitis (bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, aerobic and atrophic vaginitis), cervicitis (chlamydia, gonococcus, Mycoplasma genitalium, herpes).
Upper genital tract: pelvic inflammatory disease (endometritis, salpingitis, tubo-ovarian abscess) – often begins with chlamydia and gonococcus.
Laboratory diagnosis: vaginal pH, KOH test, wet mount and Gram-stained smear (Nugent score, "clue" cells, fungi, trichomonads, leukocytes), NAAT for chlamydia, gonococcus and trichomonads.
General inflammatory parameters (leukocytosis, CRP, ESR) in severe forms; pregnancy test; syphilis and HIV serology.
In cervicitis many leukocytes on the smear – etiology determined by NAAT; in cytology reactive inflammatory changes and organisms (Bethesda NILM).
Insufficiency of gastric digestion: undigested muscle fibers (creatorrhea), connective tissue; in achylia – fermentation processes.
Pancreatic (pancreatic exocrine insufficiency) syndrome: abundant, fatty, gray stool, neutral fat (steatorrhea), creatorrhea, amylorrhea; confirmation – fecal elastase (<100 µg/g), quantitative fat.
Hepatobiliary (hypo-/acholia) syndrome: pale (acholic) stool, no stercobilin, many fatty acids and soaps.

Small intestinal (enteral) and large intestinal (colitis) syndromes: liquid stool, undigested residues; in colitis mucus, leukocytes, erythrocytes; fermentative dyspepsia (acidic pH, starch, iodophilic flora) and putrefactive dyspepsia (alkaline pH, muscle fibers).
Syndromes of inflammation and bleeding: leukocytes, calprotectin, occult blood (FIT); parasitic syndrome – eggs/cysts, eosinophilic elements.

reference.note: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

cutoffs.value: fecal fat >7 g/24 h; elastase <100 µg/g (100–200 indeterminate)

kdl-o-282.q: Sensitivity and specificity of laboratory methods of examination?
plan: A four-field (2×2) table: true positive (TP), false positive (FP), false negative (FN), true negative (TN) – comparison with the "gold standard".

Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) – ability to detect the diseased (when high, a negative result excludes the disease); specificity = TN/(TN+FP) – correctly identifying the healthy as negative (when high, a positive result confirms).
Positive and negative predictive values (PPV = TP/(TP+FP), NPV = TN/(TN+FN)) depend on disease prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do not depend on prevalence.
Positive and negative likelihood ratios: LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity), LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity.
The choice of the diagnostic cutoff affects the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity (ROC curve); for screening high sensitivity, for confirmation high specificity.
Analytical sensitivity (limit of detection) and analytical specificity (interference, cross-reactivity) differ from diagnostic parameters.

kdl-o-283.q: Variants of presentation of skin dysbiosis?
plan: The skin microbiome is a community of bacteria, fungi, viruses and mites; its composition depends on the skin site: in moist areas Staphylococcus and Corynebacterium, in oily (seborrheic) areas Cutibacterium, in dry areas the most diverse flora.

Skin dysbiosis is a disturbance of this balance (reduced diversity, predominance of some species); a number of dermatoses are associated with dysbiosis, but whether it is a cause or a consequence is often not fully established.

Main variants of presentation: atopic dermatitis – increase of S. aureus (more in lesions, less outside lesions) and decrease of S. epidermidis/Corynebacterium; seborrheic dermatitis – association with Malassezia; acne – loss of diversity of Cutibacterium acnes phylotypes; psoriasis – altered skin and gut microbiota; alopecia areata is also being studied.

Laboratory approach: in clinical practice – culture from the lesion (for example S. aureus and antibiotic susceptibility), microscopy with KOH (fungi, Malassezia); the composition of the microbiome is assessed in research by 16S rRNA/metagenomic sequencing – not a routine diagnostic test.

Interpretation: take the sampling site into account (moist/oily/dry), distinguish colonization from infection, the result with the clinical picture; if "vaginal dysbacteriosis" is meant in the question – see the plan kdl-o-122.
kdl-o-283.note: 2026-10-09 audit: "skin dysbiosis" was written in the literal sense (dysbiosis of the skin microbiome) per PMC8936186; the official question may actually have meant "vaginal dysbacteriosis" (adjacent in the highest-category list) – must be confirmed by an expert.

kdl-o-284.q: The role of hydrochloric acid in protein digestion?
plan: HCl is secreted by gastric parietal cells (proton pump); chief cells secrete inactive pepsinogen.
HCl denatures proteins – making them accessible to the action of pepsin.
HCl converts pepsinogen to active pepsin and creates the optimal environment for pepsin (pH ~1.5–2); when pH rises (in the duodenum) pepsin is inactivated.
Pepsin breaks proteins down to peptides; complete digestion continues in the small intestine with pancreatic proteases (protein can be digested even without pepsin).
Other functions of HCl: an antimicrobial barrier, facilitating iron absorption; in hypo-/achlorhydria (atrophic gastritis, PPIs) bacterial overgrowth and impaired iron/B12 absorption.
Cholesterol is transported in the blood within lipoproteins: chylomicrons (dietary cholesterol), VLDL/IDL, LDL (the main one – ~2/3), HDL.
LDL delivers cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues (adrenals, gonads, etc.) via LDL receptors.
HDL returns cholesterol from the periphery to the liver (reverse transport), where it is converted into bile acids or excreted with bile.
Cholesterol in lipoproteins occurs in free and esterified (cholesterol esters) form; in the assay, total cholesterol is measured with an esterase.
Laboratory: LDL, HDL, non-HDL cholesterol and apoB – in which transport form it predominates determines the risk of atherosclerosis.
Physiological anticoagulants: antithrombin, the protein C/protein S system, TFPI – limit coagulation.

Anticoagulant drugs: vitamin K antagonists (warfarin – reduces synthesis of II, VII, IX, X), heparins (unfractionated and low-molecular-weight – via antithrombin), direct oral anticoagulants (Xa inhibitors – rivaroxaban, apixaban; thrombin inhibitor – dabigatran).
In vitro anticoagulants: EDTA (binds Ca – hematology), sodium citrate (coagulation, ESR), heparin (biochemistry, blood gases), oxalate/fluoride (glucose).

Laboratory monitoring: warfarin – INR (target usually 2–3); unfractionated heparin – aPTT or anti-Xa; LMWH – anti-Xa (in special cases); DOACs – no routine monitoring, specially calibrated tests if needed.
Monitoring complications: bleeding, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (platelet dynamics).

cutoffs.value: in most indications 2.0–3.0 (target 2.5); in a mechanical mitral valve 2.5–3.5

plan: Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis – 2 of 3 criteria: typical abdominal pain, serum lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN, imaging (CT/MRI/ultrasound) signs; lipase is more specific.
Determining etiology: liver tests (biliary cause), triglycerides (very high TG sharply raises the risk of pancreatitis), calcium, alcohol history, drugs.
Severity and complications: CBC, urea, creatinine, glucose, calcium, electrolytes, inflammatory markers; the enzyme level does not reflect severity.
Chronic pancreatitis: exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea – neutral fat in the coprogram) and endocrine insufficiency (diabetes); imaging is the main tool in diagnosis.
Know the causes of hyperamylasemia and hyperlipasemia other than pancreatitis (renal failure, bowel pathology, macroamylasemia).

cutoffs.value: 2 of 3: typical pain; lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN; imaging

kdl-o-288.q: Glycosaminoglycans, their importance in the body?
plan: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are linear negatively charged polysaccharides made of repeating disaccharide units.
Main groups: heparin/heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate/dermatan sulfate, keratan sulfate, hyaluronic acid (non-sulfated, not bound to protein).
Most attach to a protein core forming proteoglycans (syndecans, glypicans, perlecan, aggrecan) – a component of the extracellular matrix and basement membrane.
Functions: tissue hydration and mechanical strength (cartilage, synovial fluid), binding signaling molecules (growth factors, cytokines), heparin – anticoagulant effect via antithrombin.

Clinical-laboratory: mucopolysaccharidoses (lysosomal enzyme deficiency) – screening by urinary GAG excretion (DMB method), then fractionation and enzyme/genetic confirmation; a normal total GAG does not completely exclude MPS.

kdl-o-289.q: Diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and glucose tolerance?
plan: Diagnosis of diabetes: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 75 g OGTT at 2 hours ≥11.1, HbA1c ≥6.5%, random ≥11.1 with symptoms; the confirmation rule.
Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT): OGTT at 2 hours 7.8–11.0 mmol/L; impaired fasting glucose (IFG): 5.6–6.9 mmol/L (ADA) – both prediabetes, high risk of diabetes and CVD.
Performing the OGTT: 3 days of usual diet, fast ≥8 hours, 75 g glucose over 5 minutes, sample after 2 hours; acute illness and drugs distort the result.
GDM in pregnancy: 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks (5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 mmol/L).
Preanalytics and quality: preventing glycolysis, enzymatic methods, control materials.

pitfalls.wrong: a "sugar curve" with a 50 g load and the tolbutamide test
pitfalls.right: the diagnostic OGTT uses 75 g anhydrous glucose; criteria for diabetes/prediabetes are in the ADA tables (50 g is only step 1 of the two-step GDM screening)

cutoffs.value: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 (126 mg/dL; fasting ≥8 h); 75 g OGTT 2-hour ≥11.1 (200); HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol; NGSP/DCCT); random ≥11.1 with symptoms; without unequivocal hyperglycemia – two abnormal results
fasting ≥5.1; 1 h ≥10.0; 2 h ≥8.5 (92/180/153 mg/dL) – one is sufficient
